speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: First, dealing with Online Hostile Information Campaigns – we call them HICs – conducted by foreign parties.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I will refer to that as the HIC part.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And the second part dealing with foreign interference through local proxies.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The second part, I will refer to it as the Politically Significant Persons, or PSP part.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Members of Parliament will be familiar with the PDA.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, it is the PDA which has been brought into the PSP part of the Bill, with updating.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I will set out the reasons for this Bill, deal with some of the concerns that have been raised and deal with the proposed amendments by the Workers' Party.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: My colleagues, Ministers of State Desmond Tan and Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim, will take the Members through the detailed provisions of the Bill.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: First, on the PSP part of the Bill.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We can argue, disagree, but, ultimately, it is for us to decide.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: If I can quote what the former Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) director James Comey told the House Intelligence Committee in March 2017, "One of the things we radiate to the world is the importance of our wonderful, often messy, but free and fair democratic system and the elections that undergird it.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And so, when there is something by a foreign nation state to mess with that, to destroy that, to corrupt that, it is very, very serious and threatens what is America." The very idea of America.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We do not put it in the same grandiose terms but Singapore is important for us and we take the same approach.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The PSP part, as I said, is based on existing legislation, the PDA, ported over.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Over the years, subversion has become an even more serious issue.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Modern ease of communications, increased interactions and travel have made it inevitable that traditional spying and subversion increases in scope and intensity.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Just to give some examples from the last few years.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In 2017, an Australian former senator apparently received donations from an individual with connections to the People's Republic of China (PRC) government.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: He then advocated for China's position on the South China Sea.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: A former chairman of a European Union foreign friendship group was sponsored flights and hotel stays by a foreign government and, subsequently, voiced views that supported that government's policies on various issues.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In 2019, leaked documents revealed that the Russian government was allegedly planning to provide financial and public relations assistance to the election campaign of German politician Markus Frohnmaier, who was known to be very outspoken in favour of ending sanctions and recognising Russia's annexation of Crimea.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It was an attempt to influence senior decision-makers in Government.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Moving on to the HIC part of the Bill.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Spying and subversion in another country are age-old.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Using spies, agents, locals and useful idiots is all part of subversion.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: As technology developed, the subversion increased and adapted new technology: phone tapping, cameras, recording, microfilming and so on.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The Internet has created a powerful new medium for subversion.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Countries are actively developing attack and defence capabilities as an arm of warfare equal to and more potent than the land, air and naval forces.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It is often seen as the fourth arm of service.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The Gerasimov Doctrine, named after the Russian chief of staff, identifies issues of "protest potential" in another country, uses information operations to polarise that society and incite public disorder and keeps the target country in a constant state of turmoil.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Aggressors can more easily achieve their political and military outcomes.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: New communication tools facilitate non-kinetic forms of attack and make these harder to detect.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: For example, bots and digital ads can easily be bought to spread harmful information.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Foreign actors can blend their activities with other authentic online users, which give readers a false sense of reality.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We have an annex that sets out more details of the Gerasimov Doctrine, the new communications tools and HIC tactics used by foreign state actors.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And we distribute them together, so that it is easier.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If Members were to look at annex A, paragraphs 1, 2, 3 and 4, they refer to the Russians developing a military doctrine for the Internet age.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The doctrine took tactics developed by the Soviets, blended them with strategic military thinking about total war and laid out a theory of modern warfare.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: With this doctrine, the rules of war have changed.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Non-military means of achieving political and strategic goals without using the force of weapons, including utilising a range of actors and tools, hackers, the media, businessmen, information leaks and misinformation, are all part and parcel of new warfare.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Russians are said to have done this.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The following examples, which I will refer to, are based on reports.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Ukraine is said to have suffered extensive intervention.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Russia allegedly deployed this doctrine for many years.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: During the 2014 protests, sensitive fault lines were targeted to paint the Ukrainian government as a fascist, racist, xenophobic junta.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They claimed that Jews were being terrorised and beaten and asserted that local Jewish leaders were appealing to international bodies for help.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They tried to weaken the resolve of the armed forces and the population to build popular support for Crimea to join Russia.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Eventually, of course, we know Crimea was annexed.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And it resulted in the Czech government being unable to support the Ukrainians.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, the HICs managed to change Czech foreign policy.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Annex B sets out some of the details.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If Members were to see annex B, page 8 refers to Ukraine – look at item 3 of page 8.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Page 10, paragraph 6, the consequences as a result of the campaign.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Page 11, the interference in Czech Republic, paragraph 2 sets out how it has been successful, that 53% of the Czechs believed there is propaganda both for and against a foreign country in the Czech public space and therefore, they cannot trust anything.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That is another objective that people try and achieve: make you distrustful of everything.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The box sets out the reference to the FTA referendum.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: More recently, Russia was allegedly engaged in campaigns to erode trust in the EU’s COVID-19 strategy and to spread scepticism of Western-developed vaccines.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As I said earlier, Russia is repeatedly mentioned.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I am repeating what others have said and Singapore does not take a position on this.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Countries other than Russia are also said to have been using these strategies.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In May 2019, a disinformation network was traced to Iran.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This comprised fake persons who sought to influence US policymakers and also reporters and academics to carry their views.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Some of these were, eventually, published in legitimate publications.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Annex C sets out more details of reports that have identified Iran as a foreign state actor.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It involved the use of stolen accounts and at least 750 fake media outlets, which were amplified with the help of a legitimate foreign wire service.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, you can see the use of legitimate news organisations.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In February 2021, the social media analysis firm, Graphika, released a report on a propaganda coordinated network in favour of one country called “Spamouflage Dragon”, using a mixture of bots, fake accounts, stolen accounts and so on to push and amplify videos and media targeting issues, such as the safety of Western-made vaccines and discrediting the United States.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: A 2020 study by the Australian Strategic Policy Institute found that there has been a significant increase worldwide in foreign interference.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The international media regularly names Russia, China, Iran and North Korea.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I do not know whether these countries, in fact, did what they are said to have done.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But few doubt that they have the capabilities.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is notable that the US and other Western countries are not mentioned, generally, in these reports because they are Western media reports.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But anyone sensible will know that the United States, UK and Western countries have similar or, perhaps, in the case of the United States, even superior capabilities.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Really, there are no angels in this game.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Washington Post reported on 11 February 2020 that a Swiss encryption communications provider had sold devices to more than 120 countries.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That company was, actually secretly owned by CIA and German Intelligence.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They had rigged the devices to read the encrypted communications of all the countries, 120 odd countries, that had bought the system.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Reading secret, most confidential communications, of their own allies and, of course, adversaries.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The story was then released years after, after everything has been done and closed.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Washington Post wrote up the exposé based on a CIA internal history of the operation in 2004.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, CIA history was in 2004; the Washington Post released the story in 2020.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And they also based it on an internal oral history project by German intelligence in 2008.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But everything was kept under wraps, until simultaneously published by the Washington Post and a German broadcaster on 11 February 2020.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, it has all the hallmarks of a deliberate, planned leak.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Members might recall that at about the same time, a bit before that, but through that period, the US government was very seriously warning everyone about the dangers of relying on technology from China.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, basically, without embarrassment, this leak came out saying we did it, and now be careful about the Chinese.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But it has now got to be taken as a given that this sort of thing will be done regularly and everyone will face this.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It has become very easy and inexpensive to do.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It also gives examples of HICs targeting democratic processes, if you look at annex D.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And it is a cottage industry as well because there are reports of an active Macedonian disinformation industry.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Young Macedonians have Internet access, some basic training to create fake news websites.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Singapore – A few days ago, the French Military School Strategic Research Institute published a Report on Influence Operations.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Singapore was among the countries featured as case studies.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The report noted that there were several factors which made Singapore vulnerable: our size, hyper-connectivity, multi-ethnic and multi-religious society.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I am not so sanguine as the people who wrote this report.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Our racial and religious mix is easily exploitable by different countries and we see a steady build-up of different narratives which is being very cleverly done.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is not obvious propaganda but it conditions people to think in certain ways, particularly on foreign policy issues, often appealing to a larger racial identity beyond the Singaporean identity.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In my view, this is one of the most serious threats we face.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Our population, and I think most Members of Parliament, are not really aware of this.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Singapore has been subjected to attacks in recent times, both cyber attacks as well as cyber manipulation.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Cyber manipulation, I will give a couple of examples.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Online commentaries and videos were uploaded by social media accounts which had lain dormant for many years.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Many of these were in Mandarin and targeted our Chinese-speaking population.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: These contents were also widely circulated via chat apps and aimed to influence sentiments among Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In another case, during a period of bilateral tension with a country in 2018, we saw a large spike in online comments critical of Singapore and many came from anonymous accounts.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They sought to give an artificial impression of widespread objection to Singapore’s position.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I will say, so far, these have been relatively low level except for the strategic move, the attempts to condition our people's thinking, which are going on.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Before I deal with some of the substantive points of this Bill, let me also deal with the issue of timing.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Some have said there have been no discussions, why is this Bill being put through so quickly?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We have been talking about this very seriously for more than three years; extensively.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Select Committee heard extensive evidence in 2018 on this.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The evidence, the reports that I have been referring to so far in the various annexes, most of them come from the evidence given in 2018 to the Parliamentary Select Committee.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It sets out the discussions that have taken place and the summary of the testimonies given at the Select Committee.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Twenty different types of evidence – persons, organisations, including experts, gave evidence on the seriousness of the foreign threat.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I will touch on some of the evidence that was given at the Select Committee.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Dr Shashi Jayakumar said that it would be a mistake to assume that foreign HICs were not already happening.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Dr Gulizar Haciyakupoglu gave testimony behind closed doors, because of the sensitivity, and said there were indicators of information warfare being practised against Singapore.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Dr Liew Kai Khiun highlighted the barrage of comments by seemingly Myanmar-based user accounts on social media news portals of Singapore’s mainstream news networks.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: These were inflammatory, with Islamophobic tones, and incited backlash from Singaporean Muslims.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Dr Michael Raska highlighted that foreign states could engage in information operations that target our fault lines as a means of asymmetric warfare, given Singapore’s traditional military strength.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This is an important point that I will ask Members to take note of.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I once heard our then Defence Minister, Dr Tony Tan, describe our defence strategy in the following terms.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Singapore’s defence strategy is predicated on the superiority of our military in the region.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Our conventional military strength has got to be clearly superior; and it is clearly superior.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I will ask Members of Parliament to register this point, in particular, because our conventional military superiority, ironically, means we become an even bigger target online.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This topic was also quite extensively referenced in the Select Committee Report and discussed several times in Parliament.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And if you look at annex F(2), that sets out the discussions that had taken place in Parliament.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There were Parliamentary Questions and answers that emphasised our vulnerability.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I had made speeches in the Committee of Supply (COS) 2019 as well as COS this year, and made it clear that legislation was needed.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You can also refer to my speech at a major international conference in September 2019, pages 26 and 27.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I did, at that point, referenced Mr PJ Thum and Ms Han.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I will come back to this, but I made it clear that legislation is going to be needed.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That conference was held in Singapore on 25 September 2019, with 10 international and local speakers, experts.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Prof Allan Rock, a former Canadian Cabinet Minister at that conference, noted that tools of interference were well-known: dissemination of false information, hacking and leaking.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And he said governments have got to take this seriously and take counter measures that protect the electoral system and candidates, political parties and voters from information manipulation.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This topic of foreign interference has been extensively covered in the media as well.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If you look at the headlines on some of them, it says, "Stronger laws planned to combat foreign interference" and "Singapore to have legislation to combat increased risk of foreign interference." Annex F(4) shows – and I am giving a small sample of extensive studies internationally – Brookings Institute, RAND Institute and the Council for Foreign Relations have all commissioned and published studies.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, this topic has been extensively discussed and debated for over three years.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The other comments made: it is a very long Bill.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Members of Parliament are used to lengthy Bills, you understand the structure, you understand which are the key provisions, you understand the Explanatory Statement, you take a view and then you go through all the provisions again, look at the accompanying statements, infographics and get a better sense.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As I have said, more than half of this Bill is based on PDA, which Members will or should be familiar with.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The rest on HIC, and it is set out fairly comprehensively.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think the threat of foreign interference and its seriousness are not disputed by most people.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Most people also agree that something needs to be done.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, this is the context in which we are moving this Bill.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Before we go into the Bill, it is useful to first consider the current powers to deal with subversion.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Today, assume a person X is suspected of being a foreign agent or acting for a foreign agency against Singapore's interests.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Such a suspected foreign agent can be detained without trial under the Internal Security Act (ISA).

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Section 20 of the CPC allows the Police to ask anyone in Singapore, individuals as well as companies, for information.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Not just under SA, under any legislation if there are investigations.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Ask anyone in Singapore, individuals as well as companies for information and require them to produce any document or item for investigation.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, under current laws, suppose there is an online campaign and there is a basis to believe that this is foreign agency or entity-inspired and it is prejudicial to our national security, then investigations can be conducted under ISA.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Information, including the writer's identity, will have to be made available under CPC.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The writer and anyone else suspected of subversion can be detained.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Any challenge will be heard by the ISA Tribunal, not by the High Court.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And it is not public, unless the ISD decides to make it so.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This applies equally, whether the subversion is done online or in the physical world.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: When we talk about powers, the powers to detain, to investigate, I will refer to them as "Substantive Powers".

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The powers to enforce, like requiring the taking down of material, I will refer to them as "Executory Powers".

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There are several Executory Powers now available, including under the Broadcasting Act, which allow the Government to deal with objectionable content in the Internet space.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It allows for directions to be issued to broadcasting licensees and for content to be taken down or blocked.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Telecommunications Act gives powers to allow for directions to be issued to telecommunications licensees in the public interest, including the stopping, delaying and censoring of messages.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Public Order Act allows the Government to regulate physical assemblies and processions.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Commissioner of Police may deny permits for such events that are "directed towards a political end" and involve foreign entities or individuals.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, the issues of what directions might call the "protest potential" are regulated in the physical world.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Logically, similar rules should apply in the online space.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The current Political Donations Act requires those that are directly involved in our political processes, be they political parties, election candidates and their agents, to declare their political donations.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Act prohibits the receipt of foreign funding and has a cap on anonymous donations.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, I have taken the House through the current legal landscape.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: What does FICA add to the current powers?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Take the example I gave earlier, say, X is acting for a foreign agency.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He has an agenda to subvert our political process, subvert our sovereignty and he conducts an online campaign.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Today, as I have explained, action will be taken under the ISA.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And bear in mind that foreign agencies will often use legitimate-looking fronts.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Annex G sets out the examples of such legitimate-looking fronts.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Example of directions that can be issued include for a communicator to take down his content, for an Internet intermediary to take down the content and for an Internet intermediary to suspend or terminate the account.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Public interest is defined as including activities "directed towards a political end".

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This is taken from the Public Order Act to prohibit foreigners from organising or taking part in public assemblies directed towards such ends, and FICA applies this definition to the online space.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Executory Powers under FICA are more calibrated.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I referred earlier to the Broadcasting Act and directions can be issued.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Under the Telecommunications Act, directions can be issued to telecommunications licensees.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And, in both Acts, there are limits to judicial review.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, what in the HIC part of FICA goes further than the current laws?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Because it now explicitly includes global platforms which are often vectors for HICs.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, that updates the analogue powers for the Internet age.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: For example, in the analogue world, you have the Newspaper and Printing Presses Act (NPPA) and the Broadcasting Act.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They provide powers to proscribe foreign newspapers and broadcasting services.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In the analogue world, the Broadcasting Act provides the power to order a TV station to carry a message.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The digital equivalent under FICA is a must-carry direction, issued to communicator, social media services.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I will ask Members to refer to annex H which has two charts.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: First, Chart 1, and this is quite important.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If you look at Chart 1, the existing powers are in light green and the updated powers under FICA are in darker green.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, on the left, what is headed "Substantive Powers".

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If you look at the top right-hand side, it shows how existing laws cover foreign interference via traditional media – the Broadcasting Act and the NPPA.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And the bottom right, the light green boxes show how online, there are powers to intervene under the Broadcasting Act and the Telecommunications Act.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: What FICA does, in the dark green boxe, are targeted and more calibrated directions.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If you look at Chart 2, the existing PDA is in green; FICA in pink or red.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: On the left, the green box shows what PDA provides today.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: All the measures in that box apply to gazetted political associations.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: To use another example, suppose we discover that a Singapore company has been secretly hired by a foreign intelligence agency to put out memes and videos on social media and to spread the view that a particular ethnic group is persecuted.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And the aim, let us say, is to drive a wedge between ethnic groups in Singapore.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The company’s officers can be detained under the ISA.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This can be reviewed if their detention is under the ISA by the ISA Tribunal.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There is no judicial review except in relation to compliance with procedural requirements under the Act.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Where the content crosses the threshold of other laws like the Penal Code, of course, criminal investigations can be initiated.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The CPC comes in – that will allow any information about the company's activities or that of its staff to be obtained.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And there is a legal obligation for the information to be provided by anyone in Singapore when the Police ask for it, including Internet companies.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: These can stem the HIC without having to block the entire platform.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Social media platforms can also be asked to provide information to support an investigation into an HIC.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Today, if this data resides abroad, we cannot do so, under the CPC.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Government would also have the option of charging the company and its officers under FICA for clandestine foreign interference and prosecuting them in open Court.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, that deals with the HIC part of FICA.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There has been some degree of misrepresentation on FICA, that this Bill seeks to curtail normal interactions with foreigners.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Singapore depends for its success and vitality on being open, and a government that seeks to close down that will lead Singapore to ruin.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I actually want the House to see how our approach compares that with the US and Australia.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In the US, under the Foreign Agents Registration Act (FARA), it covers people and organisations that are under the control of a foreign government or organisations or persons outside of the United States.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Under the US' FARA, a "foreign principal" is defined very broadly, and any political activity that is designed to influence government decision-making on behalf of a foreign principal will require or trigger registration.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: For instance, take something that we take as normal.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: An American citizen meeting a US Congressman and advocating for his company's product.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If the company was a foreign company, an MNC, that will trigger registration.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That scenario will not meet the thresholds for designation of PSPs under FICA.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: On the HIC part and how it applies, I will deal with it later.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Foreign Influence Transparency Scheme (FITS) covers government-related entitles and individuals who have arrangements with foreign principals or undertake certain activities on behalf of foreign principals.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Under Australia's FITS, any activity by a former Commonwealth politician would trigger the threshold for registration.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, you could be an ex-Minister or an ex-Member of Parliament of any political party and, if you did this, it will trigger.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Singapore, under FICA, the PSP part only covers Defined and Designated PSPs.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Because we are not the US; we are not Australia; we are Singapore; we are an international hub.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Interactions with international counterparts, business people, siting of MNCs in Singapore – all of these are vital for us.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In this Bill, action can be taken in respect of HIC if the following conditions are satisfied.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Internet activity by or on behalf of a foreign principal and public interest in Singapore is affected.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: A PSP designation is possible if the activities are directed towards a political end and it is in the public interest that countermeasures should be applied.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, one of the key points for both areas is the phrase "Public Interest".

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The definition of "Public Interest" includes the requirement of "proportionality", which the Minister or Authority will have to consider in arriving at a decision.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Two academics, one of them foreign, collaborate on a paper on LGBT issues.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It will be difficult to say it is necessary or expedient to issue Directions under FICA and, really, try explaining that to a Supreme Court Judge, who will chair the Tribunal, that it is necessary or expedient.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The vast majority of collaborations, linkages will not meet the required conditions.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And they will also not meet the requirement of proportionality.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As an aside – and this has been raised by Member of Parliament Assoc Prof Jamus Lim – if a foreigner writes articles on controversial issues using his own name, or is clearly stated to be a foreigner, people can assess the value, credibility and weight, and it is generally unlikely to be necessary or expedient to issue directions.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If there is a basis to believe that he is doing so, for example, as part of a hostile campaign, or is acting for a foreign agency, with the intent of causing damage to Singapore, then directions could be given, subject to the test of proportionality.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And if he disagrees, he can appeal to the Tribunal.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Likewise – and, again, I think this arises from Assoc Prof Lim's proposed amendments – if the Economist or New York Times publishes the articles, it would not be possible to invoke FICA.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: However, if there is more to it, if a foreign newspaper is being used as part of a campaign targeting Singapore, that may be different.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But again, it comes back to proportionality, the nature of the actions, the likely effect, the likely intent, several other factors.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Newspapers – it does not mean, automatically, they are all kosher.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They have often been used as a front for such activities, which is why I put annex G in.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Legitimate newspapers, newswires have all been used as fronts.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, you cannot give a carte blanche exception but it is most unlikely that many of these would be a front unless we have very clear other evidence.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If some deception is involved in the campaign, if a foreigner hides his identity or masquerades as a local, we could, under FICA, give orders for them to be transparent, just disclose who you are, so that people can judge for themselves.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You have to go further and look at the facts.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As I said, is there a hostile campaign, is there damage to Singapore, is there a foreign agency involved, what is the extent of possible damage?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: These are non-exclusive factors nor must they all be present or any one of them present.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You really got to look at the facts, assess based on what you know and assess the proportionality as well.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But this is what the Government has been advised by AGC and that is one of the reasons for my view.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It has been suggested by some that case law means that the test of proportionality cannot be applied.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The advice I get from AGC is that it is different for this legislation because we are making clear the legislative intent for this specific Bill.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I have made similar points in respect of other legislation as well, as part of the Second Reading speech.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I will, in this context, invite Members to look at annex I.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Annex I is not in a hard copy.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Part of annex I is there but the part that I wanted to refer to, we did not have time to put that in.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: On the one side, if there is manipulation with a foreign agency involved, I think everyone will agree, it is quite clear.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: On the other side, there is foreign collaboration, bona fide work, everyone will agree that cannot be.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Or, for that matter, the range of public policy issues that are currently or which may in the future become subject to political debates, where there is legitimate reason for concerned Singaporeans to collaborate with international experts, researchers, NGOs; on the face of it, that would not be covered.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But if it changes along the lines of what I have said earlier, then there is a case for looking at it carefully.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, one has got to look at the facts, test materiality.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, some of these doomsday scenarios, that FICA is going to close off foreign collaborations, if that is correct, we, as a Government, must have suddenly gone mad.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Because in a country like Singapore, which depends so much on the flow of ideas and international collaboration, is that even thinkable?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Foreign agencies, and even non-agency, NGOs, others, will try and present a legitimate front.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, the language has got to be broad enough to cover that: that what is apparently normal but it is actually not normal.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And it is not only the classic foreign state agency subversion sort of thing.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It could be foreign associations, NGOs, even individuals, who want to change our laws, for example.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, you got to look carefully at what they are doing, what are all the factors taken in overall, using the proportionality test, what sort of issue are they focusing on, what is the possible impact, is there funding involved, but with the central guiding principle that Singaporeans should primarily decide on issues of importance to ourselves.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If you turn specifically to academics, questions have been raised about their collaborations with non-Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They collaborate, create, partner, pursue their research interests professionally.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: No HIC, it does not come within FICA.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, the Bill will not affect the vast amount of academic work that is being done.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We value the intellectual output, collaborations, exchange of ideas, the work our academics do.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And they need to link with the rest of the world; for work, bona fide and professional work, not affected; it is important for Singapore.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But in some situations, there are academics who go into a different realm around the world and they are dealt with, like we did with Huang Jing.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There is another thread to some of the points made, underlying all of these explanations and illustrations, that the Government's position and explanations are good but the powers can be abused, they can be used for a wrong purpose.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The worry is that the Government will abuse its power and shut down legitimate cooperation because it does not like it.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: One, the powers that are necessary to deal with the threat.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Second, the possibility of abuse of these powers.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So far, I have explained why the powers are necessary and why these powers are no greater – in fact, less so – than powers that already exist, and is more calibration for the Internet age.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, bearing that in mind, I will deal separately, later, with abuse of powers.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The fundamental principle is the intention – and we do not believe that legislation prevents bona fide exchange of ideas.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Any government can abuse this power and any power.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, we will come to that and what should be the checks and balances for that.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There have also been others, beyond these concerns, who have been actively trying to put out misinformation about the Bill.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Chief amongst them are Mr PJ Thum and Ms Kirsten Han.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Thum and Han, as I said in 2019, in the conference, take money from George Soros.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Some of you may recall, Soros' Open Society Foundations (OSF) has a history of getting involved in the domestic politics of sovereign countries.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They have set up an organisation called New Naratif, which receives significant foreign funding.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: New Naratif organised a series of "Democracy Classrooms" focusing on Malaysia and that was supported by the US Embassy in Kuala Lumpur.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We will say no to that in Singapore.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Anyone can organise, anyone can criticise the current state of democracy, but it cannot be funded by Soros or the US Embassy or any other Embassy.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The nature of activity and who the funding is from will have to be considered in this context.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I will say a bit more about Thum and Han before I go on to discuss their objections.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Thum wants our Independence Day to be 16 September, which is Malaysia Day.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: On several occasions, he has publicly said that Singapore should become part of Malaysia again and celebrate Independence on 16 September.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Thum and Han and some other activists met with Dr Mahathir on 30 August 2018.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They asked Dr Mahathir to bring democracy to Singapore.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I believe, I have not seen it, but I assume the Petition that the Progress Singapore Party (PSP) is presenting in Parliament is one that is inspired by Ms Han.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, I would like to know whether they agree with this statement that Singaporeans should push back and say foreigners should be able to influence domestic affairs in Singapore.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, Members can see why the two of them are very concerned that FICA will focus on foreign funding and have been mounting their own disinformation campaign.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Han has been posting on social media extensively – I am told, over a hundred tweets, posts and so on – organised a petition, sent around email templates for people to write to their Members of Parliament.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Thum has, meanwhile, written a commentary calling this Bill a "stealth coup" by me.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Basically, that I am personally going to take over Singapore and all my colleagues have to be very concerned.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I suppose a coup means that I take over from the Prime Minister.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Prime Minister needs to be very concerned too.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It requires a turn of mind, completely at odds with reality and living in fantasy, to think of a coup in Singapore.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Thum forgets that if there is this fear that I am going to mount a coup, then I or any Minister for Home Affairs has far more powers under other legislation: the Internal Security Act (ISA), the Criminal Law Temporary Provisions Act (CLTPA), the Maintenance of Racial Harmony Act (MRHA), including the powers of detention.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, Members can see there is no limit to the absurdities and fantasies that some will put out and an Oxford education, in itself, does not immunise one from spouting such nonsense.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But I can see that they are concerned.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If Singaporeans are excited about it, interested, they will contribute.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But because they will not contribute, I need foreign funding.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Terry Xu has joined Han in starting the petition, which some groups have signed up to.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I am not sure how many of these groups know what Thum and Han's objectives are.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We will look at the Petition that is being put up in Parliament by the PSP.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think Members can look at it in the context of who inspired them and how today's PSP is completely aligned, it appears, with what Thum and Han want to achieve.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There is no need to do it at another session.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Terry Xu, as many of us know, and as I said in my September 2019 speech at the conference, uses Malaysian and other foreign writers to write incendiary articles on Singapore without bylines and without identification.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The articles include a call for Singaporean civil servants to march on the streets like their Hong Kong counterparts.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, you read the articles and what would readers think?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: These are from local writers writing about Singapore in these terms.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But the articles are often by foreign writers who are paid to write these stories.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Xu and others can continue to do this even after FICA.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But a direction can be given to them to make it clear that the article is by a foreigner.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, it would be useful for Singaporeans to know whether the writer of the article is local or foreign.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The tribunal is headed by a Supreme Court judge.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Appeals are made to this tribunal and not the Court so as to protect sensitive information that may be relied on to make a decision.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: For example, we may determine foreign interference based on a tip-off or sensitive information shared by a foreign counterpart security agency.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The consequences of a leak would be very serious.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Most Singaporeans understand the need for this legislation.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They also realise the "Purposes" provision of the Bill is important – that is, clause 2 – and obviously so.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, with your permission, Mr Speaker, may I distribute a second folder which contains annexes J to L that I am going to refer to now.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If I may carry on while it is being distributed, Sir?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But we left it out because on the side of the PAP to comply with this, it is not going to be difficult because all except two of the CEC members are PSPs anyway.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, the obligations are more onerous for the other registered political parties because many, in some cases, none, of the CEC members are PSPs.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But as I said, we can agree to it if that is what Mr Gerald Giam wants.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Giam also wants DS and officers above the DS level to be included as PSPs.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They have to hold valid security clearance throughout their appointment.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They have to make annual declarations, including on investments, ownership, financial embarrassment, declarations on a variety of matters, going well beyond what PSPs have to do.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They have to declare all gifts and entertainment and they cannot work for other employers or engage in trade or business without explicit permission.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They can be directed to cease outside activities or divest investments if there is any conflict.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: A list of their key obligations is set out in annex K.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The rules for PSPs are not as tight.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Any DS or PS who accepts that will not remain in service for much after that, and they would be subject to severe disciplinary action if they contravene any of the rules.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Politicians and others who may be PSPs play by different rules, compared to senior civil servants.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If we impose on PSPs the rules that senior civil servants are under, I think it will be very difficult.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Ministers are also subject to strict rules, except that political donations are possible.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Giam and Mr Pritam Singh would be aware of these requirements, having both been public servants themselves in the past.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Gerald Giam also wants to include board members, chief executives (CEs) of Statutory Boards, CEs of Fifth Schedule companies.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: CEs of Statutory Boards, as public officers, are subject to the same rules as DSes and above, and the points I have already made apply equally to them.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As for Board Members, it would not be feasible to automatically define them as PSPs.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is preferable to use powers of designation instead.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You ask them to declare all donations received in home countries, migration benefits, all their foreign affiliations?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If we went out and asked not just these companies, but any other listed company, ask them if it will be feasible to impose these requirements on their foreign directors, they will tell you it is too onerous.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And if you take banks and you impose these obligations on the Schedule companies, but you do not impose these obligations on their competitors who might be in the same business, then you make it difficult for the Schedule companies to get good people.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is the same for Fifth Schedule companies.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, leave it to the companies to choose people of integrity and our security agencies need to be alert.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Not just about them, but other directors of major companies in Singapore.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, these additional proposals are impractical from a market point of view.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Now, I move to clause 8 as proposed by Mr Gerald Giam.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He wants to amend the definition of “directed towards a political end in Singapore”.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The context is HIC directions can be issued if there is online communications activity where material is published in Singapore, it is undertaken by or on behalf of a foreign principal, and it is in the public interest to issue a direction, such as to prevent foreign interference directed towards a political end.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And for a PSP to be designated, that person or entity’s activities must be directed wholly, or in part, towards a political end; and the Competent Authority must additionally assess that it is in the public interest for countermeasures to be applied.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, changing this definition will affect how we can act against foreign interference.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The meaning of “directed towards a political end” in the Bill has seven parts.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The first five, I think it is not the easiest to read.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think it is also in the Schedule that I have handed out, after annex M.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Pages 1 and 2 with what is proposed to be struck out.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, Mr Gerald Giam accepts all of this as legitimate, meaning legitimate for the purpose of defining what is "directed towards a political end", and that these are necessary.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But he wants to remove the last two paragraphs.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Again, it is in page 1, after annex M of the handout that has been given.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Gerald Giam wants to remove two sub-clauses, first of which reads: "(f) to seek to influence public opinion on a matter which, in Singapore, is a matter of public controversy; (g) to seek to influence any aspect, or to promote or oppose political views, or public conduct relating to activities that have become the subject of a political debate in Singapore." This is a little difficult to understand.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: To put it in the form of an example, in other words, his position is that we should not stop foreigners from interfering to shape public opinion on matters of public controversy; or to influence public views on a political debate, and this is so, regardless of whether deception is involved.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There are numerous scenarios that could fall under limbs (f) and (g) that may not be covered by one of the other limbs.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: For example, promoting some types of solidarity among members of one race or nationality, with the aim that this can eventually help them to have negative feelings towards other races, or promoting some types of religious piety, with the aim that, eventually, they may take different views on matters of political debate in Singapore.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If we believe that is being done, for example, at the direction of a foreign intelligence agency, with the ultimate purpose of creating divisions within Singapore, should we not be able to act?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If an intel agency in another country regularly pays someone in Singapore to write about these matters or support the policies of the Workers' Party, or the PAP, and gradually deepen divisions, enhance the "protest potential", as General Gerasimov might have said, that would not be covered.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: When we had the debates on CECA, were we not having a political discussion?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Under Mr Gerald Giam's proposal, any foreigner trying to influence such a debate in Parliament would be covered by FICA.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But any foreigner trying to influence the wider public on the same topics will not be covered when that discussion takes place outside, unless it can be shown that that was done in order to influence Government policy.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But Members would have seen from the examples that I have put in the annexes on foreign influence, influencing public opinion is a key aspect of foreign manipulation.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Realms and realms of examples, and look at the modus referred to in paragraphs 200 to 206 of the Select Committee report – I do not have it here but Members can check it out – where the Select Committee report says "...Russians built up internet presence in the US to influence..." and this has been done regularly in other countries.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As an example, the Guardian reported that YouTubers, bloggers and influencers in France and Germany were offered money by a PR agency with apparent connections to another state to spread falsehoods about COVID-19 vaccines.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: For example, "death rate among the vaccinated with Pfizer is almost three times higher than those vaccinated by AstraZeneca." They were asked to "act like you have the passion and interest in this topic" and avoid using the words "sponsored".

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They were instructed that "the material should be presented as your own independent view".

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But foreign-inspired subversion on (f) and (g) are okay.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But, if you look at (a) "to promote the interest of a political party" and if you look at (g) "to influence or seek to influence any aspect or to promote or post political views or public conduct relating to activities that have become the subject of a political debate in Singapore", you can do (a) in a different way under (g), that was what I meant earlier.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And you could argue I was doing (g) and not (a).

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, foreign-inspired subversion on (f) and (g) are not okay and this is exactly what the Gerasimov Doctrine seeks to exploit.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It seeks to identify issues of “protest potential”, use info operations to polarise society, incite public disorder along these issues and keep the target country in a constant state of turmoil.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Or, take another example, the Explanatory Statement to the Bill.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Say, there is a humanitarian crisis in Country Z, it becomes a hot political topic in Singapore.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Country Z then sets up Company Y, in Singapore in a bid to sway public opinion.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Company Y pretends to be a private local trading enterprise.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But it is really just a front for Country Z to influence Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: To do this, Company Y sets up multiple personas online.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It puts out many commentaries online, pretending to be "a freelance journalist" or "experts" in foreign politics, trying to manipulate Singaporeans to take a particular view of the matter.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You will also have situations, where (f) and (g) may overlap with the other limbs.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Limb (c): "influencing governmental decisions" is defined in section 9 to include influencing the public on a process in respect of the Government decision.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If this is a matter of public controversy, then it will overlap with (f).

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As I said earlier, insofar as (g) covers the influence of political views, this may overlap with matters under (a) which promote the interests of a political party; or (e) which aims to bring about changes in the law.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I have said this in Parliament, the MHA statement has stated it and the Explanatory Statement to the Bill, clause 120, explains this.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Sometimes, there may be a need to, but you cannot regularly be writing into legislation both what is covered and now also what else is not covered.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Because the above two situations are not the only ones not covered; many other issues are also not covered.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We clarified those in the press statement because people may have had these questions in mind.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But I am sure he will read them.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Clause 17 is now sought to be amended.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Assoc Prof Jamus Lim wants to remove the phrase "is likely to be".

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The phrase, "is likely to be", is sought to be struck out.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Taking one step back, I would say we are using a slide rule here to try and measure and assess people who are going to come with bazookas.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This will not work in the real world.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Even more so, when it comes to clandestine foreign interference.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Any decent intelligence service would know how to cover its tracks, conceal its linkages and disavow knowledge.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, under these proposed amendments, someone could take money from a neighbouring country, attack us, publish allegations against the Police or SAF or other institutions, cause unhappiness and unrest amongst our local ethnic communities.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This can be done covertly and not disclose that he is taking money.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Yet, if the proposals are accepted, the person cannot be charged in Court because the prosecution has to show that the person knew or had reason to believe that his actions would be prejudicial.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The person could claim, for example, that he did not realise that his post would be picked up by others and shared around.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He did not know it would be prejudicial and he had no reason to believe so.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This is so, even if we can prove that he took money from a foreign agency to put up the posts with the purpose of damaging Singapore.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is really like taking knives to a gunfight.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I make broadly the same points for the proposed amendments to clauses 18, 40 and 75.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Related to this, Assoc Prof Jamus Lim wishes to amend clause 17(2), to remove a caveat that "Y does not need to have in mind a particular foreign country or foreign principal in order to be considered to have committed an offence".

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This, similarly, narrows the mental state for the offence and means that the prosecutor must prove that the person is acting for a specific foreign principal and it is impractical for the reasons I had already given.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As matter of principle, knowledge that there is "a foreign principal" and "acting on his behalf" should suffice, even if the person does not know which foreign principal it is.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It does not matter whether you are acting for country X, Y or Z as long as you know you are acting for some country.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If I may move to clause 20, also the amendment proposed by Assoc Prof Jamus Lim.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The current wording is that the Minister may authorise directions where, in the opinion of the Minister, those conditions for HIC are satisfied.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Member wants to remove the phrase "or is suspected of being or having been undertaken".

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In practice, suspicion of links to a foreign principal would likely arise from a lead, an intelligence tip-off or other kinds of tip-off.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If there is such a suspicion, security agencies would probe further, gather data, try to corroborate the information, ascertain if the lead is reliable and they would require triangulation from different sources.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If you recall the earlier example of a state that apparently worked through a PR agency to get social media influencers to discredit vaccines, people eventually got suspicious due to a combination of indicators: suspicious instructions from the company to mask that they were being paid to push their messages; the company claimed to be based at an address in London, but turned out not to be registered there; company management from Moscow; online presence that disappeared once people started raising suspicions.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: None of these indicators, on their own, proves a conclusive link to a foreign principal.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Thresholds above do not relate to an offence.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If the person receiving the direction is aggrieved, he can appeal to the Tribunal.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Clause 21, Assoc Prof Lim wants to add in the phrase "rely on actionable intelligence”.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, we now call this agency to come and prove the actionable intelligence or we get documents and produce them?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And added on to that, Assoc Prof Lim and his colleagues want this to be in Court.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: How do you put any foreign intelligence agents on the stand?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In the real world, tip-offs come from intelligence agencies, from certain activities, associations, sometimes, it can be definitive, a "smoking gun", but in the vast majority of cases, it is less definite.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Links to a foreign state could be through ownership, funding, other associations.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It requires a piecing together of different data points.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I can tell Assoc Prof Lim from experience, if ever we said that we are going to refer what they said to us publicly, immediately they will disavow all knowledge and, thereafter, they will refuse to have contact with us.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, we need to be practical, not theoretical in this, with an understanding of how intelligence operations work.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This is in respect of appeals against our counter-HIC directions, any Part 3 direction or declaration as a Proscribed Online Location.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The question is, should the appeals relating to HIC Directions go to Court and should there be public hearings?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In a Court process, the Government may be required to set out its case in public, months in advance of the trial, documents have to be exchanged, witnesses must be available to give evidence, there will be cross examination and then the Judge decides.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Going back to my earlier example, assume we get an intel tip-off.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Foreign agency tipping us off about someone, which has happened even quite recently, and which then led to us exercising powers under the Internal Security Act.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Will we be able to get the foreign intel contact to come to Court?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As I said, they will just not hear us.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We would not even get a response and that will be the end of the cooperation.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If we think the tip-off has some merit, we do our own investigations and then issue Directions.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If the person is not happy, he appeals to the tribunal.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The tribunal members have the same immunity and protection as High Court judges.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They will consider any appeal brought under section 92.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Some countries – I am not saying we do – but some countries have human assets in other countries.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Let us say the information is obtained through such a human asset.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Depending on the country that the human asset is in, he may not live for very long after that.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And even if he lives, he would not be free.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: One could ask: can you have the case in-camera in Court?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You have to file the evidence in Court.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: A lot of parties get to see the file.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Some of this information, frequently, is often known only to two to three persons who need to know, even within the security agency.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Minister does not get to see it or know about it, unless it is necessary to brief the Minister.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There is a case pending, an application by 17 prisoners awaiting capital punishment.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They are making an application against the Attorney-General.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Various allegations have been made which the AGC considers to be completely scurrilous and without basis and being made to simply throw mud and stirred.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The lawyers will know the hearing is in chambers.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Details of the affidavits, everything cannot be published.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But details of the plaintiffs' affidavits appeared in a Malaysian news portal within a month of the application being filed and the allegations relate to, well, I was going to say there were very strong racial undertones.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Someone wanted to make these assertions in Court and then make sure they were published outside, which AGC considers absolutely scandalous.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The info should not have been made public.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The lawyer claims that his “instructing solicitor” is from Malaysia, for one of the plaintiffs.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, now you investigate and even if you take action for breach of the rules, the info is public.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In this case, the info is not security-sensitive.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But let us say you have highly secret intel information.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: First of all, does it make sense to hand it over to the very person who is a suspect or to his lawyers?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And how do you have a Court process?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As the House considers this, we must also look at this in the context of some other pieces of legislation we have in Singapore and what our approach to governance is.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We have legislation that provide for tribunals and limit the Courts power of judicial review to achieve a variety of different objectives.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And, so far, Singapore has been successful in this balancing exercise.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The starting point is always Rule of Law.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is fundamental, both for the well-functioning of society and to build a modern, economically vibrant society.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: At the same time, we recognise the normal judicial process is not best suited for specific matters; that is an exercise that requires careful consideration.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If you look at the Maintenance of Religious Harmony Act (MRHA), the Minister can issue Restraining Orders.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They are considered by the Presidential Council for Religious Harmony, which, in turn, makes its recommendations to the President to confirm, vary or cancel the order.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: During the Second Reading of MRHA, I explained that where religious issues are concerned, the trial process may not be the best way to deal with it.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It can deepen the fault lines, encourage martyrdom and inflame tensions even more.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Restraining Orders can impose a significant restraint on normal freedoms.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Restraining Order can restrain the person from addressing orally or in writing any congregation, require the person to stop communication activity, stop contributing to any religious publication, and restrain the person from holding office in an editorial board or committee of a religious publication.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Orders can be made against religious groups, to prohibit a group from receiving donations from specific or all foreign donors; require the entire governing body of the group to be Singapore Citizens; or require the group to suspend or remove specific foreigners from office.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, you can see the underlining philosophy there again – concern is foreign influence.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In some ways, these Orders are more serious than what can be made under FICA.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We talked to them, we explained how our powers can be exercised and they understood and they accepted.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Second, if we look at the Land Acquisition Act.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This is your house, you are living there.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You could be living there all your life.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Government can acquire under the Land Acquisition Act.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Any appeal against the Collector’s awards have to be heard by an Appeals Board.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Good reason: we learnt from the experience of other countries.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: A small country: we decided if we want to reshape and develop Singapore, the Government must have the power to acquire land quickly, develop it and not be tied up with the normal litigation process.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In fact, the inspiration and one of the places we looked at was India, and when it was taken, the then Prime Minister decided the constitutional protection for land which is in the Indian Constitution should be removed from our Constitution.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, a person's property can be acquired and it is the tribunal that decides on the value.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The approach to land acquisition, the policy on land acquisition, underpins our entire public housing policy, HDB policy.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It underpins our entire industrial land policy and many other aspects, just based on this unorthodox approach.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If you look at the Employment of Foreign Manpower Act, financial penalties can be imposed, other Orders can be made, appeal is to an Appeals Board, chaired by a person qualified to be a Judge of the Supreme Court.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And the Appeals Board determines its own procedures and its decision is final.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It allows us to pick up would-be terrorists, pre-emptively.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In 2017, we picked up a 22-year-old kindergarten teacher.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Do we wait until she does something, perhaps to the kindergarten children?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: She went through rehab and is now released.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In any other country, she could not have been picked up and there are countries where she could have been picked up, but I am referring to the countries that we normally refer to.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If she is not picked up and she goes overseas to one of the war zones, she might well not be alive today.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But now, she has the prospect of carrying on with her life and achieve her full potential.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: One wanted to carry out a knife attack in a mosque and the other wanted to carry out a knife attack in a synagogue.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: What would be the harm to our social fabric?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, the ISA has helped us avoid the bad incidents and hypocrisies we see elsewhere.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Recall the incident in New Zealand on 3 September 2021 where an extremist stabbed shoppers at the supermarket.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You wake up in the morning, you go the supermarket.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The attacker was known to the security agencies.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He was under surveillance since 2016 because of his support for the Islamic State ideology.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But under New Zealand's laws, he could not be picked up.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There have been other similar cases in the UK and in France.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This included Said and Cherif Kouachi, who were career criminals who killed 12 people in January 2015 in the Charlie Hebdo office in Paris.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If you turn to the US, President Obama took office in 2008.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He campaigned on the promise to close down Guantanamo Bay or Gitmo.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He did not do so during the eight years of his Presidency.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: One reason: closing Gitmo could mean that several of these hardcore detainees could be moved to the United States and many Americans were opposed to that idea.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We may be wrong about the exact number but I think it is a very low number.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The theory, and the Americans have been preaching this to us on the ISA, there must be due process, you must not have detention without trial and the State Department will tell us and publish a list.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But when it comes to the US, there is due process in the US.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They have all these hardened criminals, terrorists picked up from around the world.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, they put them in Gitmo, which is in Cuba, and then they say, well, since this is outside of the US, the US due process laws do not apply, and therefore, we can detain them without trial and they do not get the benefit of US due process.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: On top of that, basically, Members know about the atrocities that were committed on the prisoners.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Which is why I said we look at the world as it is and we avoid hypocrisies.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We deal with it in a practical way.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And, after a while, many of them are released, when they are rehabilitated.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We do not allow ideology to stand in the way of doing right for society when that ideology does not make sense.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The ideology must be to do what is right for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If you go to the CLTPA, it also provides for detention without trial.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And I am well aware that the Workers' Party has a different view both on the ISA and the CLTPA, though I do not know what will be the substance of the provisions they will replace the ISA with.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But anyway, and, therefore, it may be difficult for them to philosophically agree with this.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But I am setting out the approach the Government has taken.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is a practical approach by then Prime Minister, Mr Lee Kuan Yew.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
