text: Evidence will often not be available; people too frightened to give evidence.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In fact, we inherited this from the British and then changed it.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: People will be too frightened to give evidence.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In the longer term, more harm to society, by leaving gangsters out in society.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, better to give to the Executive these powers to deal with some types of pernicious criminals.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It has helped to keep our society safe.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If we had stuck to the approach of looking at everything on the basis only of the rights of the persons accused in the way that, say, the US or UK looks at it, and without balancing the rights of the society, we will not have the safe and crime-free society we have today.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And the rights of the accused or detainees, both under the ISA and CLTPA, are protected.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, the question for this House is: how do we view the risks of foreign interference?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: How do we place the risks in the context of the other legislation that I have referred to?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Would it be possible to deal with these issues of foreign interference through a normal Court process?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Often, we do not even name the countries involved.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Can you imagine naming one of our neighbours in Court?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: When we asked Huang Jing to leave, we did not say who he was acting for.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The foreign policy and national security implications are too serious.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The US can name any country that it wishes.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But we are a price taker in this business of international relations.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Government might ask some to disassociate themselves from foreigners if there is an increased threat of foreign interference, but we should compare that against Land Acquisition, against the Orders that can be made under other legislation that I have referred to.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: On a separate point, generally, in legislation, the usual rules for judicial review limit review of the Courts to reasonableness, legality and propriety.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That has been so in POFMA as well as in other legislation.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Members can see, therefore, various pieces of legislation have conferred the Government with generally-worded discretion.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Philosophically, the Government has seen that as part of good governance to ensure our laws are effective so that the Government can act when it needs to.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You need checks and balances, but the checks must be suited to the task and balanced against the risks.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There are risks with giving any government any power, whether or not it is appealable to a Court.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There are also risks in not giving power.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The real issue is what powers should you give.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And what are the risks in not giving the powers?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The risk here, which underlies some of the concerns that have been raised and some of the illustrations because the Government says these illustrations do not come within FICA and then you will say, what if the Government abuses its power.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And what if the Government interferes with perfectly normal collaboration with a foreigner? it will be an abuse of power.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But what if the Government abuses its power?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, you have to weigh the risks of a rogue Government doing that versus a rogue foreign interference.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The risk of a rogue government abusing its power.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: First of all, what is the power, compared with the powers in other legislation?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: All the decisions published, people can see and assess themselves.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And, ultimately, people have the final say in a highly literate population like Singapore.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: A final say of both public opinion and public opinion expressed through elections.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: People in Singapore would not stand for a rogue government.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I, like some of those who could have made comments, and I am sure everyone here, wish that there is a world where the Government has the power to act and, at the same time, there is a complete check against abuse.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If we can find that formula, we will gladly take that because that is ideal.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Then, we have to, first of all, admit that there are trade-offs whichever route you take.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If you go to Court, there are trade-offs; if you have a tribunal, there are trade-offs.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And I agree that, with a rogue government, there is a risk of abuse, as I have said, not just of this power but several other powers; and not just the Executive powers but also even powers which can be looked at or appealed to the Courts.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Just as there is a risk of an order made under MRHA against preachers on religious groups that we do not agree with, or detentions under the CLTPA, or land acquisition.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In many countries, the population would not support this kind of land acquisition powers because it only leads to some very wealthy Ministers or not much public benefit.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But in Singapore, the population trusted the Government and Singapore has developed in a way which could not even have been dreamt about in 1965.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Along the way, we have had to make these choices in a number of areas, as I have shown to Members.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And over time, people have seen how our approach proved to be good for the majority of people.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And over the same period, Singapore's reputation for Rule of Law, its judicial system, legal system, institutions, both in and outside of the legal field, were all enhanced and they were built up.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, I say to this House: this law gives the Government a set of tools that can help.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is not a complete defence against foreign interference but they can help.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Ms He Ting Rualso proposes to remove the immunity provision in clause 119.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The reason for this suggestion is not clear.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: I support the principles of the Bill as outlined by the Minister and would like to advocate the importance of having such a law to deal with hostile information campaigns (HICs).

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: I will discuss Parts 2 and 3 provisions pertaining to HICs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Foreign actors have leveraged digital technologies to carry out HICs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: We have observed that these tend to be deliberate and coordinated attempts to use information to manipulate public opinion and harm a country’s interest.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: In addition, they are often clandestine and seek to mislead the public under false pretences.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: This Bill does so by providing a set of offences and empowering the Government to issue directions to counter HICs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: The new offences in Part 2 of the Bill are aimed at acts of foreign interference by covert means using electronic communications.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Clause 10 defines electronic communications activity as the communication or distribution of any information or material through means of SMS, MMS, a social media service, a relevant electronic service or an Internet access service.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: He undertakes electronic communications activity that results in or involves publishing in Singapore any information or material.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: The offence clearly deals with persons covertly and knowingly acting against the public interest on behalf of a foreigner.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: The mere fact that communications were private, for example, an online video call between two people, would not make them covert.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: For an offence to be made out, there must be an element of secrecy or a lack of transparency surrounding the person’s conduct.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: For example, a Singaporean is paid by a foreign intelligence agency to publish a number of articles criticising Singapore’s foreign policy towards that country.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: He does so but presents it in his personal capacity as a citizen without disclosing his links to the foreign agency.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Clause 17 does not cover Singaporeans acting on their own accord or foreigners making open and attributable comments.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: For example, an article by a foreigner who openly declares his identity, published in a foreign publication, such as the Economist or the Wall Street Journal, would not be an offence under FICA.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: The same applies to foreign political observers or political commentators publishing on a social media platform or a blog, if they make no attempt to mislead Singaporeans as to who they are.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: A Singaporean shares an online video propagated as part of a foreign HIC on his social media account.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: However, he does so unwittingly and was not aware that the content is part of a HIC nor did he receive any support or instruction from a foreign principal.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: The Singaporean also has not committed an offence.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: This offence would apply if a few conditions are fulfilled.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: First, a person undertakes electronic communications activity on behalf of a foreign principal.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Second, the person does so to influence another person to undertake activity or engage in conduct in Singapore that is prejudicial to Singapore’s public interest.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Third, in doing so, the person does not disclose his links to the foreign principal.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: This is an aggravated offence because it involves a greater degree of duplicity in targeting another person to act against Singapore’s public interest.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Such acts are calculated and more likely even harder to detect, and, consequently, have the potential to cause greater harm.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: The offence thus carries higher penalties commensurate with the greater harm.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Clause 19 introduces an offence of preparing or planning for the above offences and clause 115 clarifies that these offences will have extra-territorial application.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: These offences will be investigated by the Police.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: For offences involving SAF installations, assets and personnel, Police will work with SAF.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: The Bill contains customised powers for the Government to act against HIC content online.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Part 3 of the Bill empowers different directions: (a) to obtain information about HICs before they happen; (b) to detect and prevent HICs taking place; and (c) should they occur here, to contain the HIC.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: As the Minister has stressed, the basic architecture of our counter-HIC measures is that directions can be issued only when the Minister assesses that all of the following three conditions in clause 20 are met: (a) online communications activity is undertaken, or suspected to be undertaken, by or on behalf of a foreign principal; (b) the online communications activity results in content that is published in Singapore; and (c) it is in the public interest to issue that direction.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Clause 7 sets out non-exhaustive illustrations of what would cross the public interest threshold.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: For example, in the interest of the security of Singapore, to protect public health or public finances, to prevent incitement of feelings of enmity among different groups in Singapore, or to prevent foreign interference directed towards a political end, which would include interfering in our domestic politics.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: They are not meant to constrain the interpretation of public interest found in other laws, which should be read in their respective contexts.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: The intent is for these parties to provide information or data that is useful in investigating if there is an ongoing HIC and the source of the HIC content, in particular, whether it originates from a foreign source.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: This information includes basic subscriber information that is provided when accounts are set up, such as IP addresses, or aggregated geolocation data.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: It is not MHA's intent to demand assistance that is not reasonably practicable or information beyond what is necessary.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Nor will we demand information for purposes beyond investigating a suspected HIC.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Technical Assistance Directions are subject to a non-disclosure requirement to prevent tipping off a suspect of an ongoing investigation and prevent any unauthorised external party from undermining investigations.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Recipients can specify that they received the direction but cannot disclose the substance of the direction.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Breaches of any non-disclosure requirement constitutes an offence under clause 46.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Other Part 3 directions are designed to provide targeted powers for the Government to contain the propagation of HICs and mitigate the harms caused.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: The intent of such directions is to warn the public that the content is part of a HIC.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: There are four classes of directions for different recipients.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: A Class 1 Must Carry Direction can be issued to the communicator of the HIC content to publish a mandatory message.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: A Class 2 direction can be issued to relevant electronic services and social media services to publish a mandatory message with respect to specified information or material, or identical copies of it.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: For example, if a foreign state-run media outlet posts videos on social media and these videos are part of a HIC campaign, then the Government may issue a Class 2 direction to the social media platform, to require the platform to publish a notification tagged to the video to notify the public that this video is part of a HIC campaign.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: A Class 3 direction requires providers of social media services, relevant electronic services, telecommunications services, newspapers or licensed broadcasting services to publish a general notice to end users in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: It is not necessary for HIC content to have been communicated on the service in order for a direction to be issued.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: This class of directions is intended to alert Singaporeans that a HIC is ongoing.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: A Class 4 direction requires proprietors of Proscribed Online Locations to put up a notice about its proscribed status so that any visitors to the online location are aware that it is a HIC vector.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: There are two directions to remove specific HIC content from being accessible by end users in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Clause 34 introduces the Account Restriction Direction, which can be issued to relevant electronic services and social media services and is intended to prevent specific accounts from communicating with Singapore end users.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Clause 35 introduces the Service Restriction Direction, which can be issued to relevant electronic services, social media services and Internet access service providers to stem the virality of HICs and restrict Internet service functionality respectively.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Each Service Restriction Direction will specify the actions required of the recipient.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: For example, restricting a certain function of their service, preventing harmful content from being actively recommended to end users in Singapore, or slowing down or stopping Internet access.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: MHA will work with the industry on how such directions are to be operationalised and identify reasonable and practicable interventions, given the potential significant impact on the services.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: This can be issued only if at least one direction that is not a Technical Assistance Direction or another App Removal Direction had been issued with respect to that app.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Once proscribed, it is an offence to operate this POL, provide support to it or have advertising dealings with it.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Clauses 39 to 41 give effect to these restrictions.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: To ensure that the public is aware of its POL status, a Class 4 Must Carry Direction can be issued to require the owner to put up a notice about its proscribed status.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: We also need to be able to take action against non-compliance of directions.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: This can be issued to any Singaporean, resident in Singapore or locally registered entity that has supported the HIC and it will require them to return to the foreign source any funding or material support provided.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Non-compliance with these directions will be an offence under clause 45.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: If charged, parties may raise the defence that it was not reasonably practicable to do more than what was done or that there were no better practicable means of complying, for example, due to technical impossibility.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: The Minister has provided a detailed account and these cases are well-publicised.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: In addition, threat actors are improving their tactics all the time.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Therefore, we cannot wait for harms to occur before taking action because severe damage may already be done.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Should there be credible information about a potential HIC threat, the Government must be able to act to prevent it.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Our authorisation thresholds must, therefore, be calibrated to allow certain directions to be issued even before any harmful communications have commenced.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Clause 21, therefore, provides for two specific directions – Technical Assistance Direction and Account Restriction Direction – to be authorised before harmful communications activity has taken place.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Take the following scenario, which is illustrative but not exhaustive.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: It is not hypothetical because we have seen this modus operandi in HICs conducted against other countries.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: On a social media service, a set of accounts amasses followers by first posting popular content on lifestyle matters, such as cute animal videos or funny memes.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: There are multiple accounts and the accounts act in coordination.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: For example, account A actively tries to increase account B's visibility by sharing its content and so on.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: At the opportune moment, such as election season or during a period of tension with another country, these accounts start to pivot to social and political commentaries, hoping to sway how Singaporeans vote or react to a foreign policy issue.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Assuming this happens here and our monitoring agencies detect these accounts gaining traction.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: We can issue a Technical Assistance Direction to investigate the origin of such accounts.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: If we have sufficient reason to believe that these are foreign accounts and are planning to undertake an HIC against Singapore, we can issue Account Restriction Directions to prevent them from propagating their HIC content to end-users in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: In assessing whether a HIC is afoot, the primary determinant is the behaviour of the actor involved and the entities behind the content.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: It is clear, therefore, that Singaporeans who are simply expressing their own views or engaging in the political process on their own accord are not covered and neither will the vast majority of communications involving foreigners, be it journalism or academia or online advocacy.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: MHA has also consulted the major stakeholders on the operationalisation of these directions and will continue doing so, to take into account the industry's constraints, from the technical to the legal, as we work together to counter HIC threats on their platforms.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: I have set out the clear conditions that must be met before directions can be issued and the defences inscribed in the Bill.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: I will now set out the avenues for appeal.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: This Bill will provide the right of appeal to recipients of counter-HIC directions and proprietors of POLs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Appeals will be heard by a reviewing tribunal.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Clause 23 clarifies that recipients of counter-HIC directions and proprietors of POLs must first apply to the Minister to reconsider the Part 3 direction.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Should the Minister reject the application, the appealing party may then appeal to a reviewing tribunal, which is constituted under Part 8 of the Bill.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Decisions would be determined by the tribunal and are final.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: The Minister has explained the reasoning behind the reviewing tribunal.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: The difficulty that confronts us is the suitability of making the Courts serve as an oversight body for decisions taken under the Bill, which involve issues of national security, defence and foreign policy and information from intelligence sources, not necessarily only of our agencies.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: Our own Courts have said that they have limits in these areas.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: The tribunal, in fact, goes further than judicial review in some ways in that it is able to assess the initial decision on its merits, whereas the Court in judicial review proceedings focuses only upon the legality of the administrative decision.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: The Minister and I have outlined the threat of HICs, and Minister of State Desmond Tan will speak on the threat of PSPs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: It is clear that we need to take steps to counter it.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: We have been discussing these issues in Singapore over the last three years.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: There was a major conference in 2019, and discussions at our Committee of Supply (COS) debates.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: I have brought the House through these levers and provided some illustrations of how we intend to use them in a judicious and proportionate manner.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: In addition, this Bill ports over the requirements for PSPs from the Political Donations Act and introduces a more robust framework of designations and executory powers to deal with interference through PSPs, which Minister of State Desmond Tan will elaborate on.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: There are also various safeguards, such as clear criteria for offences, clear authorisation thresholds for directions and avenues for appeal.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim)
text: This Bill ensures that we can continue to take this stance and that Singaporeans can continue to make our own choices on how we should govern our country and live our lives.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Despite the proliferation of foreign interference attempts in the digital space, we still see many instances of interference by hostile foreign actors in the physical world through compromising local proxies.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: One example that was raised in the Minister's earlier speech took place in Australia, where a former senator received donations from an individual with connections to a foreign government.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: The former senator then advocated for the foreign country's position on the South China Sea despite it being contradictory to his party's position.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Another example took place in 2015, where Reuters reported that a state-linked company was covertly backing at least 33 radio stations in countries across the Asia Pacific region to form a global network broadcasting news that placed that particular state in a positive light.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: In the 1980s, the First Secretary of the United States Embassy in Singapore, Hank Hendrickson, cultivated a group of Singaporean lawyers to join Opposition politics and contest the 1988 General Election.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: The lawyers were offered funding, and one of them was even offered refuge in the US should he subsequently run into difficulties with the Singapore Government.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: However, PDA does not cover other individuals who are directly involved in our political processes, such as our Members of Parliament.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Also, PDA only covers monetary donations and does not cover other possible vectors of interference, such as through formal affiliation with a foreign organisation and provision of volunteer services by foreigners.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: First, let me go through the individuals and entities that this Bill aims to cover.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: The Bill also empowers the Competent Authority, a civil servant in MHA appointed by the Minister for Home Affairs, to designate other individuals and entities as PSPs, if certain conditions are met.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Clause 14, read with clauses 47 and 48, empowers the Competent Authority to designate entities and individuals respectively as PSPs if: (a) they are members of foreign political or legislative bodies, or their activities are directed, in part, towards a political end; and (b) the Competent Authority assesses that it is in the public interest that countermeasures be applied.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: It is important that we have levers to designate and impose countermeasures on individuals and entities who may be at risk of foreign interference and have exhibited behaviour that points to such risk.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: It also has the effect of promoting transparency and deterring would-be foreign actors with malicious intent from trying to influence Singapore’s politics through these local proxies.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: I will now talk about the different countermeasures that will be imposed on both defined and designated PSPs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: All PSPs will have to comply with a baseline set of obligations and countermeasures.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: We will apply the most stringent countermeasures on defined PSPs as they are directly involved in Singapore’s political processes.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: For designated PSPs, in the first instance of designation, their obligations only pertain to disclosure.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: However, clause 88 provides for countermeasures to be stepped-up, if conditions are met, potentially, to the same level as those for defined PSPs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: The countermeasures on PSPs are detailed in Chart 2 that was earlier distributed.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Clauses 62 to 65 require all PSPs, both defined and designated, to disclose donations to the Competent Authority.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Smaller donations from the same donor that, when aggregated during the same reporting period, amounts to $10,000 or more, also have to be disclosed.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Donations that need to be disclosed do not only cover those that are made in cash.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Clause 51 articulates the types of donations that the Bill will cover, including donations made in kind, or the provision of goods and services for a fee below the fair market value.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: That said, the Bill does not cover all kinds of donations, only donations that are directed, wholly or in part, towards a political end.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: The disclosure requirements do not cover personal gifts, for example, as the intent of the Bill is to safeguard against foreign interference in our domestic politics.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Certain other donations or gifts may be handled by other laws.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Defined PSPs are subject to more stringent donation controls.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Designated PSPs are not subject to these restrictions at the onset of designation.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Members will see from the annex that most of these requirements already exist in PDA today.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Influence can also come about through volunteers, apart from donations.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: The Bill is not concerned with all types of voluntary services, and only prohibits defined PSPs from accepting voluntary services that relate specifically to the duties and responsibilities of the PSPs in question.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: For instance, a Member of Parliament cannot allow foreigners to volunteer at Meet-the-People Sessions or any other programmes that are organised by the political parties.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: The Bill does not cover all kinds of affiliations.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: For example, personal friendships or co-workers are not covered by the Bill.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: The Bill does not restrict association with a foreigner and is not intended to reduce foreign partnerships or businesses.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: An example of what the Bill is concerned with is foreign affiliations where the foreign principals are in a position of control over the PSP and the PSP is taking direct instructions from the foreign principal.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: For example, being an employee of a foreign company would be one such arrangement that will need to be disclosed if you are a PSP.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: These reportable arrangements are defined in clause 78.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: If there is an increased risk of foreign interference, clause 84, read with clause 88, empowers the Competent Authority to require the PSP to terminate its foreign affiliations.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Examples of migration benefits will include a foreign passport, travel identification documents, an entitlement or privilege or status to work or reside in the foreign country, or an honorary citizenship.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: The purpose of this declaration is simply for transparency.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: There would be no stepped-up countermeasures to prohibit the acceptance of migration benefits.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: The Societies Act already disallows foreigners from being members of political parties.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Designated Politically Significant Entities (PSEs), in the first instance, are not prohibited from appointing foreigners to leadership positions or accepting foreign memberships.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: If there is an increased risk of foreign interference, clause 83, read with clause 88, empowers the Competent Authority to prohibit the PSE from accepting foreigners as members or appointing them as responsible officers within the entity.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: There may be instances where the Government will need to act even before we designate an individual or organisation as PSPs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: The Bill provides for countermeasures in two of such cases.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: First, foreign states may attempt to cultivate Singapore citizens to influence our domestic politics through their involvement in foreign political and legislative bodies.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Examples of these would be a foreign political party or political advisory body.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: MHA recognises that there may be innocuous instances where Singaporeans living abroad join foreign political bodies, such as Singaporean students joining foreign political parties while they are studying abroad, out of their own personal interests.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: However, this can, nonetheless, still pose a threat, as such Singaporeans may be cultivated, approached or influenced, even unknowingly, and, subsequently, made use of to affect our local politics.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: As such, it is necessary to require them to disclose their involvement in such bodies for transparency purposes.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Second, based on our experience of seeing foreign writers masquerading as local writers in penning articles relating to Singaporean political matters, we felt that it was important for Singaporeans to be aware of the origin of such articles and perspectives.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: To be clear, this will only apply to entities that are issued with the transparency directives.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: There is no fixed expiry date for the designation and countermeasures imposed on PSPs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: This approach is the same as that under PDA.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: But the process is transparent when we designate PSPs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Clause 49 of the Bill states that when we designate a politically significant person or entity, the Competent Authority must, without delay, give the individual or entity notice of the designation.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Moreover, if a PSP wishes to challenge its designation for the stepped-up countermeasures imposed on it, it may submit an application for the Competent Authority’s reconsideration or an appeal to the Minister for Home Affairs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Clause 102 allows the Minister to consult an advisory body before arriving at a determination on the merits of the appeal.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Academic research, business partnerships, creative collaborations, cultural exchanges – such interactions will not be designated.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: An employee working for an American tech firm that is openly advocating for American technology as part of their business will not be designated as there is no public interest in doing so.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: It is also not within the Bill’s intent to prevent local NGOs from freely working with foreign businesses on their Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) projects.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: The Bill also does not seek to stop businesses and organisations from building overseas partnerships or soliciting for overseas business, networking with foreigners, going to conferences or seminars, or engaging in cultural exchanges.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: These types of activities and dealings will not be constrained in any way by the proposed Bill.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: It will be business as usual as we know it for the vast majority of Singaporeans and residents in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Allow me to give an example of how the PSP measures will apply.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Let us take a case of a Singapore-registered entity which has been actively commenting on Singapore’s politics in advocating a potentially divisive social issue.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: To ensure transparency of its activities, the PSE will have to submit donation and foreign affiliation disclosures in the very first instance.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: This is, in fact, less stringent than PDA of today.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Under PDA, if an entity is designated as a political association, the controls are the same as those imposed on a political party.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: This includes not being allowed to receive foreign funding and a cap on anonymous donations.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: If the Competent Authority assesses that there is a heightened threat of foreign interference, the PSE may be issued with stepped-up countermeasures.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: If the PSE is affiliated with a foreign group which is suspected to be taking instructions from a foreign state, the Competent Authority may direct the PSE to end its affiliation with the foreign group.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: If the PSE has been publishing articles related to Singapore politics, it may also be issued with a transparency directive to disclose the nationalities of contributors of the articles.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Where it is new, it is meant to address the gaps.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mr Speaker, Sun Tzu's Art of War has a saying, "it is better to win the heart of people than to capture the city." This saying encapsulates why we need a Foreign Interference (Countermeasures) Bill.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Historical thinkers have warned us against overlooking psychological defence in warfare.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: As the saying goes, "the supreme art of war is to subdue the enemy without fighting." In today's context, the best strategy in warfare is to win the war without the firing of a single bullet.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: One such example is Ukraine, which is said to have suffered extensive intervention during the 2014 Crimean status referendum, where sensitive societal fault lines were targeted by a hostile information campaign orchestrated by the Russians to build popular support for Crimea to join Russia.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: This, eventually, led to the annexation of Crimea.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: If we were to allow foreign interference in our domestic politics, Singapore may similarly be subject to such divisive forces.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: This may result in us losing our autonomy and becoming a vassal state of a foreign power, or a puppet of foreign forces.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: The PAP Government has always taken a firm stand that our domestic politics are for Singaporeans to decide and that we should not allow foreign actors to interfere in them.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Being a small open economy and a multicultural society, Singapore is highly susceptible to foreign interference.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: To ensure that we keep step with the evolving tactics of hostile actors, it is timely for us to update our laws to address the threat of foreign interference.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Singaporeans will still be free to express their views.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: In fact, the Government's wish is that, with FICA, Singaporeans will be able to freely voice their opinions on Singaporean matters and not the perspective of others.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: I want to remind the public that the foreign interference threat is an invisible one, and the threat that the passage of FICA aims to mitigate is one that is hard to guard against because it insidiously targets our world view.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: And once these perspectives are allowed to fundamentally alter our belief systems, it will be too late for us to take remedial action.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: The Bill provides Singapore with the basic levers to defend ourselves, but we hope FICA will raise Singaporeans' awareness about the threat of foreign interference, so that we will not, unwittingly, become vehicles for hostile foreign actors to undermine our national interest.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: My wish is for Singaporeans to commit to working together to ensure that our affairs will be for Singaporeans only to decide.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Before I begin, I do not recall coming across a Bill that is understood in such diametrically opposing ways by, on the one hand, some members of the public, including at least two Senior Counsels, many civil society activists, former Nominated Members of Parliament and journalists, and by the Executive on the other.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This anomaly in our public discourse regarding this Bill is significant and it bears deep reflection on how our laws are made and communicated to the public before they are passed in this House.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: One, is a summary of the amendments filed by the Workers' Party's Members of Parliament; two, is on how exceptional executive power requires robust judicial oversight to ensure accountability; three, is on how the Government should have sought public feedback on this Bill; and four, is on how the Government has been largely muted as to the non-legislative measures to combat foreign interference and why this needs to be corrected urgently.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Government must be accountable when it implements this law and uses executive power against individuals and entities.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: There should be robust oversight of executive action by the Supreme Court.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This must be the default position for parliamentary democracy that recognises the centrality of the separation of powers under our Constitution.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The law must more precisely scope the extent of executive powers to minimise the prospect of abuse of power.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: While the Bill targets foreign interference, Singaporeans are the central focus and it is important that their constitutional rights are respected.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: There has to be greater clarity and transparency on the entities and individuals affected by this Bill.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I note in this regard that MHA has made a statement in the middle of last week – I think there have been a few statements and comments made by the Ministry – that it will publish details of designated persons or entities, but the point is, surely, this should have been made more explicit in the Bill.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Workers' Party has no objection to the additional requirements that are ported to this Bill in connection with the porting over of the Political Donations Act into FICA.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: However, we do question whether the list of Politically Significant Persons is far-reaching enough.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I note the Minister's comments in his Second Reading speech.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But the point is our Civil Service has a significant footprint in the success of Singapore, with its central role in influencing Government policy.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: As MHA's press release on the First Reading of the Foreign Interference (Countermeasures) Bill shows, the danger of elite capture is an insidious threat.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It would be unwise to assume that only politicians, civil society activists and journalists are vectors for foreign influence.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: To this end, it would be important for the public to understand that the Government did not think it necessary to designate such individuals as PSPs in the original Bill.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I will leave Member of Parliament Gerald Giam to speak more on this subject.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Of the four areas of amendments, foremost is accountability of the Executive, because, without that, fairness in scoping powers and greater transparency are but shadow puppets.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This is why the second part of my speech is on how exceptional executive power requires the strongest of oversight to ensure accountability.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: If a poll were to be conducted among ordinary Singaporeans on concepts like the separation of powers doctrine and its centrality to our system of Government, such a poll, I would hazard, would likely elicit quizzical looks.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: One can hazard a guess that not a small number of our citizens would be unsure of how important such principles are to our political system.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Members of this House may have noticed a compact wooden bookcase at one end of the Parliament library.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This bookcase and a number of books on parliamentary and constitutional subjects were presented by the UK’s House of Commons to the then-Speaker of Parliament P Coomaraswamy on 16 November 1966 to mark Singapore becoming the 22nd nation of the Commonwealth to gain Independence.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This House passed a resolution recognising the receipt of these gifts on 5 December that year.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: One of the famous books in this bookcase is the Law of the Constitution by Albert Dicey where that hallowed phrase central to the separation of powers in all parliamentary democracies is found, and I quote: "Powers, however extraordinary, which are conferred by or sanctioned by statute, are never unlimited, for they are confined by the words of the Act itself, and, what is more, by the interpretation put upon the statute by the judges." Unquote.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The separation of powers doctrine and its close relationship with the rule of law was affirmed in the recent Court of Appeal judgment in Nagaenthran a/l K Dharmalingam v PP.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Clause 99 appears to go so far as to completely displace natural justice from the oversight process as drafted in the Bill.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: One of its paragraphs states that the Rules may enable or require a Reviewing Tribunal to hear or consider any proceedings or appeal without the person who brought the appeal having been given full particulars of the reasons for any conduct which is the subject of the proceedings or appeal.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Of course, there is a provision for a private hearing where national security is at risk.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Workers’ Party Member of Parliament for Sengkang GRC He Ting Ru will go through these amendments.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But ask Singaporeans, generally, about checks and balances and a clear majority would agree that they are important for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Power and responsibility must be divided, to empower each branch of Government, and ensure the exercise of power is not unlimited.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Which brings me to the third part of my speech on how the Government should have sought public feedback on the Bill.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In March this year, at the Committee of Supply debates, Deputy Speaker Christopher de Souza enquired what MHA would do to deter foreign influence in Singapore’s domestic affairs.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Second Minister for Home Affairs, hon Mrs Josephine Teo, addressed the query and announced that legislative levers may be needed.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I quote, "Given the recent experience of other countries, we need to consider further measures to guard against foreign subversion of politically significant individuals and entities.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This omission contradicts the position on record of the Second Minister for Home Affairs, which was to lean on the public to shape the Bill, which must surely include its safeguards.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In March this year, in his Adjournment Motion on Judicial Review and ousted clauses like clause 104 of this Bill, the hon Member for Bukit Batok and Government Parliamentary Committee (GPC) Chair for Home Affairs and Law, Mr Murali Pillai, stated that it was important for each generation of political leaders and the people to find their own equilibrium of what our people would accept without question.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This is a position I accept and welcome.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The hon Member then quoted his party Secretary-General's speech at the 36th PAP Party Conference held in November last year, when Prime Minister Lee said that Singaporeans have expressed the desire to have greater checks and balances, and that the PAP Government must change and respond to these desires and expectations.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: (In Malay):   Mr Speaker, there has been some disquiet among certain quarters about the speed at which this Bill has been tabled in Parliament.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In March this year, during the Committee of Supply (COS) debates, Deputy Speaker Christopher De Souza asked MHA about the measures that will be taken to prevent foreign interference in domestic affairs.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Second Minister for Home Affairs replied by highlighting the need for legislative levers.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: She said, "Given the recent experiences of other countries, we need to consider further measures to guard against foreign subversion of politically significant individuals and entities.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: For example, what levels of transparency in funding, support and leadership are appropriate?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This is very different from the statement made by the Second Minister for Home Affairs in Parliament, which intended to take heed of the views of the general public when drafting this Bill and its assurances.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In the same month, March this year, the Member for Bukit Batok, Mr Murali Pillai quoted a speech by the Secretary-General at the 36th PAP Party Conference.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Referring to the Prime Minister's speech, he said that Singaporeans have expressed a desire to re-examine our basic assumptions, try new approaches and have greater checks and balances.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This was preceded by the hon Member's statement that it is important for each generation of leaders and people to find their own equilibrium of what people would accept without question, under what circumstances and towards what ends.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: (In English): Mr Speaker, the fourth part of my speech is on how the Government has been comparatively muted on the non-legislative measures to deal with foreign interference.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Such measures should include educating the public to resist malignant information efforts and how to be vigilant against such interference that is commonly effected through business clans and cultural conduits, where the prospects of plausible deniability are high.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It was to be expected from the Committee's report that legislation would be used to address the problems identified.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: What is more difficult to grasp is the comparative lack of public knowledge on the non-legislative levers to address foreign interference.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Select Committee went through these non-legislative measures in a significant way.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: There have been a number of recommendations but the Government's response appears to have been focused on POFMA and, now, FICA.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The S Rajaratnam School of International Studies (RSIS) published a policy report in April this year on countermeasures against foreign influence.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This has been circulated to Members by Parliament Library staff.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Coming back to the Singapore Government's approach, the examples raised about foreign interference focused largely on long past attempts, such as the Singapore Herald and Eastern Sun episodes and the Hendrickson affair.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In a Straits Times article on 25 September, there were references to the impounding of SAF Terrex vehicles in Hong Kong and to reports of China's soft power efforts in Singapore through clan and business associations.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This begs the question: how will this Bill, in particular, if enacted, address such examples of alleged foreign interference?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Straits Times, our newspaper of record, does not make this very clear.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: What must Singaporeans do to heighten our sensitivity to such interference?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: And how is this Government ensuring that the message flows to the masses and new generations of Singaporeans, including new citizens, given that Singapore's destiny as an immigrant nation is almost certain?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: At best, the messaging is a bit unclear.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This spike in online chatter sought to give the artificial impression that there were significant and fundamental objections to Singapore's position.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This episode was also covered in the 25 September Straits Times story.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But beyond these scanty details, no further clarity and communication on foreign interference have followed.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: More fundamentally, how does the Government distinguish between a genuine groundswell of sentiment and a dedicated hostile information campaign?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I note that the MHA press release of the First Reading of the Foreign Interference (Countermeasures) Bill dated 13 September 2021 anonymised this example, although it was clear that the MHA press release was referring to the same episode highlighted by Minister Josephine Teo in her parliamentary speech.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But what does it say about the Government when it takes an arguably unclear approach to non-legislative responses?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Surely, non-legislative responses that promote a more participatory and educated citizenry would inoculate the population in a whole-of-society way far better against foreign interference.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This is an area I believe the Government needs to look into in a deliberate fashion across all levels of society.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It is my argument that the Government needs to work with the public in a far more participative way so as to strengthen the resolve of the population against foreign interference.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This apparent lack of integration of legislative and non-legislative measures to address foreign interference, in my view, is a critical omission in our public discourse on this subject.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The conclusion of the RSIS paper is prescient insofar as the discussions we have undertaken today and, more importantly, the public response to this Bill.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I quote the RSIS paper, "The manner of application of these countermeasures must be fair and necessary both in terms of process and perception without perpetuating the image of an Orwellian state.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Singapore must not appear to be taking sides in geopolitical rivalries or using foreign interference as a pretext to clamp down on local political discourse and responsible activism.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Government should not close the door on this.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: What is more perplexing is that we know that the Government had been mulling the introduction of this Bill for many months.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Why was it so difficult to undertake a period of public consultation before it was tabled for First Reading?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Hopefully, the Government will introduce such measures with the same alacrity with which it introduced this Bill.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I call on the Members of this House to seriously consider the proposed amendments and ask yourself whether you would want these amendments in place if the PAP was not in power.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The amendments are in the best interest of Singapore and Singaporeans, regardless of who is in charge now or in the future.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Whether you are reading the news, watching a TV show or doing your job, there is no escaping the influence of foreign ideas, foreign innovations and foreign interests.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This is the reality we, as a cosmopolitan and small nation, have no choice but to embrace.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I agree that we should be concerned about such disruptions and I believe most people are.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But at the same time, it is essential to be fair and transparent in how we restrict the activities of fellow Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Designing and imposing restrictions the wrong way can itself worsen the trust and stability of our domestic politics.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: With the goal of ensuring fairness and transparency, Sir, I have four points of clarification to make.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My first point is on the consultation process for this Bill.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Some residents have shared their concerns with me on this and it would be good for the Minister to clarify some of their doubts.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister share the consultation process for this Bill and whether it has integrated productive feedback from the consultation into this proposed law?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister also share how does the Ministry decide how much public consultation to hold for any proposed legislation?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Some felt that the interval was too short and, again, it will be good for the Minister to provide some clarifications on this as well.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Subsection 1(d) of section 17 requires that the person's action is "covert or involves deception".

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Similarly, subsection 1(d) of section 18 requires that the person's action "conceals from or fails to disclose" their relationship with a foreign principal.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister shed light on how an organisation can avoid being considered as having been covert, deceptive or otherwise opaque?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: If they receive a grant from a foreign principal, would it suffice to state on their website with the dollar amount received, the name of the grant -maker and the terms of the grant?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Would they need to print this material on all marketing material?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Would it need to be in their Facebook posts and their Twitter profile?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But this expectation is only fair if we make clear what reasonable compliance looks like.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Will MHA release guidelines and illustrations that can help facilitate compliance by good faith actors?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My third point is on the appeals process in this Bill.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The exception is when the Competent Authority considers it not practicable or desirable to do so.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister elaborate on when it would not be practicable or desirable for individuals to have the opportunity to be heard?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It seems odd that an individual might be denied even the chance to present their side of the story.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Providing written reasons to the politically designated person in all three scenarios would make clear that our process is transparent and fair.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My fourth and final point is on Reviewing Tribunals.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister share more about the considerations that the Cabinet should take into account when recommending the appointment of members of the Reviewing Tribunal?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: What is the profile of members envisioned for appointment to the Reviewing Tribunal?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This is important to clarify, as members of the Reviewing Tribunal may themselves be politically significant or otherwise at a heightened risk of hostile foreign influence.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In addition, section 99 allows the Minister to prescribe the practices and procedures for proceedings and appeals before a Reviewing Tribunal.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister share if these practices and procedures will be derived from the Rules of Court, practices and procedures for Court proceedings?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Will these practices and procedures follow the same principles for a fair hearing in the Rules of Court, practices and procedures for Court proceedings?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Minister has just got through two hours in this Chamber on the possible amendments.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: These are exactly what should have been done in Select Committee.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Is it realistic or fair to expect parliamentarians to understand the pros and cons of the amendments in just a few hours of debate?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, our recommendation is based on three considerations.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: One, for such an important Bill, it should not be rushed through Parliament, disregarding proper legislative processes and the feelings of Singaporeans suffering under a worsening COVID-19 crisis.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Two, countering foreign interference is an ongoing task and sufficient resources have already been deployed to it.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Do we need to restrict our citizens' freedom further to achieve better outcomes?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Three, is it wise to pass a legislation giving extensive power to a Minister without any judicial oversight?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The possibility of abuse cannot be ruled out.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Many Members of this House are probably not adequately prepared for a thorough debate today.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is difficult to understand why the Government is trying to rush the passage of this Bill or why the debate on this Bill cannot be postponed by three to six months to allow for proper scrutiny and consultation involving a wide range of stakeholders.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Just earlier this year, the Government established a two-month-long public consultation process for the Copyright Bill.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The POFMA Bill also went through a long consultation, lasting more than a year and, in addition, through a Select Committee, before it was passed into law.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, where is the Select Committee for FICA which, arguably, should be held to even greater scrutiny in light of the removal of judicial supervision of the Government's usage of FICA's powers and our citizens' constitutional rights?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We should also delay the reading of this Bill because we should be now focusing our resources and attention on the worsening COVID-19 situation in our country.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The number of infections has shot up exponentially and there are more and more distressed situations amongst many of us Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is a time when Members of Parliament should be busy helping constituents get through the many challenges in their lives due to the current COVID-19 crisis, instead of being distracted to mull through and digest this draconian Bill.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: On the other hand, the Government is not new to dealing with foreign interference for which it has been well-equipped to deal with after many years of experience.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: PSP recognises that foreign interference had existed in the past and will continue to exist.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But countering foreign interference is an ongoing task and this Government already has substantial resources to deal with it.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As I said, do we need to restrict our citizens' freedom further to achieve better outcomes?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We deploy substantial resources to national security every year.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This makes a total of $22 billion accounting for more than a quarter of our operating Budget.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There are also tough laws in place to deal with internal security and public issues.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: To start with, we have the Internal Security Act (ISA) which was passed in 1960 when we were still part of Malaysia.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Court of Appeal's ruling that the ISA was subjected to judicial review was already overruled in a legislative amendment in 1988, giving the Government wide powers in administering the ISA.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Incidentally, Malaysia had repealed its ISA in 2012 while our ISA is still in force.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Then, we have the Newspaper and Printing Presses Act (NPPA) since 1975, which is designed to ensure there is no foreign control on Singaporean newspapers and limits the circulation of foreign printed media.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There is also the Broadcasting Act 1994 which requires online sites discussing Singapore's political issues to register for a licence with conditions covering foreign funding and interference.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The NPPA and Broadcasting Act allowed the Government to have almost monopoly control over the narrative on major policies and issues through the mainstream media.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: That was until the rise of social media as a strong alternative platform from around 2010.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
