text: As a result, the Protection from Online Falsehoods and Manipulation Act (POFMA) came into being in 2019 to allow the Government to tackle the spread of fake news and false information online.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Between the ISA, NPPA, Broadcasting Act and POFMA, this Government already has extensive powers to deal with any internal security threat, manage public opinion and prevent the spread of false information online.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, is there a need to give this Government further powers to deal with foreign interference at the expense of our citizens' constitutional rights?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As there is no urgency but ample reasons why we should delay the Bill, we should then make best use of the opportunity to evaluate the implications of FICA properly.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We understand all that has been said about combating foreign interference.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But we cannot ignore the basic principles of democracy, which is not based on a benevolent ruler but on separation of powers and checks and balances.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A law like FICA, which ignores those principles, ought to be considered carefully and over a long period of deliberation.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Thus, FICA appears even worse than the Internal Security Act.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There are many more provisions and, to me, all sounded like a joke for someone living in a modern democratic society, based on the rule of law.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Or, in more accurate English, tyranny in the name of law.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: (In Mandarin):   My Singapore compatriots, FICA, in name, is a law to prevent foreign interference, but, actually, it is a tiger in sheep's skin and may severely infringe on our democratic and civil rights.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: National security is, of course, something that we are very concerned about and we also support giving the Government enough resources to deal with it.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Through the Internal Security Act, the Newspaper and Printing Presses Act, the Broadcasting Act and POFMA, the Government has, basically, controlled threats to domestic security, public opinion and the transmission of fake news online.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Hence, FICA is really a law that is unnecessary.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It gives the Government the power to deal with citizens who hold dissenting views.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We should learn from history, such as the lessons of militarism in Japan and Germany.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Every time a government moves towards authoritarianism, it can bring about disastrous consequences for the country.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The country needs checks and balances between the Government and the people in order to have lasting peace and stability.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: FICA is a law that could suppress public opinion and civil rights.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Do not think that FICA has nothing to do with our everyday life.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: (In English): Mr Speaker, the excessive controls of FICA over civil rights would not stop a determined foreign state from conducting foreign interference.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: While our capable security agencies and diplomatic channels are dealing with it, the best defence against foreign interference is not more laws to control our own people but to raise the awareness of our people towards national security threats.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Hence, the anti-terrorist awareness campaign, SGSecure, which is aimed at all Singaporeans, is a wise move.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Like what the Leader of the Opposition has commented just now, this Government should be more proactive in educating Singaporeans on what is online foreign interference, so that every citizen can be its eyes and ears.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Accordingly, we should not have laws to restrict and control Singaporeans' interaction with foreigners.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But we should encourage more interactions so that we know first-hand if there are developments of concern to the interest of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I, as do many Singaporeans, urge you and all Members of this House, to delay the passing of this Bill and allow for public consultations and the appointment of a Select Committee to scrutinise the Bill.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: You have the power to do so, Mr Speaker, under Standing Order No 68.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And how each Member votes on this Bill will represent his or her legacy to the present and future generations of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A yes vote means the Member is willing to sacrifice the rule of law, which is the foundation of all democratic nations.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For the sake of Singapore and Singaporeans, Mr Speaker, I urge you again to exercise your power, under Standing Order No 68 to refer the Bill to a Select Committee.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And I just received a message from a Singaporean through my handphone which says, "I want freedom of information.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: As my Workers' Party colleagues will point out, we believe in giving relevant authorities clearly defined and effective tools to counter actual acts of foreign interference.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Our objections, however, are raised in both the drafting of wide-ranging powers, the problems with oversight mechanisms and also the way the Bill has been presented.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Outside this Chamber, Singaporeans are just starting a second week of yet another set of tightened COVID-19 rules while navigating a system of confusing quarantine and testing programmes and regulations, scrambling to adapt to more home-based working and learning.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Our healthcare workers are strained and we have resorted to activating SAF to assist the system that was overwhelmed only one month after we further loosened restrictions.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I would therefore, like to seek clarification from the Minister about why the pressing need to forge ahead with this Bill now.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: While I reiterate that the Workers' Party agrees that appropriate measures need to be put in place to counter the threat of foreign interference, we would like to understand what is the real and imminent threat that Singapore faces that warrants such a rush in passing the Bill.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: And more crucially, why are the specific powers and tools contained under the Bill so urgently required by the Minister and various Competent Authorities that would mean the Bill needs to be rushed ahead and passed into law without further delay at this particular juncture?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I also want to stress that this Bill is not an obscure one that, once passed, will have minimal impact on the lives of Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Already, we have seen numerous voices from a Senior Counsel, various NGOs, Singaporean academics, including a senior research fellow at IPS, speaking up to voice their grave concerns not only at the speed at which the Bill is to be passed, but also about the substantive provisions contained in the Bill.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: There is a fear from many that in the rush to pass the Bill to counter foreign interference, we may be throwing the baby out with the bath water and end up catching many legitimate and innocent people, entities and projects in the dragnet.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: A fear that has been repeated by numerous voices including those of, in particular, my colleagues Assoc Prof Jamus Lim's and Mr Gerald Giam's amendments.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The impact of the Bill is not reserved just for the few who are active in politics.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The way it has been drafted and passed has the potential to adversely affect ordinary Singaporeans in ways that may not be initially obvious.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It is like a trojan horse that appears benign at first, but unravels upon passage in two main ways.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This means local content creators, local activists, local academics, their retraction from our public spaces will mean that we will be worse off, and this will dampen the richness of thinking and dialogue on issues that matter to all Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Could this be a slippery slope that would lead to less checks on how these powers are wielded?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: And ultimately, in the hands of possible future rogue Ministers and officials, damage Singapore's reputation as an open global business hub where enforcement and application are predictable and certain.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Together with the hasty passage of significant Bills, such as this, with limited or rushed debate, these would risk chilling investment and job opportunities in the process.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I must also sound a note of caution.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We must ensure that we do not end up being so shrill and fearful of the threat of foreign interference that we end up neglecting an even more insidious threat, one where domestic players could seize an easy opportunity to whip up nationalism and anti-foreign sentiment to further their own political goals, nefarious or otherwise, in the flimsy name of protecting national interest and sovereignty.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We have seen this happening since 2016 in movements and campaigns like Brexit, Pegida and Make America Great Again.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: There has been a rise of far-right governments from Brazil to central eastern Europe; formerly fringe parties, such as the Front National and the Alternative für Deutschland, have acquired national platforms.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: All of them have built their success on twisted versions of patriotism and national identity and sovereignty.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: If similar homegrown ideas and movements are allowed to take root here, whether from the ruling government of the day, opposition parties or otherwise, the damage done to a small society like ours could be catastrophic.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Moving on to the proposed amendments by the Workers' Party, I will speak on those standing in my name, which are amendments to clauses 92 to 104, which fall under Part 8, Oversight Arrangements.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: First, the rights of appeal; and second, the judicial review of the clause.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I turn, first, to clauses 92 and 93 which deal with the rights of appeal against decisions made under the Act by both the Minister and the Competent Authorities.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This section is important as it prescribes the methods and processes in place to protect citizens against an abuse of power by the government of the day.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The Government appoints these individuals, and the chair of the tribunal has to be a Supreme Court Judge.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: There are no other specific requirements in the Bill relating to the remaining two members of the tribunal.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The tribunal can hear appeals on too narrowly and clearly-defined circumstances for a person issued with a Part 3 direction, that is, a direction to counteract harmful foreign online communications activity of the proprietors of a Proscribed Online Location, which are locations that are declared by the Minister to be purveyors of hostile information content.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It is notable that the drafting of this section shows that the draftsperson is able to very narrowly and precisely define parameters when it is desirable to do so.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Additionally, all appellants must have first requested the Minister to reconsider the earlier decision before they can be taken to the tribunal.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: In particular, it is not clear how, or even whether the tribunal will be able to consider appeals on the substance of the exercise of the Minister's powers to issue Part 3 directions, given that there is no obligation in the Act for the Minister to explain how he exercises his powers of considering Part 3 directions issued by the Competent Authority under the Act.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Also, I note that the tribunal is only empowered to either dismiss the appeal or revoke the decision.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It is not within the tribunal's power to make any amendments.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Their only route is through the Minister himself and the Minister's decision is final.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I	also	note	that	our	proposed	deletion	of clause 119(2) is a consequential amendment of having deleted the provisions relating to the Reviewing Tribunal.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The Workers' Party's position to the approach taken above is that oversight mechanisms proposed are insufficient to ensure the Act is not abused.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: First, the Minister is in almost all cases the final decision-maker.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Only a limited and very narrowly defined subset of cases are subject to appeal to the Reviewing Tribunal.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This would mean that he would, effectively, be asked to make his appeal partially blindfolded.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: In view of this, we propose that in line with the doctrine of the separation of powers, the judiciary is the appropriate organ of state to exercise oversight over the broad powers granted under this Bill.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This proposal means that any person who is subjected to a determination order or decision under the Bill has a right of appeal to the judiciary, that is, to the High Court.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The Reviewing Tribunal is clearly not an effective substitute for the Courts.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This is also problematic as the tribunal effectively is appointed by the Cabinet, in what is effectively a check, by the Executive, on an Executive decision.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This is a classic case of, in the words of the Leader of the Opposition, “Ownself Check Ownself”.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The tribunal is also, unlike the Courts, not part of the Judiciary established under our Constitution, whose independence is also enshrined in our Constitution.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Under our Constitution, judicial power is vested in the Courts.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Carving out matters that should be properly determined by the Courts for review by a tribunal that cannot be held to account is deeply problematic.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: There is also no mention of either the tribunal or the Minister being guided or bound by precedents of previous decisions which are often instructive and valuable.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: To address concerns that judicial trials may compromise national security because of the sensitive nature of a matter, our proposed amendment also allows for such hearings to be held in-camera, without the public being allowed to attend, if the Court is satisfied that it is in the public interest to do so.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The ouster clause is a breach of the principle of the separation of powers: the Government should not be using its legislative authority to oust the rightful constitutional oversight of a co-equal institution in the Singapore system.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It means that no decision under FICA should be challenged through the process of judicial review, apart from the very narrow grounds of purely procedural compliance with the Act not being properly followed.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Many of our leading jurists have also expressed their discomfort with ouster clauses.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The Court of Appeal has expressed concern in Per Ah Seng that ouster clauses “can be regarded as being incompatible with the rule of law because it should be within the Court’s purview to declare the legal limits of discretionary powers”.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Our former Chief Justice Chan Sek Keong, too, has suggested that ouster clauses, "may be inconsistent with Article 93 of the Constitution, which vests the judicial power of Singapore in the Supreme Court".

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The latter two limbs of judicial review are key in ensuring that, as captured in Chng Suan Tze v Minister for Home Affairs, "All power has legal limits and the rule of law demands that the Courts should be able to examine the exercise of discretionary power".

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: And we must, as legislators, have the rule of law in mind as we consider the balance of, amongst others, natural justice, national security and the separation of powers as we decide whether or not a judicial review ouster clause should stand.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: For illegality, this arises when a decision-maker exercises a power wrongly, or improperly purports to exercise a power that it does not have.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The Courts, in their role to check and balance powers granted to bodies, ensure that nobody overreaches and goes beyond the powers given to them.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: For irrationality, it allows a party to challenge a decision by a public official or body if “it is so unreasonable that no reasonable authority could ever have come to it”.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Disallowing judicial reviews on the grounds of illegality and irrationality takes away an important check on the powers granted to the Government.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Imagine, if one day, the Competent Authority designates a six-month-old baby a PSP under Part 4.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This decision is final and cannot be set aside if the Minister upholds this upon appeal.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It will not be allowed to be set aside on the grounds of irrationality since judicial review on these grounds are not possible!

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: While this situation may be dismissed as outlandish and would never happen, it is theoretically possible under the provisions of the Bill.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: While we might say that we have confidence in current policy-makers' intentions and policies, yet, no one can guarantee the conduct of future Ministers and competent authorities and their commitment to acting rationally and legally.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: In fact, were we not told that the logic for the constitutional amendments surrounding the establishment of the Elected Presidency and, in 2016, changes in the remit of the Council of Presidential Advisers, have to do with putting in safeguards in place against the possibility	of	irrational	or	unreasonable	behaviour	by	top decision-makers?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Why do these safeguards not apply here, especially as we are granting wide-ranging powers to the Minister?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I wish to also point out that judicial review does not review the merits of cases.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Instead, it is a process by which the Courts exercise supervision over decisions made by Ministers and other public officials and bodies to ensure that legal limits are enforced where public power is exercised.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: In other words, we believe that the "sunlight of scrutiny", to use the phrase of our esteemed colleague Mr Murali Pillai, is more crucial than ever in needing to be applied to this Bill and the broad and alarming powers it purports to introduce.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This sunlight is what helps both shine a light on malicious foreign activity and, at the same time, assures all of us that we do not need to worry about the over-expansive use of Government powers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This principle of non-interference per se is unobjectionable, and the Workers' Party stands behind the notion that domestic political matters should, indeed, be determined by our own people.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But the proposed language in a number of areas spelled out in the Bill are troubling.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In this speech, I will provide justifications for the amendments that the Workers' Party has proposed in my name.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: These pertain to clauses that leave the scope of foreign interference troublingly vague and, relatedly, proposed an insufficiently steep hurdle for the applicability of the law, one that we believe begins to border on the policing of thought.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The common thread among these amendments is that we need to satisfy a reasonable standard of proof and intent when we claim that an individual has acceded to the influence of foreign principals.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: We can all accept that there are threats out there that have to be dealt with.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: We can all accept that some threats are subtle and, by design, evasive, and, hence difficult to identify and prove with absolute certainty.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And we can all accept that establishing facts, even by the strict legal standards upheld in a Court of law, will seldom be definitive.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Even eyewitnesses could easily differ in what they perceive – or believe to have observed – from an event.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Film classics like Rashōmon and Virumaandi, and parables like the Blind Men and the Elephant, remind us that objectivity may be elusive, even in fair, carefully-litigated circumstances.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Consequently, society – and the legal system – have allowed for a comparatively high burden of proof for claims and accusations, which (at the very least) requires a comparatively high probability of an outcome or event being true.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: We also have well-understood channels of appeal, to allow for the possibility of overturning rules that subsequently turn out to be false positives.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But this does not appear to be the case in a number of clauses in this Bill, notably, the amendments we have proposed to parts of clauses 17 through 18, 40, and 75.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The dictionary definition only states that something that is likely “will probably happen or is expected”; it does not attribute any probability to this likelihood.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Statistically, any outcome that has the greater probability of being realised could be anything ranging from 51% to 99%.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Thus, establishing that a given action will amount to an offence will require an estimation of a likelihood.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While courts have a long history of attributing just cause based on strong, credible evidence, this is an enormous leap of faith for any single, largely unchecked individual.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The desire to draft a law robust enough to capture such possibilities is a sound motivation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But at the same time, we cannot deny that the vast majority of such communications activity – even when framed in a manner that is potentially incriminating to its sender – could well be innocuous; the frivolous or unfiltered rantings of a troubled mind.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Possibilities are insufficient, especially when they call for predictions of an uncertain future.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Were this Bill be passed into law as it stands, we will require not just that our Ministers or relevant Competent Authorities speculate on the likely mindset and possible actions of individuals, but that such individuals themselves possess the ability to predict whether the information they communicate will affect security, public good, domestic harmony or international relations.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Experts can barely venture such forecasts successfully, much less an average person.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: As much as I may be a fan of Tom Cruise, Stephen Spielberg and Philip K Dick, "suspicion" or a "reason to believe" does not rise to the level of actual crime, but represents anticipatory action.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: At its best, it runs the risk of abuse and misuse, short-circuiting the free will of individuals to change their minds before they act.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: At its worst, it rises to the level of thought policing, pinning on suspects actions that they have yet to be realised.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Even conspiracy – a very indirect attribution of potential involvement in illegal activity – requires solid evidence.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Short of this, we are relying on gut feeling and instinct to play with people's lives.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: One potential objection to this set of amendments is that the Minister or the relevant Competent Authority will always act judiciously and with care.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This claims that, bereft of the flexibility to act on their suspicions, we will compromise the ability of our authorities to properly protect our citizens.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But this calls for us to enshrine into law the propensity of a political office holder to always act in the public interest.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: What if, God forbid, an irresponsible party forms the government or someone in the government goes rogue?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: We are walking dangerously close to Manchurian Candidate territory here – and I know I am citing a lot of movie references.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The purpose of the law in any society guided by rule of law is to bind the hands of policymakers, regardless of their benefactions, from the most egregious exercises of arbitrary decision-making.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Do these specific sub-clauses satisfy that standard or should the language of the law be rendered as clear as possible?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Furthermore, we cannot exclude the possibility that even an entirely well-meaning officeholder may carry suspicions, even firmly held ones, that could well turn out to be erroneous.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The proposed amendments to clauses 17(2) and 18(2) are meant to refine intent.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While we agree that clandestine foreign interference may well involve multiple principals, expanding the applicability of the law to include instances where individuals "need not have in mind any particular foreign country or principal" veers uncomfortably into territory where we criminalise those who may have been deceived or misled.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Yet, the explanatory notes of the Bill clearly expressed that covert activities are "not intended to cover circumstances where a person undertakes an activity with no knowledge, awareness or direction from the foreign principal or where the relationship between the person's activities and the foreign principal's interest are merely coincidental".

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Will we then charge those who have been unwittingly made to operate as pawns of a more sophisticated principal?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Lest we rule out as the domain of the naive and, hence, inapplicable to PSPs, it is useful to remind ourselves of how often even sophisticated experts may end up being duped.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Just think of the victims of Bernie Madoff's Ponzi scheme, the Envy Global nickel investment scam or Elizabeth Holmes' Theranos, currently playing out in US Courts.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: To compound matters, allowing for such possibilities would be extremely costly in terms of resources.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Think of the time, energy and resource that would have to be expended to investigate and prosecute cases where it is unclear whether any specific foreign actor is even involved.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It could also give rise to either an excessive number of frivolous accusations or, conversely, inhibit actual victims from stepping up to alert authorities if they suspect they may have been manipulated.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The coincidence of interests, another dimension highlighted as notes, remains poorly excluded by the overall language of the Bill.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Part (iv) of clauses 5 and 48, where we have not proposed amendments, refers to the term "collaboration", which is undefined but as the notes explain, takes on its "ordinary meaning".

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While we understand that the purpose is to capture nefarious collaborations, perhaps inspired by the case of former Lee Kuan Yew School of Public Policy professor Huang Jing, such broad language raises both theoretical and practical concerns.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: For starters, there is very little reason why the simple act of working together, the dictionary definition of "collaboration", with a foreign entity need give rise to subservience or, for that matter, even mild influence.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I am certain we all have had colleagues with whom we disliked but, yet, we are forced to work together on projects and would never imagine nor wish to emulate or even learn from.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Hence, there is little logical reason why one would link collaboration with influence or, more intrusively, interference.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Moreover, in any collaborative relationship, especially when parties carry equal standing, it is frequently impossible to attribute who actually exerts control.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: By a similar token, it would not be unusual for working relationships dealing with public policy to venture into politically sensitive, controversial – this is the wording in the Bill – issues.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Think matters, such as climate change, vaccinations, free trade and gender issues, all of which are controversial and often evoke partisan leanings, regardless of whether there may have been any intent to direct such effort towards a political end.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This could have a chilling effect on already guarded national discussions by constraining the ability of our citizens to work with foreigners on matters of national importance so long as they happen to be politically controversial.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Taken together, including the exceedingly vague term "collaborations", into the scope of activities subject to FICA, it becomes inherently problematic.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Is it sufficient for us to claim that casual transparent interactions do not entail collaboration but deep engagement does?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: How much must one actually work with another before they are deemed to have collaborated?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: To engage, however, includes the possibility of working with and, indeed, even working for somebody else.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Surely, it must bother us that we are choosing to define into our laws the possibility of catching, in Minister K Shanmugam's words earlier on, a one in 1,000 chance but glossing over the far greater likelihood of throwing up many, many more false positives.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: These theoretical observations are further compounded by the fact that, in practice, Singaporeans routinely collaborate with non-Singaporeans on all manner of critical and non-critical operations.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Top generals conduct joint military exercises on a regular basis and we often send our best civil servants on overseas assignments where they may gather knowledge and experience from citizens of other nations.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Our political officeholders are often called to perform global public service, serving on committees in international organisations where they collaborate with high-level officials from other countries.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Surely, it is possible that an individual might independently choose to pursue a given course of action, bereft of external influence.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Yet, this choice could still be common knowledge.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: By a similar token, the definition of foreign principals may be excessively broad.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While we understand that malicious intent is subsequently captured by clauses 5 through 7, exclusionary language, especially for these two very general categories, may be warranted – something to the effect of a sub-clause that explicitly spells out how these entities are engaged in political activities.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Alternatively, examples and counter examples could be provided of businesses and political organisations that would be captured or not by said definition.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In contrast, the amendments we have proposed for clause 120 are one of omission, namely, the fact that the law fails to incorporate public assurances by MHA.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Given how there is always, by definition, at least one political party in Government, these proposed amendments serve to clarify some of this distinction in the text of the law, not with this current administration or Minister, but, potentially, with future ones.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Ensuring that political speech is legally protected goes beyond guaranteeing that citizens can speak freely about political matters that are near and dear to their hearts.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: As a child, I learned how "boh sompah, buay pasah".

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Children, evidently, intuitively, understand the importance of codification of promises.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The proposed amendments to clause 120 essentially do the same for the guarantees promised by MHA rather than leaving it to the vagaries of enforcement by the government in power.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I shall close, Mr Speaker, with a more general reflection of what FICA could mean for a globalised city state, such as Singapore.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In our Sitting just a mere three weeks ago, we spent enormous amounts of time debating on the merits of economic openness, both historically and for the future of the survival of our nation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This openness comes at a cost, of course, and it is one that we must surely manage.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: It does not engage in petty partisan politics.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Any harm arising from these are of our own making.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: After all, it is the mark of all free societies that we take this form of the rough with the smooth.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Accepting these rough edges, we must, therefore, accept that we will continue to make mistakes.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: There will be those who believe their ideas are good when they are poor.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The Bill is no arbiter in this contest.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: What it will do is to make sure that all ideas to come into our political arena do so through the front door, through an open political contest and that they cannot sneak in through the back, under technological cover, wearing a false face and pretending to serve the public interest when they are in the back pocket of foreign or private actors.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: This Bill stands against those who are knowingly malicious and against those who have been unknowingly used.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: It is the latest in a long line of efforts to keep Singapore free. "Freedom" is a word not used lightly in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The idea of freedom means something specific to a small country in a volatile neighbourhood.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: It means an often taken-for-granted, but still slightly cherished power to decide our own fate, because this freedom is hard-won and because the battle remains as fierce today, as it did in 1965.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: We must see what laws can best serve to protect it.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: This Bill targets the enemies of this freedom so that we can fully exercise the larger internal freedoms that I spoke of earlier – to ensure that our civil liberties and our political contests remain our own.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: In fact, it lasted eight days in all.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: So, when the hon Mr Leong Mun Wai says there was not enough evidence gathered or consultations done, I am not sure what he makes of these 169 written representations and the 65 oral evidence from individuals and organisations.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The issue of foreign interference is a complex and enduring one, made more powerful in recent years by technological platforms.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: We must be clear that these technologies are not neutral between public good and harm.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: We cannot leave these untended and expect ordinary citizens, who already have so much cognitive tax in their daily lives, to be inoculated against these malicious campaigns.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Our digital lives have opened many new possibilities, but, along with the sunlight, we have an infestation of lies.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: He said, "Today, information can easily be weaponised by foreign actors, at low cost, and with anonymity and impunity.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: This is asymmetric information warfare, fought in a theatre and era with no distinction between war and peace.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: In this battlefield, Singapore, an open, democratic, digitally-connected and diverse country, is especially vulnerable.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: We are a young country with sensitive fault lines that foreign actors can exploit to foment distrust and ill-will among our various communities." Sir, at the time, Mr Edwin Tong was responding to a Parliamentary Question.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: This was again, let me repeat that, 2019.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: But the stage had already been set a few years earlier.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: We have heard these issues discussed deeply at the Select Committee hearings.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: We have heard evidence from experts during the Select Committee hearings that hostile information campaigns are becoming cheaper to mount and becoming more prevalent.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The point of these campaigns is to weaken the target country, turn brother against brother, countrymen against one another, race against race, undermining social cohesion with fights constructed with false sticks and stones.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: A third foreshadowing of this Bill happened at the Committee of Supply in 2019 and again in 2021.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Government Ministers then spoke about how foreign interference laws would need to be introduced and its efforts in tracking the legislative response in other countries.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Fourth, this has been a hot issue discussed among our think tanks and at the Universities – most notably, at the Foreign Interference conference organised by Nanyang Technological University (NTU)'s RSIS in September 2019.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: This topic has, certainly, long been on the radar of both the Government and the people.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: It is not new and certainly does not lack airing or consultation.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: So, for those who ask why are we "rushing" through this Bill and ask for more consultation, I hope we realise this Bill has been in the works for some time already, a few years in the making actually, and there has, certainly, been no lack of consultations and feedback.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: To the Leader of the Opposition, hon Mr Pritam Singh, who referred to Mr Christopher de Souza's Parliamentary Question in March this year and Second Minister for Home Affairs Josephine Teo's reply, let me remind him that this was at the Committee of Supply 2021 debate.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: I should reiterate that this process started way before March 2021 and this was also not the first time that MHA has stated the need for such a Bill.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: My second point has to do with the signature of our defence against external threats.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Unity has been our clarion call since the nation began.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Against the call of race, religion and the multiplicity of the Babel Tower of languages, we formed our own tribal instincts.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Today, we have more need than ever for such instincts – this communitarian commitment, which is not natural, but chosen by all of us who have decided to call this place home.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: This injunction to think beyond oneself, this seeking for things that matter, this Singaporean spirit is one that we must seek to grow and nourish.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: We cannot do this if we keep using the infantilising versions of these words of "safety and protection", which can degenerate into nothing more than an entitled demand for special accommodation, for "care” for oneself and a refusal to follow the same rules that apply to everyone else.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: To see what true public interest comprises, against a private, self-regarding clamour, we must have space for open, transparent and accountable debates.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: We must see that all disagreements among ourselves are taken seriously and welcomed, and that it is our joint duty to ensure that such debates reflect our own views, rather than those of outside agents.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: This Bill is not a molly-coddle of resources to "protect" and bubble wrap Singaporeans, but a sword, so that we are armed against those who seek to harm us.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: It is a true countermeasure, a necessary response to attacks – attacks, which I am quite sure, will come.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: So, the earlier we are prepared for it, the better.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: This Bill gives us the power towards early detection and exposure.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: We have always relied on this sunlight in the past and we must do so again.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: As for the criticism of this Bill from activists and academics, MHA, the Minister himself, have already responded to some of these.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: As a Member of Parliament in this House, let me say this with ample evidence from our own history – there can be no civil liberties if activists can be bought or sold; and there can be no academic freedom if our Universities are homes for foreign agents.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: It will be naive to believe that all activists are high-minded patriots, just as it is mere pretence that all academics are cultivating young minds for the good of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: In the real world, there are active, hostile and intentional actors working against the public interest of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: All of us, on both sides of this House, would have failed in our duty if, in the face of such clear and present danger, we stand by and fold our hands.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair at 5.45 pm.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended  at 5.25 pm until 5.45 pm.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: I do not know much about espionage other than what I read from newspapers or see in James Bond movies.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: I had not intended to speak, until a few doctors and the Singapore Medical Association (SMA) staff approached me privately and separately to raise their concerns.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: So, how could FICA affect those of us in medicine?

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: Some doctors have patients who are political officeholders in other countries.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: SMA is part of the Medical Association of South East Asian Nations (MASEAN), Confederation of Medical Associations in Asia and Oceania (CMAAO) and the World Medical Association.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: SMA also works closely with MOH on local healthcare decisions.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: As many of you here would know, Dr Poh Soo Kai was one of the founders of SMA and served as its first Honorary Secretary from 1959 to 1961.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: He was also arrested and detained without trial during Operation Coldstore in 1963 and under the Internal Security Act in 1976.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: I was born in 1980 and grew up without much knowledge of such matters.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: What is past is history and I do not question it here.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: My being here now, as a Nominated Member of Parliament and being the current President of SMA, has made the wearing of multiple hats complicated.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: I state for the record that I speak now, as an individual, to seek clarity on the intent, and the extent of FICA.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: I agree that there should never be foreign interference in a country’s politics.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: As an ordinary citizen, I have remained blissfully unaware of how threats to Singapore have manifested, except for what is reported in mainstream news.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: Arresting a human agent with proof of radicalisation or obvious threats to the stability of Singapore is easy for us to accept.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: But in the modern world, it is scary to learn that modern threats can be subtle, through social media, bots, ads, sponsored articles and posts to erode trust in the Government and take advantage of social fault lines and sow discord.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: This is a real threat, and we, as a nation, have to learn to defend ourselves against these threats.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: Where my opinion differs is how best to tackle it.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: The Bill grants extensive powers to the Minister to enforce and regulate anyone or any organisation with an online presence, from the content produced down to the operations.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: While this may scare off the malicious, I am afraid that it may also scare away people who are genuinely interested in improving our nation.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: This brings me to my first concern that we need to leave some space for people to participate as active citizens in shaping our future.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: Desiring to influence public opinion or decisions is part and parcel of advocacy.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: Increasing reporting requirements opens up a small organisation to potentially being targeted and increases the barrier for a citizen who wants to participate and contribute, or just to simply air their views.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: My next concern is about how Singapore relates to the wider world.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: Singapore is an open country with organisations forming many collaborations, especially NGOs that might need the scale to ensure that their services are accessible to others.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: It seems impossible to expect that people should be deterred from seeking sponsorships beyond Singapore and also that volunteers and manpower should only be limited to Singapore Citizens.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: Singaporeans may, ourselves, shy away from working for NGOs for fear of being unwittingly implicated, real or imagined.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: But this requires a lot more trust and faith in the people to do the right thing.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: It is a lot of power in one man’s hands.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: How can we protect it from future abuse?

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: Not just to the different branches in the judiciary, but also across the people.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: Let them call for accountability and transparency in the organisations they work with.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: Let organisations regulate amongst themselves who are the right people to seek sponsorships or volunteer work from.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: Let safeguards be what they are: limited protections for the worst case scenario, not pre-emptive strikes against people who may be just trying to do the right thing.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: Quoting the MINDEF website, Total Defence involves every Singaporean playing a part, individually and collectively, to build a strong, secure and cohesive nation.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: The six pillars are military, civil, economic, social, digital and psychological defence.

speaker: Dr Tan Yia Swam (Nominated Member)
text: In this digital age, foreign interference is no longer a problem that should only be left to the Government to guard against.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: (In Mandarin):   Like many Singaporeans, I also desire world peace.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Most of us have no quarrel with the rest of the world and try to be kind to others.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The adage that one does not hurt others, does not necessarily lead to the conclusion that others will not seek to hurt us.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Across the span of history, there has always been strife between different countries.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Even in relatively peaceful times in the world today, foreign forces do often seek to influence the policies and affairs of other countries for their own political, economic, or military purposes.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: With the development of science and technology, these interference methods have become more sophisticated, and have the potential to cause significant and destructive impact in a short period of time.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: I think the comparison made by Mr Leong Mun Wai just now is rather inappropriate.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The Nazis were a totalitarian government, whereas ours is an elected government; what the Nazis did was ethnic cleansing, whereas we have been advocating racial harmony all along.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Singapore is a democratic, independent and autonomous country.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: To have autonomy means to be able to make decisions freely and independently without being coerced or influenced to do so.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: However, foreign forces can use various hidden tactics to manipulate our country’s policies, public opinion and exploit existing faut lines amongst our people.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: As the saying goes "It is easy to dodge a spear from the front, but hard to avoid an arrow from behind." These actions directly jeopardise our ability to make independent and autonomous decisions.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: To protect our basic rights, we must consider ways to effectively resist foreign interference.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Today, I will give my opinion on the Foreign Interference (Countermeasures) Bill.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: It exists in a zone that has seen perennial disputes among major and regional powers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Located in the Straits of Malacca, Singapore is an important international waterway connecting the Pacific and Indian Oceans.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: It operates the most important energy supply line in the world and is, therefore, one of the most strategically significant cities in the Pacific.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Today, with globalisation, Singapore has become an important transportation, trade, financial and information hub in Asia.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: In today's international environment where competition among major powers is intensifying, Singapore is inevitably a contested space and platform among major powers jockeying for strategic superiority.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Holding Singapore under control is tantamount to holding the lifeblood of Asia's transportation, trade, finance, and information.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: In recent years, disputes over territorial sovereignty and hegemony in the Pacific have been common and countries involved have been looking to meet their own needs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Against this backdrop and in this complex international environment, other countries will pay attention to the attitudes and propositions held by Singapore and will even influence or interfere through various ways.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: These practices are not mere imaginations, they have been happening in fact.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: He disclosed confidential state information to them and advocated the positions of other countries on sensitive issues of national security.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: In Singapore, in December 2018, tense bilateral relations between Singapore and our neighbours became a hot topic.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Most of these anonymous comments were critical of Singapore.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Covert foreign intervention efforts can change individuals institutions and even entire societies, in an unnoticed manner.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The cohesion of a nation, the fighting spirit of a people, can be corrupted and defeated without a fight.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Let us imagine what would happen, if Singapore allows other countries to interfere in Singapore’s affairs and influence public opinion, and our autonomy was really manipulated by foreign forces.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Singapore would very likely become a puppet at the mercy of foreign countries’ manipulation.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Our nation-building philosophy, lifestyle, safety and interests may all be weakened or subverted.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: For example, if foreign forces intentionally drive a wedge along racial lines, can our racial harmony be maintained?

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Would our racial and religious equality still be possible?

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: If foreign forces were to use Singapore’s land and resources to meet the needs of their own countries, could we then continue to protect the interests of our people?

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: If foreign forces try to involve Singapore in geopolitical disputes or become a battlefield for wars between other countries, would our children not also get involved and be sacrificed?

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Just now, some Members said that there was no need for a new law to counter foreign interference.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: I hope that these Members can realise that Singapore’s unique characteristics make us more vulnerable to external interference.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: First, Singapore is a multiracial, multireligious and multicultural society.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Instigating inter-ethnic, inter-religious and inter-cultural relations is a likely avenue of intervention by foreign forces.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: At the same time, people of different races or religions may have stronger cultural and historical ties with some countries.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: They may have a sense of friendliness or belonging to a certain country or a spiritual leader, which makes it easier for other countries to target these people and make use of them.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Second, Singapore is a very open society and maintains a high Internet penetration rate, which allows other countries to achieve their propaganda purposes through anonymous, fast and efficient information dissemination.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Many countries have the technological and financial capability to expertly create misleading information, incite intimidation and sway the minds of men.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Through highly paid mercenaries and the use of sophisticated tools, such as software and hackers, they are able to penetrate into our society and sow discord.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Third, Singapore is a small country, which is like a small boat in the sea.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: If we do not pay attention and endeavour to resist foreign interventions, it will be as if someone is jumping around, and our boat can be easily overturned.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: What preventive measures should we take to minimise the risks of foreign intervention?

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: As such, there is nothing to worry about for most people and entities, as the Bill will not affect their daily activities.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Obviously, political parties, people holding political office, and Members of Parliament are defined as "politically significant".

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Their actions can directly influence national policies and public opinion.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: As the saying goes, "One who stands upright does not fear a crooked shadow." Such persons and entities should have nothing to worry about if they do not harm Singapore’s public interest.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Second, the Bill is not intended to prevent individuals, companies, and organisations from establishing international relationships.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: We strongly encourage individuals, companies and organisations to participate in international exchanges and international cooperation to make our country more dynamic.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: It organised cultural exchanges, education and training activities throughout China, Southeast Asia and other regions, reflecting the importance we attach to overseas connections.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: We continue to encourage companies, associations and social organisations to visit overseas and conduct cooperation projects with other countries.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: To do business abroad, our companies will, inevitably, deal with local governments or government-related organisations.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Of course, we should also abide by their local rules when dealing with them.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: If a Singaporean businessman interacts with a foreign government or government-related organisation and discusses national policies, that is not an issue.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: However, if the other part tries to get the businessman to lobby a Singaporean Member of Parliament or asks the businessman to widely spread the other side’s position in Singapore, then the businessman ought to be more vigilant.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: In addition, if a Singaporean organisation organises an exchange event and receives sponsorship from a foreign party, the general approach should be to be transparent about the sponsorship in the event materials, so that the process is transparent.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Some local individuals may also accept titles granted by overseas governments and institutions.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: It does not target personal, business and cultural exchanges outside of these areas.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Third, the Bill will not affect free speech.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: True freedom of speech is when people can speak freely without interference.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Free speech is undermined if foreign actors use hostile information to manipulate and influence public opinion.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Singaporeans can still express their personal opinions about our politics.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: For example, if a businessman is dissatisfied with Singapore’s policies and believes that it has affected the industry he is involved in, he is free to express his views and provide feedback to the Government.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: In this case, the new Bill does not apply.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The Bill is not aimed at personal opinions and is not meant to curb freedom of speech.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Its purpose is to ensure transparency of information and create an environment where discussions in the public sphere is free from foreign interference and manipulation.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Malicious foreign forces may incite controversial debates in order to sow discord between different groups, sway public opinion towards their intended narrative on sensitive issues, confuse people or weaken the public’s trust in the state’s institutions, thereby undermining the security and stability of the target country.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Hostile information can sometimes involve Singapore’s national defence, security and diplomatic issues through intelligence and other means.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Therefore, it is necessary for us to protect sensitive information needed for Government decision-making and we cannot make hasty conclusions through common legal procedures.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: We must formulate a customised legal framework to protect sensitive information and the individuals who provide the information.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: For issues involving national security, state secrets and diplomatic relations, we should all focus on the broader context.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Singapore is not the first in putting national security matters outside the court system for independent review.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: For example, in the United Kingdom, the review of investigations by British intelligence agencies is placed in a review court independent of the court system to protect sensitive evidence from being disclosed.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Israel also has an appeal procedure hosted by a special court to protect sensitive evidence provided by the state during the review of administrative detention.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The discussions on how to effectively guard against foreign interference have been discussed for quite some time.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: An important means of hostile information campaigns is false information on the Internet.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: In fact, as early as January 2018, the Government commissioned a Select Committee to study the dissemination of online falsehoods.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: In March 2018, we held an eight-day hearing to listen to public feedback.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Among the 65 people who came to the Select Committee hearing, 18 spoke about the use of hostile information campaigns intervening in domestic affairs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: For more than three years since, different institutions and scholars have participated in discussions on foreign interference.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: There have also been frequent discussions in the newspapers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: At the same time, other countries are also actively enacting legislation.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: After such lengthy discussions, we need to take action.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: I hope everyone will be united in our efforts to guard against foreign interference.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: In the face of foreign interference, it is important that we stick to our principles and put the interests of the Singaporean people first.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: If we were to learn from the history of other countries, the most important lesson will be to counter foreign interference and extreme ideologies.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Singapore, as an independent country, must stay clear-headed, focus on the big picture, learn lessons from history, and resist all forms of foreign interference.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Social and Family Development (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Not only should we stress the importance of personal ethics and responsibility so as not to be used by external forces, but we must also ensure that our Government, social organisations, and individuals will not be tempted or misled by foreign forces to harm our independence and the foundation of our democracy.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: (In Mandarin):   Here, I would like to ask Minister of State Sun Xueling two questions.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Can you give an example where a country in Asia was affected by strong foreign interference?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: If you have no intention to commit a crime, then no matter how harsh the law is, it does not concern you.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: The Minister has been talking about this principle, and now the Minister of State is also talking about this.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: (In Mandarin):   Earlier in my speech, I gave an example.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: This is to answer the Member's first question.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: Can the Member repeat his second question, please?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: (In Mandarin):   My second question is: is there such a principle in law where if you have no intention to commit a crime, then even if the Government introduces harsher laws, it does not concern you.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: (In English): Okay, the saying that if you had no plans to be against the law, so the law should not concern you.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling
text: I hope that all the Members here will consider the big picture.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Some of my constituents have written to me expressing their concern with the Bill's over-reach.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: They are reflective of the disquiet felt by many.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: If these draconian measures are not properly limited, they could have a chilling effect on freedom of speech and the exchange of information among Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: At the same time, FICA seems to be lacking a sharper approach to deal with real threats that Singapore might face.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Elite capture can, potentially, have a far more negative impact on public policies than influence campaigns on the general public.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Fundamentally, no legislation can effectively counter foreign interference in our politics by itself.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Public education and a freer press are also needed to inoculate our population against these risks.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The definition of public interest in clause 7 includes the prevention of any foreign influence or interference directed towards a political end in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: In turn, clause 8 defines an activity to be directed towards a political end in Singapore if its purpose includes influencing public opinion on a matter of public controversy or if it promotes or opposes views on a subject of a political debate in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Public interest is one of the basis for the Minister to authorise Part 3 directions, anticipatory directions, designations of Politically Significant Persons (PSPs) or entities, Technical Assistance Directions or directives regarding donors.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: With the inclusion of clause 8F and G, the Bill's interpretation of political end covers an extremely wide variety of policy matters and issues which may be discussed by Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Public discussions on these issues, invariably, involve the views and voices of foreigners.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: FICA sets a low bar on what constitutes public interest.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
