text: It empowers the Minister to block public discussions if it is, in his opinion, in the public interest to take action.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This gives the Minister for Home Affairs a very wide discretion to authorise Part 3 directions or designate PSPs.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: It could stifle genuine political debate by discouraging Singapore Citizens or local non-government organisations (NGOs) from speaking up, even in good faith, for fear of being issued a directive under FICA or designated as a PSP.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: While the Government might argue that having a directive issued against, say, a Facebook post, is not a death warrant, it carries a reputational risk to the target of that directive.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: It would be very unfortunate if an NGO engaged in advocacy work, for example, speaking up on migrant workers' rights, is designated as a politically significant entity.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I note that MHA has tried to give assurances that this type of activity will not be stopped.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Removing these two subsections will not hinder the Minister from applying the brake on hostile foreign influence operations that could harm Singapore.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Clause 7 already has a list of actions that are contrary to the public interest which the Minister is empowered to authorise Part 3 directions against.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: These include threats to public health, finances, safety, tranquilly, peace and order as well as incitement of feelings of enmity, hatred or ill-will between different groups of people in Singapore which may endanger the public peace and public order of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Setting one race against another or using religion to drive a wedge between religious groups could be considered incitement of feelings of ill-will between different groups of people in Singapore and will already fall under clause 7D.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: A foreign agent promoting harmful falsehoods, for example, about approved vaccines, could be reined in to protect public health under clause 7B.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: In short, our amendments to the Bill will not prevent the Minister from acting against foreigners seeking to do harm to Singapore but they will go some way in preventing genuine political discussions from being stifled either deliberately by the government of the day or, inadvertently, due to their mere presence.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Next, I wish to highlight an area where the Bill does not do enough of, which is preventing elite capture.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: While high-profile influence campaigns tend to hog the limelight, clandestine foreign lobbying of individual elites is, by definition, done in secret.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The most likely targets of this secret influence operations are our political elites.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Many democracies have countermeasures in place to deal with the risk of such influence operations.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: These agents must disclose their agreements with foreign principals, report the funding they have received and provide a log of all activities performed on behalf of the foreign principals.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The Singapore Government would be familiar with FARA because agencies like EBD, STB, Temasek Holdings and the Government itself have already been registered as foreign principals.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: These registrations are transparent to the public and can be downloaded from the FARA website.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Australia has the Foreign Influence Transparency Scheme Act, which has a Registry of Interests.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Taiwan has the Sunshine Acts, which require public officers from the President all the way down to the Administrator for Company Registrations and their immediate family members to make public declarations of their assets, which help combat both graft and foreign influence operations.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: In addition, most of these democracies provide for independent legislative review through regular select committee hearings.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Policy-making in Singapore is highly concentrated in the top ranks of the Government and the civil service.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Many policymakers regularly exchange ideas with one another in informal settings like golf courses and exclusive clubs like the Pyramid Club.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: These are places where informal discussions on policies may take place well before they are discussed in the media or drafted into law.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Yet, in the Bill, the list of defined PSPs excludes senior public officers.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: These officials lead the formulation and drafting of legislation.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: They are the subject matter experts who provide important policy advice to Ministers almost on a daily basis.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The Minister has argued that civil servants are subject to the Instruction Manual and various rules and declaration requirements, which are, cumulatively, stricter than the FICA requirements on PSPs.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This is even more reason to include PSes, DSes and Statutory Board CEOs as PSPs.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: FICA will provide a stronger layer of public transparency, accountability and oversight without making it more onerous on them.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Their names will be made public on the register of PSPs and any foreigner dealing with them will know that they are PSPs and vice versa.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The chairpersons, board members and chief executives of Statutory Boards also have important roles in influencing and implementing Government policies.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I cannot agree with the Minister that it is impractical to define this group as PSPs just because some of them are foreigners.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The fact that many Statutory Board members are foreigners is even more reason to impose transparency requirements so that the public and the Government can be more confident that they are acting in the best interest of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Surely, we can all agree that these decisions must be guarded against any malign foreign influence.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: All these influential individuals should be subject to the same level of scrutiny of their foreign connections as election agents and candidates, the latter of whom are already on the list of defined PSPs but are much less influential in policy-making.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Lastly, central executive committee members of registered political parties are included because they have a role in setting the policy and political positions that parties take into elections and Parliament.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The last part of my speech will focus on the other actions that are essential to our efforts to combat foreign interference and protect our core national interests.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: We need to focus much more on public education and avoid over-relying on legislative measures to curb hostile foreign interference.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This is a point made by the Leader of the Opposition earlier.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Back in 2019, Minister Chan Chun Sing also said that a discerning electorate is the best defence against foreign influence.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Given the growing sophistication in the way foreign powers conduct their influence operations, which Minister K Shanmugam has taken us through in his handouts, we need a whole-of-society approach to counter them.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Sustained public education of both the young and old will help remind us that we are a sovereign nation with our own core interests.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This requires a consciously planned and sustainable approach so that Singaporeans are aware that other countries have their own agenda and our national interests are not necessarily aligned with theirs.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: For example, some countries, to further their own agenda, may insidiously play up their cultural affinity card.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: They may, for example, appeal to Singaporeans of a particular ethnicity to share with their friends their pride in that country's military and economic progress and they might even chastise their own Government for not showing sufficient deference to them.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Yet, the vectors of this campaign may not even realise it.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Issuing directions under FICA to block the transmission of their messages may be like cutting off the head of the mythical hydra.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: A new head will grow again until these Singaporeans are convinced that they have been deceived.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This is not something that a legislative hammer like FICA can easily achieve.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: We need more frank and open discussions about the tactics used by foreign powers to influence our population so that Singaporeans will recognise them and will not unknowingly spread foreign propaganda without realising their goals and origins.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: As a small country which seeks to be friends with all countries, large and small, it is sometimes inconvenient for the Government to front  public discussions and education of this nature.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Some countries might bristle at being called out by the Singapore Government and this could impact diplomatic relations.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Academic institutions, NGOs, researchers and even school teachers should step forward to play a greater role in this national effort.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: These independent organisations and individuals will have more freedom to educate the public or their students without being seen by foreign powers as Government spokespersons.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: They can, therefore, be more candid in sharing their views, even in public forums, without Singapore incurring the ire of other countries.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Government agencies, especially MFA, MINDEF and MHA, should regularly engage these groups and individuals in closed-door sessions to share the Government's perspectives on our core interests, but without dictating what they should or should not do.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: He was later charged and pleaded guilty to lying to the FBI.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The ambassador was later prosecuted in Sweden but acquitted due to insufficient proof.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This could handicap our efforts to weed out hostile foreign influence.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: We cannot rely only on legislation or law enforcement or intelligence agencies to stem foreign influence.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Given the risk that foreign interference poses to a small and open country like Singapore, we need to use more tools in our arsenal to counter it by drawing on a wider range of intelligence, including research and exposure by the press.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: A free press which invests in investigative journalism can shine the light on shady activities as well as inform and educate the public and policymakers about hostile information campaigns taking place on our shores.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: My Workers' Party colleagues and I have proposed some very reasonable amendments to the Bill to prevent over-reach, ensure greater transparency and provide more judicial oversight.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: With these amendments, FICA will retain all its teeth to keep foreign interference at bay while assuring Singaporeans that its fangs will not be used unjustly on our own citizens.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I appeal to this House to seriously consider these amendments and approve them for the benefit of all Singaporeans and our future as a country.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In 2018, I submitted written and oral representations to the Select Committee on Deliberate Online Falsehoods.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I raised the need for us to be mindful of the power of lobbyists with political or commercial objectives, who may fund the spread of falsehoods online and cause divisions in our society.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I expressed that social media and online news websites should be transparent on their funding and/or political affiliations.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I was concerned about sinister campaigners meant to spread disinformation, evoke emotions and provoke reactions to advance a certain agenda.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Intrinsic in what I said, was how easy it was for any foreign principal to interfere in our social compact and political institutions if there are no checks on transparency or accountability.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In this speech, I will focus on foreign interference by electronic communications activity.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: My speech will be in three parts: first, my thoughts on the threshold proof required to best protect our national interests; second, my clarifications in relation to the mechanism to safeguard our collective interests; and third, the importance of maintaining trust and defending the institutions of our country, which I will deliver in Malay.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The foreign interference threat that Singapore faces can take various forms and employ different tactics.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: These tactics evolve over time and are difficult to track.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In New Zealand, the ministry of justice in a statement on mitigating foreign interference stated that: "… due to its covert nature, direct evidence of foreign interference on our democratic system, and its impacts, can be difficult to obtain, and often emerges post-facto." The situation in Singapore is no different.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: By the very nature of foreign interference, direct evidence of the same is very difficult to find, much less to prove.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Often times, if we wait for such direct evidence, it would be too late.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: There are two main categories of amendments which I am concerned with.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: First, the amendments relating to the mental state of mind of the perpetrators in clauses 17, 18, 20, 40 and 75 of the Bill; second, the proposal to introduce a new threshold of proof in clause 21.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It will be too easy for perpetrators to just disclaim knowledge that something is, for example, prejudicial to the security of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Specifically, on the proposal to remove clause 17(2)(a) and clause 18(2)(a), this effectively means that a perpetrator must have in mind a particular foreign country or principal during the activity.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: However, in reality, foreign state or principals are likely to disavow any links to Hostile Information Campaigns (HICs).

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I think it matters less who that foreign principal is, so long as we know that the perpetrator is acting on behalf of a foreign principal.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The fact that one is a puppet on a string is enough; without needing to know or prove who the puppet master is.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This means that the Reviewing Tribunal or the Courts can be guided by past case law and decisions to assess if, indeed, the Minister has fulfilled the legal threshold to issue such anticipatory directions.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: On the contrary, there is no established standard for an “evidence or actionable intelligence” test in the common law or Commonwealth jurisdiction.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Ultimately, I think the Member and all of us here want the same thing – which is, greater certainty and clarity before the issuance of such directions.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In practice, the test on reasonable suspicion is objectively met if there is a reasonable suspicion or belief and that it is in the public interest to do so.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This is based on Court of Appeal cases that have construed the meaning of reasonable suspicion test.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This is based on case law with a judiciary that carries out its duty with no fear or favour.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I now move on to my second part on the clarifications to further safeguard our national interest and Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: First, in relation to clauses 17 and 18 of the Bill, is it a requirement for the perpetrator or accused to actually know that the proxy was indeed acting on behalf of a foreign principal?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: What if he or she does not even know that the proxy was acting for a foreign principal?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Alternatively, he or she may not know that the proxy was acting on behalf of an undisclosed principal.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I ask these questions because it should not be made easy for perpetrators to disclaim actual knowledge in situations when they could or ought to have made reasonable enquiries with the proxy regarding the principal.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This is not an ordinary crime or offence we are talking about here.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The stakes are too high given the harm and prejudice that can be caused to our country.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Second, with regard to clause 16 on determining the purpose of an activity or conduct having regard to the intention or belief of the persons involved, what is the threshold of determining such intention or belief?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Does such belief need to be objectively ascertained on a reasonable basis?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Also, what is the approach, assuming there is more than one or competing beliefs or intentions?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Third, on what is to be determined as covert or clandestine, may I ask the Minister what about communications over WhatsApp or other end-to-end encrypted messaging platforms or communications through VPNs?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: These are widely available and are platforms commonly used.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Do we consider the varying degrees of concealment?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: On the flip side, if there was no attempt at all to hide the prejudicial interference, then I think the perpetrators should still not be allowed to get away with it.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Fifth, I feel that it would be useful for the public to know on a periodic basis the types of threats and attempts of foreign interference made.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In this way, Singaporeans and the public can appreciate the good work done behind the scenes by the men and women of in our Public Service to protect our national interests and, at the same time, maintain and increase public confidence in the Public Service and the Government.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: (In Malay):   Every country takes part in activities to influence, shape perceptions and make decisions in other countries.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: However, these activities reach the level of interference when it is deliberately done in an irresponsible manner to damage the sovereignty of other nations.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: First, our country’s high level of digital literacy means that online intervention campaigns can be carried out very easily.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Therefore, it is right that we, as one country, seek to further strengthen our solidarity and our mutual trust with the Government by reviewing the legal framework to combat elements that want to divide us.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In my English speech, I recounted my experience as a community leader and lawyer when I was providing evidence at the Select Committee on Deliberate Online Falsehoods in 2018.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I stated my concern that social media and online news websites should be transparent in their sources of funding or political links.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: What was inherent in my evidence was my worry that any foreign actor can easily interfere in our country’s politics and disrupt the stability of our social and political institutions.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In fact, many other observers and individuals have voiced similar concerns to the Select Committee, as what was listed by the Minister earlier.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In my role as Vice Chairperson of the Government Parliamentary Committee for Home Affairs and Law, I have also been involved in various discussions and consultations on the issue of foreign interference as reflected in this Bill.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Therefore, the discussion on the threat of clandestine foreign interference has been going on for more than three years and not just recently, as portrayed by the hon Leader of the Opposition, Mr Pritam Singh.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In fact, Mr Singh was also a panel member of the Select Committee in 2018 and he was present during my testimony on 27 March 2018.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Their activities or plans are difficult to detect and sometimes we should take immediate action before it is too late.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: As a lawyer in international cases in Court and arbitration, I had to often accept urgent orders to preserve certain evidence or assets temporarily before the case goes to Court for trial.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: As for this Bill, in order to balance the rights of an individual with our public and national interests, the Bill provides the space and opportunity for the accused to submit appeals and provide evidence to the Reviewing Tribunal that reviews MHA's orders.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I feel that the proposed process in this Act is reasonable.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This is in view of the pressing situation to prevent interference by foreign parties and the adverse consequences to our country and citizens if such interference is implemented successfully.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In this way, no clandestine enemy can divide our plural society.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This is based on the definition grounded in previous case laws.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: But in my experience, for serious criminal cases especially against the country and our entire society, the Ministry will not simply accuse a person without any reasonable cause or proof.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: However, the battle to colonise the minds of our people still exists.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Let us unite and strengthen the trust between us and within our institutions.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: (In English): Mr Speaker, Sir, in conclusion, the law and our public officers operate in the light to protect us, while sinister, clandestine actors operate in the shadows against our collective interest and our country.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Hence, we should even the odds in this fight.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Let us put our trust in the men and women of our Public Service and grant them the tools that they need to uphold their sworn duty to protect our lives and our Singaporean way of living.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Given the nature of FICA, there are, expectedly, numerous questions from various quarters on what FICA is, what does it cover or not cover, who or what is affected by it, how will it change the current operating models of NGOs that are part of a larger global body, or whether FICA will end up as a political muzzle on active citizenry and citizens’ participation in politics.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: These questions are clearly important and should be thoroughly addressed and debated so that all Singaporeans will have a clear understanding of what the Bill entails.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: History is replete with examples of how different states and state-sponsored actors had tried to influence the course of political and social development in other states.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In modern times, foreign influence might take the overt form of Embassies and Foreign Chambers of Commerce lobbying and advocating for their interests.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It may also take the covert form of actions, such as state-sponsored actors conducting black ops and clandestine disinformation campaigns, that sow discontent and distrust between the government and people and discord among citizens on contentious social issues.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Such operations can also create an impression of mass support among the country’s citizens for a foreign country’s position on important bilateral issues.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Such pernicious foreign influence creates a drip effect that can change the attitudes of citizens towards their own government and even towards their own fellow citizens, leading to the destabilisation of the country in the long run and the weakening of its position vis-à-vis that of the foreign country that could be behind, exerting the covert influence.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This is why an open economy and a small country like Singapore needs intelligence and counter-intelligence resources to help manage such threats.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In the hyperconnected world that we are in today, everyone, individuals, organisations and governments, are susceptible to online attacks.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Such attacks can be conducted by hackers who are motivated by monetary gains or by state-linked groups that are trying to make a political statement.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For example, the hacking of Sony Pictures, an entertainment company, in 2014 by the “Guardians of Peace” who supposedly had links with a North Asian nation.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Cyber attacks can even be sponsored by foreign states as part of political espionage to retrieve embarrassing information about politicians or classified government information from rival states.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I know that Singapore has always tried to be diplomatically sensitive when disclosing information on foreign influence.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I do understand the need to be diplomatically sensitive, but if we were to act against the agent of that particular foreign entity, then should we also not make that entity’s identity and activities known so that we can, as a country, take a particular united position against that particular other country?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For example, if Country X is behind certain activities that could be deemed detrimental to Singapore and Country X is known to be popular with Singaporeans, either as a tourist destination or perhaps a country that Singaporeans tend to purchase goods and services from, then exposing this country as a country that does not have Singapore's and Singaporeans' interests at heart might allow us, as Singaporeans, as one people, to take a stand of solidarity and take a position against Country X.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: After all, why would we want to contribute to the economy of a country which is determined to affect Singapore negatively?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I said earlier that Singapore is a small country, and, as a small country, we might not have much of an impact on that particular country’s economy, but it is important to take a principled stand, in a show of collective Singaporean solidarity that you cannot mess with us, you should not mess with us.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: My next point is countermeasures for donor activities funding from overseas sources for NGOs.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Clearly, we should not allow foreign entities to indirectly influence or get involved in Singapore’s politics via donations they make to PSPs.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: What would the Government’s position be if the local chapters of global NGOs happen to be supporting a particular cause that might be regarded as not being fully in alignment with what is best for Singapore?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Because, sometimes, those issues are a bit grey, they are matters that are open to debate and interpretation.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Some of this information could be deliberate attempts by nefarious foreign entities to shape and influence our opinions on certain social and political topics.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In an ideal world, we would be discerning enough to differentiate between genuine information versus attempts to influence.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: But sadly, we are living in a less than ideal world.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: With that in mind, I end my speech in support of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Some Singaporeans might think that this is an arcane and obscure Bill that will probably only impact those politicos who comment on or get involved in politics.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Should we not be spending the time talking about COVID-19 jobs and other bread-and-butter matters?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: They are subtle and we do not notice them and, like the proverbial frog boiling in water, one day, after many of these changes, we will wake up and find that we are no longer living in a democratic society envisaged in that most Singaporean of documents, our Pledge.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: If our rules become more and more tilted, biased and skewed towards the Ruling Party, the government of the day, against critics, alternative parties, or even independent-minded citizens who simply have a point to make in the public square, even at a time when our citizenry is more educated and politically aware than ever before, wither Singapore?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: What will happen is that our politics will become less accountable, less contestable, less meaningful.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The ideas that get raised in the public square may become more and more limited to a narrow field of opinion.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Abuses or mistakes may not come to light or will get glossed over in public debate when they do.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Fear of the enormous discretionary power of the Government may poison political discourse.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: And if all of these things happen to our politics then that will affect our policy outcomes on COVID-19, on jobs, on HDB lease decay, on retirement adequacy, reducing inequality and much else.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The thing about giving the Executive government more and more power in exchange for stability and economic benefits is this: it is that if that government turns rogue one day and that stability and those benefits no longer get delivered, well-meaning patriots and alternative parties may struggle to change that entrenched government because the legal and institutional tools to bring about that change are all stacked against them and, by then, it will be too late.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Some may say that such new laws, like POFMA, have not stifled debate.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: There is still debate and criticism of the Government in the public square.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: It is hard to know what the effect of these laws has been in the past on the quantity and quality of debate versus if these had not been passed.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: That could well happen one day if a Ruling Party in the future, for example, faces a political crisis of confidence and decides to use the most draconian provisions latent in these laws to suppress criticism so as to stay in power.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: That could well backfire and create ammunition for those who want to disrupt our society, those who want to turn people against the state, those who want to turn people against one another.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: No, the first impulse should be to build independent institutions and education amongst our citizens so that we respond as a society to meet that threat, as the Leader of the Opposition alluded to, and he spoke of non-legislative measures.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The Minister is also subject to error, even with the best of intentions, as are all of us.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I am not singling out any party or Minister for blame here.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The Government may respond to such arguments by providing assurances that they will not use the broad powers in FICA in ways that are inappropriate.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: It is a bit like saying that I should give you a blank cheque but I assure you that I will not write a figure on that cheque that is more than what you agree to pay.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The language of the Bill should reflect intent; language of the Bill, not assurances given outside of that language.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Or to follow the Latin expression "quis custodiet ipsos custodes", who watches the watchman?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Surely, foreigners with malicious intent would seek influence over those holding more power, first of all, and that means Ministers.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In the rest of my speech, Sir, I will touch on three broad themes.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: What redress does Singapore have in cases where malign foreign influence succeeds in influencing Government Ministers or even the Prime Minister, and Minister for Home Affairs himself or herself?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Thirdly, on the theme of oversight, I shall explain the rationale for the amendments I am moving to this Bill.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: First of all, Sir, I would like to speak on the danger of foreign interference, or FI, successfully directed at Ministers or even the Prime Minister or Minister for Home Affairs.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Of course, I am not suggesting that that has happened in the past or is happening now, but it could.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: What recourse do Singaporeans have were that to happen?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: What is to be done if the FI is directed at him or her and succeeds?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Some academics refer to such a scenario as elite capture.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: It is not hard to understand why this can happen.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: A malicious foreign actor bent on interference may find that they have more power to influence Singapore’s politics if they can bring a Minister or even the Minister for Home Affairs himself under their influence rather than an Opposition politician.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: For a malicious foreign actor, influencing the Prime Minister and his or her Ministers brings more bang for the buck.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: This scenario is not academic, arcane or improbable.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In the USA, one popular narrative that became a significant political issue, and I am not stating that this is ever true, was that the previous President of the United States had been suborned by a foreign power.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: This unpacks itself into a few distinct questions.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Thirdly, is there going to be a FICA Office under this Bill, along the lines of the POFMA office, staffed by trained professionals who could, in theory, investigate Ministers?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: And if so, how would their independence be established in cases where MHA office holders are themselves the target of investigation?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I do not have the time to elaborate on this here but this is a Workers' Party Manifesto proposal and I spoke about it at length during the debate in this House last year on access to justice, including rebutting objections to the idea.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The office of a public Ombudsman would, if properly designed and resourced, be a good receptacle for public complaints of FI directed at Ministers and would have the organisational independence and separation from the government of the day to be able to investigate Ministers credibly.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Before I leave this subject, I would like to pose two very distinct questions to the Minister for his reply during this debate.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Media reports have described the work of a gentleman residing in Europe who runs a Facebook page that makes frequent interventions concerning partisan politics in Singapore, often to defend the Ruling Party and criticise the Opposition in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Just a short quote from one of his more recent posts: “People often accuse me of bias because I never criticise the Government in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Does this extend to volunteering for the People’s Association, or PA?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The PA works with grassroots advisors who are Ruling Party Members of Parliament or individuals associated with the Ruling Party.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: It does not formally work with Opposition Members of Parliament.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Much of the work of the PA serves to build political capital and visibility for the Ruling Party by way of the Ruling Party Member of Parliament or individual gracing events as the Guest of Honour, being featured in publicity materials and so on.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: This is problematic, given the potentially deleterious effects which such a Part 3 direction could have on the reputations of individuals and entities.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Will the Minister commit to such a timeframe?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: These reportable arrangements are defined broadly and could cover arrangements where the PSP, in her private sector capacity, secures a new foreign client for her business, for example.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The language of the Bill repeatedly states that such arrangements are reportable even if not directed at political ends.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: This would be very onerous to PSPs who depend on doing business with foreigners for a living or for certain individuals who work with foreigners frequently, like academics, for example.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: What will the Government do to minimise the onerousness while maintaining the flow of information that is potentially actionable?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: For example, can the reporting arrangements be made to report on classes of foreign clients and partners, such as, for example, multinational companies in France or academics in Italian business schools, rather than being required to specify each and every one of the names of the foreign individuals or entities which the PSPs have dealings with?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: This still flags out the countries that the PSP has dealings with.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: At this point, I declare my interest as the CEO of an international research consultancy.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I ask this question notwithstanding the fact that my colleague, Sengkang Member of Parliament Ms He Ting Ru, has argued for replacing the Bill’s Review Tribunal mechanism with appeals to the Courts, a proposal I agree with.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Fourthly, in the Explanatory Note on page 205 on defining the offence of clandestine acts of foreign interference by electronic means, one example cited might suggest covert links to a foreign principal would be if the person moves communication with the foreign principal to an encrypted communication platform.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Does communicating with a foreigner on such a platform like WhatsApp, for example, in and of itself, constitute proof that the communication is covert and clandestine?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: To turn to my third and last broad theme, Sir, I am moving amendments to this Bill, specifically clauses 47, 48, 78, 79, 81, 84 and 85.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I do not propose to repeat these amendments here word for word.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: These are set out in the Order Paper Supplement.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: This will allow the public to understand the reasons behind the Government's actions to form their own conclusions about the justifications for those actions.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: This is important because how FICA's powers are used is a matter of public interest and deserves scrutiny.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: These amendments require the Government to publish this information over the Internet in a searchable, sortable and downloadable manner without charge, in the words of my amendment to clause 81 to which other amendments make reference, and this is for the sake of transparency and should be self-explanatory.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: An exception to transparency in publicising the register of PSEs and PSPs is made on national security grounds, but under the amendments moved by my colleague Ms He Ting Ru, this would be subject to appeals to the High Court and judicial review.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In clause 48(1)(b), I am moving an amendment to add the word "reasonable" for the Government’s ability to designate someone a PSP if their employment and activities are not obviously political.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: This enables a person to apply for judicial review of executive action taken against them under clause 48(1)(b).

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The amendment to clause 78 requires reportable arrangements to be made public.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I would add that our call here is for such publicity to be made with due cognisance taken towards commercial sensitivities and individual privacy.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: This call should be seen in conjunction with my earlier suggestion to make these reportable arrangements less onerous.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In general, published information should be concise and focus on key types of foreign interests associated with PSPs and PSEs.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: First, the Government did not say that it would publish the reasons behind their FICA decisions, which my amendments to clauses 47, 48, 81, 84 and 85 require the Government to do.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Second, there is an amendment to clause 48 that requires the Government to exercise its executive discretion in designating PSPs reasonably.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Third, the amendments call on the manner of publishing to be over the Internet in a searchable, sortable and downloadable manner without charge, centralised for ease of use by stakeholders and for accountability.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: There must be rule of law, not rule by law.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: However, the Bill, as it stands, has insufficient independent oversight, enables government over-reach and overlooks real dangers like foreign interference directed at Ministers.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Like all dangers Singapore faces, the solution should never be to simply give the Government more and more broad discretionary powers that can be used against citizens, critics and Opposition parties, among others.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Mr Perera, could I invite you to wrap up your speech, please.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: I wish to speak about their concerns today.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: I will focus instead on two issues: one, the apparently sweeping scope of powers provided in this Bill; and two, the desire for transparency in the Government's administration of these powers.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Youths are understandably worried if their everyday interactions with foreign friends will run afoul of this Bill.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And more precisely, whether any activity or conduct critical of the Government or Government policies and with any shade of foreign involvement, will be hit by FICA.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: If one reads the proposed legislation with its plain meanings, one can, quite naturally, come to these conclusions and concerns.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: But at the same time, a foreign principal with malicious intent to interfere with our affairs can very well exploit, or may already be exploiting, the cover of seemingly innocuous day-to-day activities or conduct, to achieve its insidious objectives.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: That is the whole point of artful interference and manipulation: to operate under cover.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And this could certainly involve a seemingly innocent collaboration with another party.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Let us take an example, a foreign principal can collaborate on a song about vaccines.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: We already have a song, a collaboration, may I add, about 菜饭, "Economical Rice".

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: So, I think we can all agree that a song about COVID-19 vaccines is entirely conceivable.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: The song could be about the supposed superiority of certain vaccines and/or the alleged risks of certain other vaccines.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: If the song is catchy, if it is funny, engaging and sung with passion, it will have the potential to viral, no pun intended.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And the foreign principal can very well do this in collaboration with some other parties.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: A foreign principal can also exploit the pretext of collaboration to create memes, videos, articles, even games, essentially, any number of platforms, to achieve its sinister objectives.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And so, herein lies the central paradox that we have to deal with when we discuss our approach as a people to counter foreign interference.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Because the tactics of foreign interference can be so sophisticated, so clandestine, these efforts slide themselves effortlessly into our everyday lives and can so easily masquerade as normal activities and conduct.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: So, to counter these, we really need to fight these forces where they are, in other words, our laws and actions will have to operate within the realm of everyday activities and conduct in order to be effective.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: It touches a raw nerve and it causes worry, rightly so.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: But the basic point I am making is that, ultimately, we are contemplating laws like FICA, which can intersect so much with the realm of our daily lives, only because the very threats that FICA seeks to counter have invited themselves into our daily lives first, whether we want it or not, and the powers of FICA scoped on the basis of this fundamental reality.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: The real and only threat is insidious foreign interference from overseas, not alternative voices, whether domestically or abroad.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: So, there is a whole toolkit of directions, directives and countermeasures, but all these tactical modalities are, ultimately, to serve a very narrow purpose that FICA is intended for.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Third, the principles of FICA are neither unique nor novel.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: In other words, Singapore is neither the only nor the first country moving such laws.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Their definition of activities "on behalf of" a foreign principal is similarly broad.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: One can also certainly say that Company A in this illustration is working "in collaboration with", in its plain meaning, the foreign government.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: So, Australia has defined these activities quite broadly and the principles behind FICA are really no different.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: I will also note that none of the amendments that the Workers' Party has moved actually touches on clause 5, on what constitutes activities or conduct "on behalf of" a foreign principal.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: So, I am glad to see that the Workers' Party agreed on the definitions in clause 5 of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Having said all these, how can we then assure Singaporeans, nonetheless, and keep their confidence in the Government's judicious administration of FICA?

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: We should recognise that any government, today or in future, as Executive of this and other laws of the land, will be held accountable to the people and by the people in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And, in turn, we, the people, should have a key interest to choose suitable persons who will exercise these powers, any legislative powers, discretionary powers under the law, judiciously and wisely.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Notwithstanding this, secondly, I think transparency and timely disclosure by the Government to the public in its Executive actions under FICA will go a long way towards modulating the Government's administration of the law and keep trust with the public.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: In this light, I agree with the spirit of the amendments to clauses 78, 79, 81, 84 and 85 moved by Mr Leon Perera.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: These commitments generally go further than Mr Perera's proposed amendments which do not cover Part 3 Directions and do not cover some of the stepped-up countermeasures for Politically Significant Persons.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Except for the public disclosure of individuals who are reporting to the Government on their involvement in foreign political organisations and public disclosure of individuals and entities reporting certain arrangements to the Government, these are what Mr Perera has proposed to disclose, but I agree with the Minister that information reported by individuals and entities in general to the Government should not be publicly disclosed if the key intent of transparency is really to hold the Government accountable for its actions.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: At it stands now, clause 116 of the Bill already provide that authorities may make public any designation of Politically Significant Persons and and any stepped-up countermeasures for these Persons, and any transparency directive.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: So, the commitment that the Minister has expressed on transparency goes even further than the clause 116 in the Bill itself.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: In that number one, the Ministry will make public these actions and two, it will include Part 3 Directions against harmful foreign online communications with one exception.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: These proposed amendments will capture the Government's definitive commitment to public disclosure and transparency under FICA and I look forward to the passing of these amendment at the Committee Stage later.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: At this point, I would like to seek some clarifications.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Two, will the reasons for actions taken under Parts 3, 4, 5 or 6 also be published, as much as practicable?

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Three, will the Registry or Registries be accessible online, free of charge, searchable, sortable and downloadable, so as to maximise its intended potential for public education and awareness?

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And four, will appeals made and decided under FICA be similarly published?

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Can the Minister assure that the Singaporean youth working overseas and writing, posting from overseas about his or her racialised experience with previous job searches or employers in Singapore will not be deemed a vector of a Hostile Information Campaign and thus, slapped with some Part 3 Direction under FICA?

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Can the Minister assure that indeed, students, lecturers, academics in our schools and Institutes of Higher Learning here, interacting with foreign students, discussing, exchanging views on any number of political issues will not find themselves subject to designation as Politically Significant Persons?

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Can the Minister assure that patriots, well-meaning Singaporeans who want to lend their own voices to civic discourse here, no matter how critical of the Government and Government Policies, will not be caught by FICA, simply on account of any actual or suspected interaction with a foreigner?

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: The Select Committee on Online Falsehoods heard evidence in 2018 on a troll farm cottage industry in Macedonia.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Macedonian teenagers worked in these farms and subverted the US presidential elections in 2016.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: They might very well have zero actual interest in US politics and it is unclear if they were taking directions from other foreign state players.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: But it was clear that they did this to earn money through advertisements.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: One teenager reportedly earned US$16,000 – more than 40 times the average monthly salary in Macedonia.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: There were even dedicated classes to train young Macedonians in this trade.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: One, the content created by this troll farm were not all "fake news" or falsehoods per se.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: So, not everything can be caught by POFMA.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Second point and equally fundamental is that the Select Committee report came out in 2018.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: We are debating FICA today, three years later.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Indeed, it would be fair to ask, what actually took us so long?

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: But Singaporeans, including youths, are concerned and I implore the Government to double down on transparency commitments as well as constantly communicate on the narrow intent of FICA so as to assure Singaporeans while ensuring that the Government has the wherewithal to effectively protect us against a common threat.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Ultimately, each government will be held to account by Singaporeans through the exercise of our individual democratic rights.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: To end, I would like to touch on Mr Gerald Giam's proposed amendments to clause 8 on what is defined as being "directed towards a political end in Singapore".

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: It is a bit like saying, let us fight with one arm tied behind our backs, or maybe more, because we are worried about the power of having two arms.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: All those are already in clause 7 and so there is no reason why the Minister cannot use those clauses to invoke directions in the public interest.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: I do not believe it is necessary to have such a broad and wide sweeping catch-all clause, which is what we believe parts (f) and (g) are, in order to give the Minister the power that he needs.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: He has already all the power that he needs.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan
text: So, as we debate FICA, I think it is quite clear and we can all agree that the same logic and the same definition should apply to even more nefarious and insidious threats in the online space that can apply to both Singaporeans and foreigners.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan
text: Mr Gerald Giam mentioned clause 7 in FICA, specifically, I think, clause D.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan
text: In fact, it has an additional word, "hostility".

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: Clause 7F leads on into clause 8, where it defines the political end in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: So, I think it is important for us to understand that we want to scope down the Bill to make sure that we focus on the acts that actually cause harm to Singapore, not provide a catch-all phrase inside the Bill for the Minister, if he cannot find anything else to use, to use that as a tool against harm.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: There are specific qualifications for what qualifies as harm against public interest, against public health and so on.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: I have given examples on how, let us say, if there is a threat to public health, the Minister can take action on that.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: There is nothing preventing him in this Bill from taking action and the Bill has many other strong clauses to give the Minister the power to be able to take action.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: So, nothing is preventing him from doing that just because (f) and (g) are removed.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The outcome of such a process where areas of agreement are identified would possess the unique legitimacy of all voices in this House.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The hon Leader of the Opposition started his speech by observing that there are quarters outside this House whose views on this Bill are diametrically different from the Government.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: But what is more important is to make it clear, as elected representatives of our people, where we stand, either together or apart on matters under deliberation – not just the broad strokes but the detailed issues as well.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I had carefully reviewed the proposed amendments of the Workers' Party.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: We only have a few matters upon which we disagree.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It enumerates the areas of public interest, including to prevent any foreign interference directed towards a political end in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The hon Member Mr Gerald Giam wants to be more specific about what is meant by the meaning of this clause.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In my mind, we should equally be mindful of the agreed position of what is not the intention of the clause.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It is not to curtail political activity by Singaporean civil society or politicians.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: There is also consensus on what constitutes Politically Significant Persons and the responsibilities they should assume.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Such persons, because they carry political weight, there is a need to ensure they do not become pawns for foreign influence.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It is noteworthy that the hon Member Mr Gerald Giam wishes to enlarge this list in the clause further to include more classes of people.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The Bill, as it stands, requires the Government to make a case if there is any other person outside the list it feels should be designated as PSPs.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The hon Member Mr Gerald Giam's rendering puts even more people on this list.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: That is to say, this Bill has a net which the hon Member Gerald Giam wants to make larger.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: We are, after all, talking about actions of spies and saboteurs.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The hon Member Assoc Prof Jamus Lim wishes to limit the ambit of the clauses to only criminal acts that the accused knew would be prejudicial to the security of Singapore as opposed to acts that are likely to be prejudicial to the security of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The focus here is on the impact of the accused's action.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: But before that, he has to be proven to be acting on behalf of a foreign principal.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I turn now to the proposed authorisation of the Minister to issue Part 3 directions under clauses 20 and 21.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: There is, again, broad consensus to allow the Minister to issue directions, including anticipatory directions where in his opinion there is online communication activity being undertaken by or on behalf of a foreign principal in or accessible in Singapore to protect public interest.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Here, the hon Member wishes to limit the Minister's powers to circumstances where he secures a higher threshold of evidence of foreign interference instead of reasonable belief or suspicion.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Given the protean nature of foreign interference, this has to be resolved on the basis on which wording protects Singapore's interest.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Currently, the Police powers of investigations are triggered as long as there is reasonable suspicion of a commission of a crime.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The question arises as to why should there be a higher bar to trigger appropriate action when it comes to foreign interference affecting Singapore's security interests?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This House is unified on the point of vesting in the Minister the power to issue the 14 types of directions to various entities – known as Part 3 directions – in particular, to social media companies described in clause 29 to protect public interest.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: There is consensus to vest in the Minister the power under clause 24 to Proscribe Online Locations which would be subject to Part 3 directions.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: There is agreement to criminalise behaviour that involves the making of money or providing financial support to Proscribed Online Locations.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The only difference here, again, based on the proposed amendment by the same hon Member is on the ambit of evidence required to make out the offence.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Again, this issue is a narrow issue that has been dealt with on the basis of which wording would better protect Singapore's interest.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: On the measures of designating an entity or person as a PSP under clauses 80 and 81, there is full agreement on the ability of a competent authority to designate an entity or person as politically significant entities or Politically Significant Persons.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The additional point here, as proposed by the hon Member Mr Leon Perera is that the public list of politically significant entities and persons be maintained unless there is a national security ground, not to name these persons or entities.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: What is proposed here again by the hon Member Mr Perera is for such disclosures to be made publicly available.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: From a practical perspective, it seems to me the sting behind this provision will be to deal with the consequence on the part of the PSP for failing to file the report.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I say this because if a PSP files a report stating that he has dealings with a foreign principal, directed to a political end in Singapore, it is likely to spell the death knell of his political career.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In other words, the publicness of the report maybe neither here nor there.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Turning to the arena of requiring disclosure of foreign involvement in publication of political matters, I know again there is consensus in vesting with the competent authority the power to issue transparency directives to newspapers, broadcasting services and PSPs requiring a disclosure of foreign principals and links.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: There is consensus in the ability on the part of the competent authority to issue directives to PSPs to end their afflictions with foreign principals and foreign volunteers.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The additional suggestion made by the hon Member Mr Perera that is being made here is that to have these directives together with any other modification of cancellation made public.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: There is broad agreement on what constitutes exempt activities, that is activities that should not be covered under this Act.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The hon Member Assoc Prof Lim proposed adding in this list an exemption on the part of Singaporeans exercising their right to discuss politics and foreign individuals and publications commenting on Singapore politics in an open, transparent and attributable way.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I do not disagree that such acts should be outside the jurisdiction of this Bill.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The only issue is whether it is necessary, given that the structure of this Bill already makes it clear that it is not intended to stifle such activities.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: My objective here is simply to point out to the fact that there is much more agreement on significant matters than disagreement.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This may not be apparent to members of public outside this House.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In my view, the most substantive area of difference lies with the redress mechanism under the Bill which I now turn to.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The hon Member Ms He Ting Ru, proposed that appeals be heard hurt by the High Court, with the right of further appeal.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I appreciate that her motivation is to provide checks and balances.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I would respectfully demur with her suggestion although I must acknowledge there are merits to the broad rationale behind her proposal.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: As for my reasons for demurring, I need only refer to my Adjournment Motion speech made recently this House when I spoke about judicial review in March 2021.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Both the hon Leader of Opposition and the hon Member Ms He, kindly referred to some parts of my speech today.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I said then that each generation of political leaders and people must find their own equilibrium on what is acceptable.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: They will also recall that in my same speech, I went on to state that, in my view, the status quo should be preserved for the ISA.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I recounted the point made in 1991 by Prof S Jayakumar, the former Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Home Affairs in this House that when it comes to issues of national security, putting a Court to scrutinise exercise of powers would be tantamount to giving the Court, an unelected body, the final say on such matters.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Also, in my respectful view, since we are dealing with issues of foreign interference affecting public interest, as defined under this Bill, a different form of procedure to ensure the swift and agile handling of cases and judicious safeguarding of sensitive information will be needed.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: (In Malay):   Mr Speaker, first I would like to thank the hon Leader of the Opposition, Mr Pritam Singh for commenting on the speech that I delivered in March.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I said that each generation of political leaders should find and achieve their own equilibrium, of what our people would accept.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The Leader of the Opposition would probably remember that I also said, with regard to the ISA, I am of the opinion that there is a reasonable reason to maintain the status quo as it is a bill that is crucial for the security and stability of our country.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: FICA is a similar Act like the ISA, because we are discussing about national interests and the country's sovereignty being threatened by foreign interference.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Due to this, I can understand why the Reviewing Tribunal should hear appeals in FICA instead of the courts.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This does not mean that there is no protection for an individual.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The courts may still hear appeals and the case if there an overreach in power or in certain matters.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: (In English): The hon Member Ms He referred to the point I made in my speech in March this year on the need for sunlight of scrutiny of Government action.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: She may also remember that I stated then in my speech that ISA did not act and does not act in darkness, having regard where checks and balances embedded in the Act and the Constitution.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I think it is worthwhile holding up again this handout, page 36, which the hon Minister Mr Shanmugam showed us earlier.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: What FICA aims to do is to give targeted powers, and you see that in dark green.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I heard the hon Member Mr Perera saying just now a theory about FICA having some latent powers being embedded which can be used later on by a Government which is malevolently intending to use these powers.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: If that is really the case, it will be better to use the latent powers already embedded in the current Acts.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: You do not have to pass FICA for that.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: So, with respect, I have difficulty following his argument.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Notwithstanding what I said, I have a few questions on the redress mechanism concerning the Reviewing Tribunal under clause 92 of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I also note that the decision is to be made by the President on the advice of the Cabinet.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I seek the hon Minister's explanation on this matter.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Next, may I ask if the Reviewing Tribunal will be a standing tribunal that is appointed at the outset for a period of time or will it be an ad hoc tribunal that is created as and when there is an appeal?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: My preference is that it should be a standing tribunal to ensure transparency.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Moving on to the powers of the Reviewing Tribunal, is it contemplated that the Tribunal will have powers to compel the appearance of witnesses and production of documents?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This does not appear to be specifically referred to in the clauses that I have reviewed.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I now turn to appeals to the Minister against decision of competent authority's decision, designating a person as a PSP or given a directive to comply with on that basis.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: How would the public know that the Minister is not following the Advisory Committee's advice in making the determination on an appeal?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I have argued, however, there is a lot more agreement on the main issues.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I have seen more that unites than divides us.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I acknowledge there is one major sticking point on whether the review should be a political or legal matter.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I argued that, like other matters of national security, it ought to be a political matter and hence should rest with the Minister.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: An important point of agreement, however, is where and how we disagree in such matters, such as public interest.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The PAP and the Workers' Party may disagree on what this interest is, both in substance and form and in the matters, both trivial and significant.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: But we both agree that such discussions must remain our own.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: It is a new piece of legislation and this is one more piece of legislation for which we have an ouster course.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: And would the Member also not agree that there has been no equilibrium sought from the people by virtue of an absence of public consultation as to whether this ouster clause has been considered by the public?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: And the question, as I understand, posed to me, is whether there has been an equilibrium reached within the present generation of political leaders and the people of Singapore on the matter involving FICA, which contains an ouster clause.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: The point I wish to make is this.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: In my earlier speech in March 2021, I have already stated that when it comes to issues of national security, a different approach should be taken.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: What you see here are powers that are already reposed with the Executive.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: In cyberspace, the cyberattacks and hostile information campaigns have increased in complexity and have become more illicit, masking themselves in seemingly innocuous ways.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Therefore, these risks should be actively pre-empted and addressed for the national security of Singapore.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: I believe in the legislative intent of the Bill.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: However, I have concerns about certain aspects, namely transparency and the need for more checks and balances.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Is there a way we can realise and uphold the good intentions of the Bill while at the same time provide some amendments which can address the concerns?
