speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: First, on the possible avenues of check and balances that can be incorporated into the Bill.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Second, on how we can increase the transparency of this Bill.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Thirdly, I will speak on how the definition of foreign principal may bring about potential discrimination which may affect Singapore’s reputation as a global hub.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: First, the Bill grants considerable powers to the Government.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: I understand that in cases of foreign interference, speed may be of the essence and information received must be acted upon quickly.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Moreover, this information may be sensitive and require confidentiality to be preserved.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: However, provisions can be enacted in the Bill to require that sensitive information be sealed or otherwise not disclosed in the Court hearing such as to allow a judicial review to still be carried out.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: We have seen some precedent for this in the treatment of whistleblowing information and whistleblowers' identity in court proceedings.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: If time is of the essence and there is need for judicial reviews under this Bill to be expedited, surely this can also be provided for in the Bill as well.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: A reviewing Tribunal, even if presided by a High Court judge cannot replace the role of judicial oversight.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: We must strive to maintain Singapore’s reputation of holding and protecting the rule of law while recognising the ills of foreign interference.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Second, there have also been concerns about the transparency of the Bill.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: One example is the criteria on who can be designated a Part 4 PSP.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: This is further elaborated on in sections 7 and 8 of the Bill.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: These definitions, though, are still broad and not easily understood by the community.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Section 20 will also grant the Minister for Home Affairs powers to issue directions to various entities such as social media services, relevant electronic services, internet access services, as well as persons who own or run websites, blogs or social media pages, to help the authorities investigate and counter hostile communications activity that is of foreign origin.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Although it does not apply to Singaporeans expressing their own views on political matters, unless they are agents of a foreign principal and it may not be the intent of the Bill to stifle political speech, there are some members of the community, for example, members of academia or humanitarian and advocacy groups who have genuine concerns about this.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: These groups have many foreign connections due to their nature that encourages cross-border collaboration.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: The fear is that their work, which may touch on complex local political issues, and their ties with foreign entities, foundations and states as well as associated funding, may mean that they are at risk of running afoul of the law.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: It may be argued that this does not cross the threshold of “public interest”.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: However, there is a sense of unease on the ground and reasonable concern that the current non-exhaustive way that “public interest” is defined in section 8 would still mean that their activities fall under it.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Could more be done in the wording of the Bill to provide greater certainty to organisations on the types of entities that would be designated a Part 4 PSP and subject to directives, such that it avoids casting a shadow on their activities?

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: After all, unless winter is coming in Singapore, surely it would be in the country's best interest to avoid casting a chilling effect on such complex cross-border research and activities.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: I am also concerned about how our youths have received this.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Youths include Singaporeans, foreigners and PRs among them, interacting together.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: And our youths value the ability to talk about potentially politically sensitive and difficult topics and is increasingly comfortable doing so on an online platform.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Would these regulations give the impression that the Government is discouraging this?

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: If it does, it will cast a shadow on the trust that the youths have for the Government which is something we should guard against.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Youths are our future and trust is essential for governments to effectively lead.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: This is something we should always be vigilant about.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: I fully agree that Singapore must always be prepared against the threat of foreign interference.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Hence, I am glad that three years later, after the recommendations of the Select Committee, discussions in Parliament, conferences, publication and speeches during the Committee of Supply, we are ready to debate this piece of legislation to protect our national interest.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The threat of foreign interference is a global problem and the threat to Singapore is real, is growing and we need to enact strong safeguards to protect our “national sovereignty and security, social cohesion and democratic institutions”.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In protecting ourselves from foreign interference, there are several factors that makes it even more important for this Bill to be enacted.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Sensitive issues of race, religion, foreign workforce versus local hires, can be easily manipulated to sow social discord.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We cannot allow others the chance to destabilise the delicate balance that we have continuously been working on.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: International investors from various industries are attracted to set up operations in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: These are all foreign companies that have established substantial operations in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We value the partnerships we have forged with each one of our trading partners and we seek to continue to be able to balance their needs while propelling our national interest forward.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, the increased Sino-US tensions will invariably affect Singapore.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We will have to be able to assert our neutrality and independence to maintain the balance that we have.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We must prevent foreign interference from destabilising what we have.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We must keep in mind to pursue what is best for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As Minister Vivian aptly said in a CNA interview, there is a big difference between “being useful” and “being made use of”.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We are not isolated from the impact of foreign interferences, as Minister Shanmugam had mentioned earlier.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: With the rise of technology and even more ubiquitous use of social media, these interferences are expected to be more frequent and more sophisticated and they will attempt to sway public opinions and even destabilize the precious balance that we have so carefully cultivated.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I understand that there are some reservations to this Bill.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, let me just point out that such legislation to ensure non-interference by foreign agents are currently already in place in countries such as Australia, EU, US and Canada.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: They have laws to prevent, detect and disrupt foreign interferences conducted through hostile information campaigns and the use of local proxies in their domestic politics.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: These examples serve to illustrate the fact that it is only expected that states will have to protect their self-interests and prevent foreign intervention especially when its intention is to harvest protest potential.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Notwitstanding the above, I wanted to share a concern which was addressed by the Minister in his speech earlier.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: One concern was from foreign businesses and Singaporeans working in MNCs on whether discussions between a Singaporean and non-Singaporean individual on policies which may affect their business may be seen as foreign interference and captured within the scope of the Bill especially if it is done on an online platform.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This has been of particular concern, especially in light of the current labour crunch causing delays and pushing up the cost of doing business.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This labour crunch is brought about by border restrictions, the lack of access to foreign labour and the perceived increasingly anti-foreigner sentiments exacerbated by the current COVID-19 environment.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: (In Malay):   The Select Committee on Online Falsehoods was established three years ago and comprises Members of Parliament from both sides of the House.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: After considering 169 written representations and oral evidence from 65 individuals and organisations, it has concluded that the spread of online falsehoods is a "real and serious problem" in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The Select Committee was also presented with evidence that information operations sponsored by foreign countries were carried out against Singapore.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Since 2018, the threat of foreign interference has been discussed repeatedly in this Chamber and in online media and publications.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It is time that our laws deal with the threat of foreign interference which is increasingly threatening our national security.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: There are other factors that make it important for this law to be implemented.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Imagine, two-thirds of respondents inadvertently believed an article that was manipulated by the study!

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: And imagine if article is manipulated by those who seek to divide our society.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We should and must overcome such online falsehoods, especially when it is done through foreign interference.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The spread of online falsehoods through foreign interference is a real and growing problem around the world.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: One of the ways it is done is by using fake social media accounts to influence and divide a harmonious society by using sensitive matters such as racial and religious issues.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This prompted many Americans to attend the protest with one protester reportedly carrying a gun.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In Singapore, we are not immune from the impact of foreign country intervention.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As we strive to improve the law to address this problem, we should also realise that we can play a role as Singapore citizens.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We must be more careful and sceptical of what we read on social media including the comments and we must not be easily influenced that is not based on truth; especially on sensitive issues which are more easily manipulated to heighten racial discord.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We should check the source of information so that we can get the accurate information.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: If in doubt, we should not share the messages in case we spread the wrong information.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Therefore, this law is an important step that should be taken to protect our national interests and also protect ourselves from being used by those with nefarious intentions.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We have sensitive issues like race and religion which can be easily manipulated by foreign actors to fracture our social cohesion.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As we chart the path for Singapore forward, we need to have open conversations, open conversations with all Singaporeans but protected from foreign interferences which may not be in the best interest of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As such, Mr Speaker, Sir, this is an important step to take.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: As a sovereign country, we must always ensure that there is no foreign interference in our politics and in our political process, whatever the intentions.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: As citizens of this land, we are solely and ultimately responsible for the governance and the future of this country, and we live with whatever the political outcomes and its consequences.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: As key stakeholders in the economy and society, it is in the businesses' interest to see political and social stability in the country and that the democratic processes are carry out in an orderly, transparent and legitimate manner.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: While the intent and purposes of FICA is clear, there are some who still felt that this Bill could make Singapore seem less welcoming of others.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: In a Business Times article on 1 October titled "FICA could affect perceptions of Singapore as global hub", it raised a number of concerns.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The article also questioned a situation in which a multinational company's (MNC) employee is vocal about Singapore politics and policy, whether that would be construed as undertaking on behalf of the MNC and hence will come under the ambit of FICA.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Thirdly, the article also mentioned that FICA "is designed such that there will be little opportunity for the Courts to interpret and define the scope of its provisions", unlike the Common Law.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Can I ask the Minister if he could address those issues raised and whether there is a basis to be concerned that FICA could impact our status as a global hub?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mr Speaker, having heard the speeches of several Members of Parliament, my overall feeling is that we have one key consensus on this Bill, and that is: we do not want external forces to interfere with our internal affairs and weaken our sovereignty as an independent country.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Our own affairs should be resolved by ourselves and there is no need for foreign political forces to interfere.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Some of them may even harbour ill intentions.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: In the recent US elections, we have seen from media reports of alleged foreign interference during the elections.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: During the 2018 Yellow Vest movement in France, the French government was also aware of the presence of clandestine foreign interference that exploited existing social conflicts to stir up public resentment and incite riots.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: During the 2019 unrest in Hong Kong, the Hong Kong government repeatedly mentioned that the demonstrators had received funding from foreign organisations.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Of course, the business community also hopes that Singapore's economy and society, as well as the democratic process can develop steadily, and that our society will operate according to the rule of law and public opinions, and not be influenced by external forces.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: However, some business, especially those that often do business overseas, still have concerns about this Bill.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Singapore is a small island state, lacking a large and high growth domestic market.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Hence, our economic development strategy must be open and connected to the world.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: It is only natural for local companies to seek business and growth opportunities through internationalisation and cross-border operations.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Singapore companies that do business overseas will inevitably have dealings with organisations that are connected to the local Government or semi-Government organisations.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Sometimes, they may also have exchanges with these local entities in cultural, educational or ancestral matters.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Some of these companies support various exchanges between the two countries in the form of sponsorship, charity or donations.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: For example, at anniversary celebrations, trade associations or clan associations may receive congratulatory support from foreign organisations or receive goods, sponsorships and donations according to etiquette.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Not all businesses are familiar with the intricacies of FICA.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Some are concerned that they may inadvertently be caught under the new law.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: We all know that in the eyes of law, ignorance does not mean you are not guilty.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Hence, they are worried that their past interactions and future engagement with overseas organisations might cause them or their company to be listed as being politically influenced.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: I hope that the Minister can give a more detailed and simpler explanation of the coverage of this Bill, what is allowed and not allowed.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: It is best to illustrate with situations that we often encounter, for example, how the authority designates individuals or organisations as "politically significant persons/entities".

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Given that the conditions in different countries are different, will there be room for flexibility under the Bill?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Will the Government set up a consultative mechanism to allow companies to discuss and communicate with relevant authorities so that the business community can better understand the purpose of the Bill?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: In this respect, I feel that if trade associations can participate more in the communication, the objective of the Bill can be better achieved.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Businesses in overseas markets often have to follow local customs and contribute in many ways to the local community and society.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: These acts of kindness are sometimes recognised by the local government.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Here, I would like to seek clarification on these matters too.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I will first address some of the points made by Members of the Workers' Party.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Pritam Singh spoke about the need for engagement and responding to feedback, but it appears to me that the Workers' Party has really not substantively engaged with anything that I have said.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I explained in detail in my opening speech where we agreed and also where we disagreed and why.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I replied on many of the points and why some of the proposed amendments will not work.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He also referred to the concepts that were recently affirmed by the Court of Appeal in Nagaenthran a/l Dharmalingam.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: These are the principles that underpin much of our success.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I said in my speech, the starting point is that the rule of law is fundamental to our existence and our well-being as a country.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And that is shown in our consistently high rankings on law and order indices and our good international standing.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is also fundamental to ensure that we have good investments; low unemployment; healthy economy.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But as I also have explained, we have never taken an absolutist approach.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And if you take a dogmatic absolutist approach, it will not work for us and it is not working for many other countries.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You can come to this House and have soaring rhetoric.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Rhetoric has not solved the Gitmo problem of the United States.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: President Obama said, "The choice between liberty and freedom or security.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Why is it that we continue to be colonised in our minds that there is only one way of doing things properly?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I said what is the answer to the problems we have – practical answers, not just rhetoric.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I said we need to see how checks need to be made suitable for the context and the risks we face.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I said how are you going to deal with the risks of leaks in open Court hearings or in-camera?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: What are the objections to the Tribunal chaired by a High Court Judge?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, what we had was not a debate because we are not dealing with these points.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Parliament is not just a forum for reading out speeches with an intent of putting it out in social media eventually.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Or do they accept that these are needed?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And, if so, why do they say we should not deal with the issues relating or covered by FICA, some part of it, through a Tribunal, given the National Security considerations?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Is it the Workers' Party's position that all these tribunals established under all these laws that Parliament has approved should be abolished because it offends the principles of separation of powers and the rule of law?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If we did not and if we did not have the rule of law in Singapore, I would not be here, Mr Singh would not be here, this Chamber would not look this and Singapore would not be like this.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In fact, none of you would be here.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The reason we are all here is because this is a country run according to the principles of rule of law.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We do not mind listening to lectures on rule of law but we subscribe to them too.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: All the laws that have worked well for us.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We would have to subject all our laws to judicial review.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In matters of national security, immigration, religious harmony?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, it is not a reflexive answer each time there is a problem to say that there is only one solution.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The point is, as I have said, what is the problem?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: What is the best solution for this particular problem?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: How do you make sure that the Government is given sufficient powers and how do you make sure that there are checks and balances?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, there are the risks, and the checks and balances.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Why are countries in Western Europe, the United States being opened up by foreign adversaries?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: All the evidences that we have seen in our list.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Why is it that they are so open to foreign attacks?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Is it because they do not have the technology?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There is such thing called political will and political courage and there will have to be a recognition that judicial process will not be appropriate.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, Parliament is not just a place where you come and because you see that there are some people who are saying certain things, you resort to rhetoric without offering real suggestions.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It requires some courage to say this is a problem and we will deal with it.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This is the way we will deal with it and offer solutions.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And in so far as I have seen, the solutions: I have explained why the High Court process, open court process does not work, and I have heard nothing in response.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Courts themselves, have recognised their limitations in such matters.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In Chng Suan Tze, the Court of Appeal recognised that where a decision – say the ISA detention – was based on national security concerns, judicial review of that decision would be precluded.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Court acknowledged that what national security requires has to be left to those responsible for national security, that would be the Executive.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And in such situations, we have found alternative ways of providing for checks and balances with the view that we must maintain accountability.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: What happens if the Prime Minister or the Minister for Home Affairs are suborned?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Well, what happens in any other country if a prime minister or minister for home affairs or any other minister is suborned?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In the case of the US, have we seen the United States Supreme Court intervene?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But do you expect the people as a collective body to deal with day-to-day problems of foreign interference?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That is why we are elected and we are in Parliament here to debate what is the best way possible for the people.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We have had consultations for three years now.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Singh read out an answer given by Second Minister Josephine.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We have to bring people in, and this is what we have been doing from the Select Committee hearing.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: For three years we have been doing that: conferences, Select Committee hearings for over eight days, if I recall rightly, discussions in Parliament, speeches, extensive discussions.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In fact, if this Government had not stuck to those principles, fundamentally, and had not recognised that that is the foundation of our existence – rule of law, separation of powers, doing things according to the law – we would not be here.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: PAP would have been long out of power but Singapore would not be here.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, yes, Executive powers must be subject to checks and balances.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The question is in what form and that depends on what is appropriate for the situation.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: When the Courts are not suitable, we have introduced other types of bodies or tribunals with statutory imposed safeguards.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The further safeguards here, like requiring a Supreme Court Judge to consider the matter.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I have taken this House through various pieces of legislation, where we have vested powers in tribunals as an alternate to the Courts as a form of check and balance.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And we also have a series of cases where ouster clauses have been upheld by the Courts.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: These relate to areas which are traditionally regarded as non-justiciable.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: National security and foreign relations are classic areas.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Ms He Ting Ru made some points on the Tribunal: the scope of what they can review and their independence.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: She seems to be under the mistaken impression that the Tribunal’s remit is narrow.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And the Tribunal, chaired by a Supreme Court Judge, will look at sensitive intelligence and information.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Perera, I think, called it the Government-appointed Committee.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Singh pointed out that under clause 99(2)(b), the Tribunal will be able to consider a matter, without the appellant being given full particulars of the conduct which is the subject to the appeal.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But I also explained why sometimes we cannot give the full evidence.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I said that in my opening speech which Mr Singh did not refer to at all.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There might be times when the evidence would have to be given to the Tribunal for it to look at and decide for itself whether it makes sense to make the orders and it is proportionate to the kind of orders that can be made.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We are not talking about the liberty of the individual.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Also, clause 99(2)(f) allows the Tribunal to give a summary of any evidence to the appellant.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Singh highlighted the importance of education about foreign interference and its dangers.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I have explained that FICA is part of a comprehensive strategy to deal with foreign interference.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Powers under FICA are only part of the picture and I have said that it is a calibrated piece of legislation to allow us to act surgically against threats.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Besides legislation, we have been and will continue to strengthen other defences – detection and response capabilities, Singaporeans’ ability to discern legitimate and artificial online discourse, though that is going to be very difficult, to counter the threat of foreign interference.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: On public education, the Government has introduced various programmes.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Digital Media and Information Literacy Framework was launched by MCI in 2019.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It educates the public on using information responsibly and the risks and benefits of technology.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Source, Understand, Research, Evaluate Programme by the NLB educates the public to be responsible producers and consumers of information.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Media Literacy Council also runs programmes to promote responsible online behaviour.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And we have had extensive communications efforts over the past three years, which I have detailed.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Giam is right that a whole-of-society effort is required for public education.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, we will welcome everyone's assistance in helping to engage and educate the population.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But these efforts have to be complemented with laws, which is the focus of FICA.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: At the same time, this is something that has been considered at length for at least three years.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We have engaged the media to put out examples to increase awareness of the threats happening around us.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We have also engaged various stakeholders since 2019 and their feedback had been incorporated into conceptualising the Bill: Internet companies – over a period since 2019 and senior lawyers, academics, security experts, students – many of them were closed-door discussions; some were open Panel discussions.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, it has been going on for three years which is what Minister Josephine Teo mentioned.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think, perhaps, Mr Singh misunderstood that to mean that it will be post whatever she said some months ago.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: What she meant was during this entire period.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Local academics have also written various commentaries and these were published online.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Some of them were mentioned in Annex F which was distributed earlier.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Articles have been published, written by security experts from RSIS.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Moving on to foreigners who comment on Singapore politics and whether they are liable.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Again, I think he either missed it or was not listening to my speech, I dealt with it in my opening speech.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: A foreign commentator putting out his name and commenting is unlikely to be called "covert" per se.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Depends on the facts and I said this arose from something that Assoc Prof Jamus Lim had put out in the context of his amendments.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If a foreigner puts his name, writes articles, people can assess for themselves what is the weight to be attached.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It probably will not come within the proportionality test.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But depending on the facts, there is some covert action, some other factors, or the intensity or the nature of the matter, there are a variety of factors to be considered.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The other 60 pages are the Explanatory Statement which is to help Members and Members will know more than half it, as I said, is based on the Political Donations Act (PDA).

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Now, I will go on to the points made by other Members that I have not touched on.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Members brought up questions and suggestions in five main areas.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Second, the scope of the Bill and its application.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Leong Mun Wai asked why is FICA necessary when we already have extensive powers and substantial resources to deal with foreign interference.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I have, in my speech, pointed out how the Internet has opened an entirely new front for hostile action.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Assoc Prof Jamus Lim asked how MHA came to the conclusion that Singapore was being attacked in 2018 when Facebook’s assessment was that there had been no cases of foreign influence operations targeting Singapore since 2017.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We do not know how Facebook makes its assessment and whether it depends only on Facebook.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We look at the wide variety of communication tools.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Based on the information we have available to us, we reached a different conclusion.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And I would say to Assoc Prof Lim, matters of our national security should not be outsourced to private companies and they should not be made to decide what our fate ought to be.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Dr Tan Yia Swam and Dr Shahirah made the point that there are extensive powers given to the Minister and that provisions are not clearly defined.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Xie Yao Quan asked that we explain the targets of the Bill and how the law will be applied, especially with regard to young people.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Various Members, several Members have asked if FICA would affect various types of foreign interactions with academics, businesses, NGOs, clan associations, whether there will be a chilling effect on freedom of speech.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I mentioned this in my speech earlier; I will just summarise.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As long as these are done in an open and transparent manner and not part of an attempt to manipulate our political discourse or undermine public interest such as security.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It will also not cover Singaporeans expressing their own views.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It goes without saying Singaporeans have every right to speak up on our domestic politics.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They are also free to engage in advocacy.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Louis Ng and Mr Zhulkarnain asked how the Government decides what is covert or deceptive.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is an assessment that has to depend on many factors.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: No different from many of the other things that the Government does.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Primarily, we have to examine the behaviour of the actor involved.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Indicators of covert or deceptive behaviour will include attempts to mask their tracks, misrepresent their identity, attempting to launder their narratives by having them amplified by sympathetic or unwitting locals.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Tactics will continue to evolve and become more sophisticated, and I even attempted to set out the full list of tactics or factors that might be used or need to be considered.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In response to Mr Zhulkarnain and Mr Perera's questions on the use of encrypted messages, VPNs and so on, use of such services is common.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The fact that communications is private, on its own, would not make it hidden or covert.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The use of such messages or VPN to intentionally avoid detection could be a factor in an assessment but it really must be taken into account with all the other facts and circumstances and the legal requirements set out in the law including proportionality.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Zhulkarnain asked in relation to the offences in clauses 17 and 18, why we should allow an individual to "get away” if there is no covert or deceptive behaviour.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I had previously said that this Bill was calibrated, and this is one example of how.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There is a line, a fine one, between a campaign to persuade and a campaign to manipulate.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: When campaigning is done openly, Singaporeans know who the content is from.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They are able to make up their own minds and are free to agree, disagree, depending on whether they are persuaded.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, in our view, that should not be criminalised.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But separately, directions can be given against a foreign party, depending on whether the thresholds have been crossed, which I explained earlier.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Leong Mun Wai said someone can be arrested, no reasons given, and if the evidence is offered later, the Government is not entitled, or not obliged to reveal a source.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, you can be detained, trialed in absence, and there is no judicial review for all the actions taken against you Now, this one, of all the things that have been said today, this one takes the cake.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I do not know if he has read the Bill.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Or if he has read it, I do not know if he has understood it, because I think we are talking about two different Bills.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: All of these statements are completely untrue, so I do not know what Mr Leong has read.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I will ask him to read the Bill carefully and also ask him to make some preparation before he comes to Parliament and also listen to what is going on in Parliament, including the Minister's speech.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, to suggest that someone can be detained, trialed in absence, no judicial review?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I do not know where he got these ideas from.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It brings to mind another debate we had a few weeks ago, but this one goes further.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There is the power to give some directions, so perhaps that might help him change his mind on the Bill now that we know that he has been talking about some other Bill.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: These clarifications also address Assoc Prof Jamus Lim’s concerns on whether we will charge those who were duped into committing harmful activities.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In such circumstances, the elements of an offence would not be made out.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There would be no basis for any criminal action.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The question really is what kind of powers are needed and how we make the processes work.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Murali Pillai and Mr Louis Ng asked how do we select and appoint members of the Tribunal and the rules that will be set out, including whether the Tribunal will provide written reasons for their decisions.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Zhulkarnain asked if there are safeguards to ensure that the Tribunal does not disclose information they have access to during the proceedings.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There will be a few discrete and fixed panels set up, members will be selected for their areas of expertise, they will have to undergo security vetting because they will be receiving highly classified and highly confidential information.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They must be people with experience and standing, just like any other tribunals or independent committee, like the ISA Advisory Board.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Members will be given the same protection and privileges as a Supreme Court Judge and they must protect secret information, under the Official Secrets Act.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Pillai raised the concern on separation of powers and suggested consulting Chief Justice for the appointment of the Chairperson rather than for the Cabinet to advise the President.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: While it is not written in law, that is the way Supreme Court Judges are appointed to panels.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We consult the Chief Justice and he suggests some names.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I have spoken to the Chief Justice to suggest some names.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We will work out the specific rules for the Tribunal in the coming months as subsidiary legislation.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Some broad principles: (a) the Government will have to present the evidence to convince the Tribunal; (b) Tribunal will have powers to call witnesses and compel the production of documents; (c) information will be disclosed to the appellant to the extent that it is not sensitive from a national security perspective; (d) the Tribunal can take an inquisitorial approach when the information cannot be given to the appellant and (e) the Tribunal will decide whether to uphold or overturn directions.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Zhulkarnian asked about the expeditious proceedings of the Tribunal.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Tribunal can consolidate and hear similar appeals as a single case, or they can take one case as a reference point that will apply to other similar cases.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They can also dismiss frivolous or vexatious appeals.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Rules of the Tribunal will be set out in subsidiary legislation and the key features drawn from reviewing bodies in other laws.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Pillai asked why is the Minister, and not a reviewing tribunal, the appealing authority for PSP decisions, and why there is no requirement, similar to the Tribunal, for the Minister to review the appeal expeditiously.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think Mr Perera may have raised the same question.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The level of authorisation required for various powers is calibrated based on the impact of the directions and countermeasures.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: PSP directions are targeted in their applications and scope.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They are issued to a specified individual or entity.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The impact of the directives are limited to that person or entity and compared with a HIC.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The appropriate appellate authority is therefore framed by reference to the level of authorisation and the respective direction appealable to the next level of authority.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Liang Eng Hwa asked for more details on the process to how a Competent Authority can designate someone as a PSP, and whether businesses can take rectification measures to remove their designation as PSPs.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The processes for designation and appeal are spelt out in clauses 47 to 49 and clauses 100 to 102 of the Bill.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Being conferred with an honorary title or degree by a foreign state or University alone is unlikely to be sufficient grounds for designation as a PSP.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is not FICA's intent to stop these types of interactions and activities.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But, again, we will look to see whether there is an attempt by a foreign actor to cultivate a Singaporean to undermine our national interest.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The committee will comprise third parties to render advice to the Minister.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In response to Mr Louis Ng's question on whether individuals will receive written responses to explain decisions made by the competent authority on designating PSPs, this would be done as the specific activities that qualified them for designation will have a direct impact on how the controls will apply to them.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: For instance, a designated NGO that advocates on a variety of issues will have to report donations that it specifically receives for its activities that are directed towards a political end.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The explanation will be important in setting out which are its activities of concern and those would be the donations that have to be disclosed.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Louis Ng asked if MHA will release guidelines and illustrations that can facilitate compliance by good-faith actors.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Liang Eng Hwa asked if there will be engagement to help businesses navigate how FICA applies to them.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: A recipient of a direction who fails to comply, can be prosecuted.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We agree with the intent of Mr Ng's and Mr Liang's questions, there is a need to help good faith actors comply.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We will continue to engage stakeholders including tech companies and Internet access service providers to understand their capabilities and constraints, identify suitable modes of compliance and we will continue to work with our stakeholders to operationalise.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The exact mode of compliance with disclosure and declaration obligations and other requirements from counter-measures that they may be subjected to will be articulated in subsidiary legislation.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But the vast majority of foreign dealings between Singaporean companies and their business counterparts will continue unchanged.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Xie Yao Quan asked where will Part 3 directions be published and whether the reasons for actions taken under Parts 3, 4, 5 and 6 will be published.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Zhulkarnain suggested giving a report on the FICA offences or directions without the need to go into specific details or naming the foreign principals.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Darryl David suggested informing the public when there is sufficient evidence that there is foreign interference and said we should make the entity's identity and activities known so that we can take a united position against such a country.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We have taken the approach to not name the foreign state actors whom we suspect to be involved in these foreign attempts.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There are wider national and foreign policy considerations in doing so.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: However, we will alert Singaporeans when such communications activity has been detected and if FICA directions were issued to block and contain such foreign interference.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As Mr Xie has pointed out, national security concerns may make it impracticable to publish the reasons for actions taken.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Where possible, we will inform the public on the broad grounds for issuance of directions.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In response to Mr Xie's question on whether appeals made and ruled under FICA would be published, we can consider, although it would depend on the facts and circumstances of the case.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The more sensitive the information used, the less likely we are able to do so.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Xie suggested making the Registry of Foreign and Political Disclosures accessible online, free of charge, in a searchable, sortable and downloadable format, to maximise its potential for public education and awareness.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Zhulkarnain pointed out that it is easy for a person to deny that he is aware of the purpose of undertaking an activity and asked for the threshold in clause 16 in determining that a person has intention or belief to undertake the activity for a particular purpose.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He also asked if a person would be held liable if he was not aware that he is acting on behalf of a foreign principal.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Given the sophistication of threat actors, this is more than likely.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And making out that case would be the job of our law enforcement agencies.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Referring to clause 49, Mr Louis Ng asked for clarification on what would not be practicable or desirable for individuals to have the opportunity to be heard.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Also, if we have received intelligence that a target for designation may already be compromised and counter measures are required immediately to mitigate the threat, it may not be desirable to wait for the hearing before designation.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: These are important to ensure that Singaporeans continue to make our own choices on how we should govern our country and live our lives.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There is also the question of the Petition as I said in my Second Reading speech.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I will start with the first which covers the Second Minister for Home Affairs, Minister Josephine Teo's comments at this year's Committee of Supply.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: It seems to me that it is not a misunderstanding of this but it is probably more accurate to say that, that does not seem to be an answer as to why the Bill could not be put before public consultation, like other Bills are.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: This is an omission for which I do not think we have heard any responses yet.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: The second point pertains to the role of the Courts, which I think is the fundamental disagreement between the Government and the Workers' Party (WP)'s position is the oversight mechanism.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I think there is scope to discuss some of the other points and I think Minister has agreed with some of our amendments but Minister referred to the case, the 1988 case of Chng Suan Tze v Minister for Home Affairs.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I refer to the Constitution of the Republic of Singapore (Amendment) Bill.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: A debate that took place on the 25 of January 1989 and it also dealt with, the main debate also dealt with Internal Security Act (ISA) (Amendment) Bill, which sought to abolish appeal to the Privy Council in case of review of ISA cases.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Then, Minister K Shanmugam, as a backbencher said the following and I would start with the reference to Chng Suan Tze and Minister said, "It will be useful to consider exactly what the Court of Appeal said.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: It did not say that it can itself decide whether or not the detainee posed a threat.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: The Court said that it can consider, within broad parameters, whether or not there was any ground at all for the detention.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: It will set aside the detention only if there were absolutely no grounds for the detention, that is, it takes the view that no one in his right mind could possibly have concluded that the detainee posed any threat to national security.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Otherwise, it will not interfere with the Minister's decision.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: This Government believes it has never abused the ISA and there is nothing to fear.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: The Government works on the basis that the persons in Government should be upright, moral and only do what is good for the country.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Thus, the people have nothing to fear, despite the powers that the Government has.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: These powers will never be abused because they are so effective, they help the Government govern effectively for the greater good of all.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: So, that has worked." And Minister says this, "But can we be sure that down the road, the situation will be the same?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: We cannot guarantee that the future government will comprise of honourable men." Minister then goes on, "An argument, therefore, can be made out that there must be checks and balances within the system.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: And I was listening very carefully to the other People's Action Party (PAP) Members who spoke and I compared the speeches of those Members with the PAP Members who spoke in 1989.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: The Minister was not the only one who was concerned about an appeals mechanism or other appeals mechanism and that there be appropriate checks and balances.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I am not going to go through the entire debate, but I think the point is, the WP does not understand at the very base level, why it has to be limited judicial review in this case.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I think Minister gave some reasons and the Minister referred to leaks – that there could be leaks in the system, when you go to Court.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: So, that question, I think if you ask me on balance, should a Court at least look into and review the decision of the Minister?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Should judicial review be allowed to be captured in its entirety by a Court of Law?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I think the answer is yes and that is a fundamental difference.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Notwithstanding this, Minister makes the point about national security and so forth, which is why the Workers' Party Members have proposed potential in-camera hearings and files can be sealed after that as well.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: My third clarification, Sir, is a bit more specific and this pertains to designated PSPs.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I am not sure it is appropriate for me to direct this question at Minister because it would probably be more appropriately directed at the other office holders in MHA who spoke on the Bill and this is with regard to designated PSPs.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Let us assume there is a cause-based, a single cause-based NGO in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Their cause is, they are very aghast at the idea of foreign workers being transported at the back of hard-top lorries.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: This is their single cause, they are all Singapore members and they regularly write to their Members of Parliament and encourage their Members of Parliament to bring this issue up in Parliament.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Let us assume this NGO receives foreign funding.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: It receives foreign funding from another International Organisation, whose main object is that they seek to ensure and uphold the human rights of foreign workers all over the world.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: That means will the Competent Authority say, "No, sorry, you cannot receive this funding." Because, I know under stepped-up countermeasures, you can do that.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Because this has knock-on implications for other arguments that the Government and other Members of Parliament have made.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: If you work with climate activists, for example, there is an international solidarity movement on certain issues.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: How will this be addressed and considered by FICA?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: This, I hope explains Mr Gerald Giam's amendments for clause 8(f) and (g), as to how do we balance this exercise.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Because if you compare clause 8(a) to (e), there is a very clear target – legislature, presidential counsels, trying to change the laws – but the last two limbs are far more broad and that also explains why the Workers' Party proposed additional oversight arrangements.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: On what the Second Minister said, I thought I was quite clear.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: What she was saying and this is an answer I myself looked at, previously.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We have seen the experiences of other countries.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We have to consider what further measures are necessary.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: For example, what levels of transparency in funding, support and leadership and for whom?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The public has a big part in this to shape the proposals on these further measures to give the eventual safeguards their strongest support.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: What have we been doing with the public for the last three years?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In fact, we have taken into account the viewpoints that have been given to us by a wide variety of actors.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We need to bring the entire society together.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We need to do a lot more to bring and shape public thinking.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, there is a long haul ahead of us and the public has to be involved in that.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The public has been involved, primarily, experts, in the thinking through of the Bill too.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: To take that and say – that means for the drafting of the Bill, the public will be involved and how come it was not involved – that is a misreading of that statement.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Let us go to the second question, which I think is the crux of the difference between the Government and Mr Pritam Singh and his party.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I did not only say it in 1989.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If you went back and checked, I think I have said it at various points – 1989, 1990.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I have said it just for the record since it is all in Hansard anyway.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I have said it in respect of the original MRHA.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I have said it in respect of the CLTPA and I have said it in respect of the Internal Security Act.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I have given this answer to your colleague, Mr Dennis Tan, when he asked me, probably trying to suggest that I am being inconsistent.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: A person who is prepared to be thinking about issues sometimes has to change his views when he is faced with the real world and experiences.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In 1989, I was a lawyer four years out of law school, four years after being called, and like many other lawyers, my assumption was every problem, the solution is in the Courts.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Just like Mr Pritam Singh and others, I also take the separation of powers very seriously.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The constitutional principles, the independence of the judiciary, all of these, I take very seriously.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I believed in it, I believe in it and I believe we try and uphold it.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, any time when there is an approach that seeks to cut back on judicial review or take away the powers of the judiciary, my instinctive reaction is negative.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I do not like it, I do not want to do it and I instinctively try and see if there is a different way of doing it.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Which is why when the MRHA was originally brought in, I expressed my discomfort within the bounds of what is possible for the backbench Members of Parliament of the ruling party.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Likewise, I expressed my concerns about the CLTPA.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Likewise, I expressed my concerns about the Internal Security Act.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Likewise, today, I said, if we can find a better model, I will be the first one to do it.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think, Mr Pritam Singh, based on what he says, he obviously does not deny that there will be leaks.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Do you want us to take the risks?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Will there be a possibility of a leak with a Tribunal?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: To the point of being close to zero.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You look at the way the Americans have dealt with it.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You see the issues around the world where lip service is paid to all these grand concepts but the societies live in utter misery, where rule of law is a concept for lawyers but it does not operate in the real world.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, I look at all of this experience practising in the Courts and too many years as a Member of Parliament.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Long conversations with the late Mr Lee Kuan Yew, discussing, I would say arguing though it is not easy to argue with him, discussing, tough discussions and then I began to understand the meaning of his original speech to the Law Society when he said, "Law and order, I reverse it.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Order first, before law." Because if you do not have order, you cannot have law.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: When we all read it, we think we understand it.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But I do not think we really do.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You need to really imbibe what is the meaning of that.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If you cannot have the CLTPA and arrest the gangsters, how are you going to have law?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But if you can bring order into society, then your law will take full effect.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is halved and the reason is as society develops, as society progresses, as there is stability, as there is order, the law takes stronger and stronger roots.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If you get that wrong, you will neither have law nor order.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, I began to understand why we have a strong commitment to the rule of law, a strong commitment to the separation of powers and at the same time, in specific areas, there are some exceptions.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: For example, I said the Land Acquisition Act.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Your property could be worth millions of dollars.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Government could acquire it and you could be asked to leave.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is a social policy and there is a need for that.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You look at all the countries in the post-colonial world.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They inherited the institutions from the British – a civil service, a judiciary, laws, schools, education.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Most of them have gone down the tube while they have grand rhetoric.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: What has Mr Lee and his team done with it?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Built up our civil service so that it is a strong, outstanding, excellent civil service.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Built up the other institutions, including SAF, the Police force, our education system, our middle class.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But making the exceptions where necessary and I took you through the exceptions.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: To me, the best example of how this operated in practice is when I saw how the Americans were struggling with it.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They had an ideological commitment to due process.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But then, they have these, I do not know, hundreds or a thousand plus terrorists whom they do not want to give a trial to.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: America was never under an existential threat as a result of 9/11; never like the threat that we faced.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But when they did it, they said Guantanamo Bay is in Cuba, our rules and laws do not apply there, there is no due process, we lock them up and we throw away the keys.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That is why I said, let us get out of this colonisation of our minds.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Let us look at what works, what is fundamental.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But what is wrong with the checks and balances we have built in here?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, yes, I am not embarrassed to say that I had certain views, straight out of law school the first four years.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The only mistake is I should not have become a Member of Parliament when I was 29 years old.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But I am not embarrassed to say those were my views and those views have changed because of the realities of life, not because I became a Minister but because over time, long before I became a Minister, I saw how laws are meant to operate and where the exceptions have to be made.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Because Singapore believes in the law, so we put forward the law, we give ourselves legal powers, but in reality, the kind of threats we face, the kind of adversaries and the resources they have in terms of manpower are far greater than what we have.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, that, and our people have not even begun to realise what the problem is and the nature of the problem despite all the speeches and the conferences and the seminars and the Select Committee hearings.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If anybody else from the Workers' Party wishes, I will give you the references to my different speeches where I have expressed my views so that I do not have to keep coming back to the speech once every year or two years.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: On the first point about Second Minister Josephine Teo, I stick to my position that I do not believe it was a misreading.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I think I can leave that at that.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: The point about judicial review, again, that reflection of how one's views changes over time is not something that I take lightly.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I think all of us go through such a catharsis in our lives as we build up a crucible of experience.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: But I would like to ask whether the Ministry considered judicial review in the usual sense and not limited judicial review.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Why was it that illegality and irrationality were deemed, that they ought not to play a part in this Bill.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: We are talking of a different sort of threat.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: But we are only asking the Court to just look at the lawfulness of a decision.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Nobody is asking the Court to substitute the Minister's decision.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: And this, I believe is an important matter because we cannot use the experience of having legislation with ouster clauses to justify new legislation with ouster clauses.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: So, I think each legislation must be unpacked to why judicial review has to be limited.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They could be from a variety of different intelligence sources.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As I said, I am not saying we have the human assets but a variety of different types of assets.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: While the actions we take are nowhere near as serious as the Internal Security Act, nevertheless, in some ways, the Internal Security Act is often focused on the people within and we will be able to have our own evidence that would be able to be used.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Here, we would have to depend on other types of evidence, other sources, whether our sources or partner sources, and there is a great deal of requirement for secrecy and confidentiality and this should not go to the Court process at all.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But we all agree there needs to be a robust process for making sure that the process we set up can properly look at what the Minister has done.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, the direct answer to the question is we assess that that the kind of information we will be looking at and assessing on deciding would be much, much, much more confidential and secret.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And really, in ordinary circumstances, it would be known to no more than one or two persons.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And we have to rely on that kind of information, sometimes for this.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But if there are suggestions on how we can make it more robust, because we want it to be robust.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That is why we have a High Court Judge sitting there.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As I said, even though it is not in the Bill, I have asked the Chief Justice for names.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And if there are other suggestions to make it robust without affecting the secrecy and confidentiality, we will be very happy to consider.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: And I thank the Minister for his extensive discussion about our questions.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: I have three clarification questions for the Minister.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: And if I appreciate the point that he raised, that we should not outsource our national security to a private company.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: But by the same token, I am sure he will appreciate that the tools available to large and sophisticated Internet companies such as Facebook might indeed throw additional light on an issue.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: So, for me, the question is, does this apparent disagreement not already raise caution about how the Competent Authority's suspicions may not always be correct?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Or does the Minister believe that MHA will always retain its own Counsel on what he believes to be true.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: My second clarification has to do with the standards of suspicion embedded in the Bill.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: I ask this because for starters, this was not codified specifically in this form in the Bill.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: And that is part of the reason why, for me at least, this hurdle remains a little too low for establishing offence.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: And my last question has to do with whether the Minister continues to believe that there is a misunderstanding of the law by those who have raised reservations.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: I mention this because the reservations brought by scores of academics, activists, other lawyers who have all scrutinised the Bill and thought that the language was vague.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: So, for me, it seems like either the language is indeed vague as claimed and hence subject to misunderstanding.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Or it is not vague, in which case, then these individuals should not be accused of misunderstanding.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: On the first point, do we believe that there was a foreign state involved response.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So I think Assoc Prof Lim's real point is, "Facebook says, there is no such thing.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Doesn't that throw into question your credibility of assessment?" Let me try and give Mr Lim some examples, or at least one example.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: At many stages, Facebook has denied something only to come back and reverse itself.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I am not saying, therefore, they do not really mean what they say when they have not seen any state attack.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I also pointed out that Facebook is not the only medium.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There are a variety of other medium, other than Facebook.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And I do not know if they have considered a complete survey.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Minister for Communications in Sri Lanka called up Facebook to say, can you do something about this?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This is a riot being organised on Facebook in order to kill other people.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Their definition of what is or is not a foreign hostile activity, may well be different from ours.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, if I organise a pogrom to go and kill people, that apparently does not breach Facebook's community standards.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Does Assoc Prof Lim think that a responsible state authority should outsource the way it handles law and order to Facebook, whose primary concern is, how much money it can make with the best thrill in the world?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: When someone took Nancy Pelosi's speech and re-did it to make it look as if she was drunk and slurring, Facebook also felt that in the interests of free speech, that does not breach their community standards.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I do not know what their definitions are.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I do not know what are the different types of medium they considered.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, I cannot comment exhaustively, nor can I take it at face value that if they say, so it must be so.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And I am not going to all the details.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As I said, we are a price taker, we do not name countries, we cannot afford to.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Another question by Assoc Prof Jamus Lim is, do I believe there is a misunderstanding by all those who have raised issues?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think in any debate, again, after long years of experience in Parliament, my view is on any debate, it broadly breaks out into some who are honest and they understand; a large group who do not follow very carefully and may have views which are not accurate.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: How many people look at even the detailed newspaper reports?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And viewpoints tend to be impressionistic; and often impressionistic viewpoints tend to be inaccurate.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But for good reasons – people have busy lives and they have a limited bandwidth.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I do not know about Assoc Prof Lim, but if I was not doing this job and I was a lawyer in private practice, I would also have very limited time to understand what is going on in Parliament, which Bills are coming up.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I will probably have, perhaps, a little bit more than the average layperson's understanding.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But all our viewpoints tend to be impressionistic on areas that we are not directly dealing with because we all have busy lives.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And then, there will be a small group which will go out to deliberately misinform and confuse the population.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There will always be that group and I have indicated that some of that has been happening too.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Quite apart from that, on language, let me try and explain to Assoc Prof Lim one more time.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is going to be 10 o'clock but I will try again.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I said in my Opening Speech, I think I said out of 10,000 people, you are trying to catch that one case.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Even in that one case, the foreign agency will try and make it look like it is a normal case.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, the facade will be normal, everything will look normal.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In fact, if they are worth anything, they will make it look very normal.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, you have to have definitions; just because it looks normal does not mean that you do not have the powers.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: How do you go behind that, how do you deal with it.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, that is why you say it is to foreigners' involvement affecting public interest.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The way in which it is done, I have explained the framework.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If the idea is hostile information campaign, foreign state agency, payments, covert activities, I think it is quite clear.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
