text: But there are also situations where it is not so clear, and that is where you build in the proportionality test.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And it seems to me quite a few of the commentators do not understand the proportionality test.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That is why I made it a point to say AGC advised me; that test is there.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: When you do not understand the proportionality test, then you say, "Oh dear, it says 'collaboration', so, any collaboration with a foreigner on a matter that is of importance to Singaporeans could potentially run afoul", because you misunderstand the proportionality test.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Again, there are people who fall into those who deliberately push this line but there are also a large number, genuine people, honest people, who are genuinely concerned.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I would not say a large number of people are concerned with this Bill.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In fact, our assessment is that, by and large, a large number of people understand, a vast majority of Singaporeans understand the need for FICA.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, of the very small group who are concerned, a significant number you can put down as honest people who, either for impressionistic reasons or other reasons, may have had some misunderstanding and like the two Nominated Members of Parliament who spoke up, say, is there a possibility of abuse.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And that lies behind some of the points that have been made outside.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Yes, if you apply the law as you say it should be, and if you apply the proportionality test correctly, yes, then it will be done properly.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And my answer to that, I gave an extended analysis this morning about how abuse can take place under any legislation.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, our task is to continue to explain to people how this law works and, over time, just as with the many other pieces of legislation, if the Government operates it properly and honestly, it will be understood.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If it operates it wrongly, the people will express their views in a variety of ways.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think Mr Perera said, "Trust in institutions should be built up".

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think listening to Mr Perera over the years, his ideal state, if you take the UK or the US, they have all the things that he says we should have – Freedom of Information Act, they have all these other bodies, many things go to the courts, they do not have an Internal Security Act.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Can anyone tell me why the trust in their Congress in the US, I think, is now down to, perhaps, a single digit or maybe low double digits?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Why is the trust in the Government in Singapore so much higher?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Trust depends on how you exercise your power and your track record.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Trust depends on whether people's lives have really improved and whether you work to improve people's lives.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Trust depends on whether you have the courage of your convictions, in the face of some opposition, to say this is the right way, this is the way I will explain and I will do it for the benefit of people.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Trust does not depend on putting in a series of legislation, just copying others whose trust levels are abysmally low.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Assoc Prof Lim asked me about the phraseology "the authorisation by Minister for anticipatory direction".

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think the phrase used is "suspects or has reason to believe".

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: One, basically, the question revolves around what the Leader of Opposition has also been asking.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: I do not think the Minister has given enough convincing arguments about what is the hurry, why FICA is needed and why the judicial review is not needed.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: First of all, my first question, what is the hurry.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: The Minister has been saying for hours that three years of consultation has been done, they have done a lot of things and all that.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: But what we have heard here is that those things are about identifying what need to be done and what are the threats, what are the foreign interference threats and all that.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: But just now he mentioned something that, oh, he also consulted some Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: But at the end of the day, I think we can all agree that there is little consultation of the general public.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: And what the Minister was trying to say just now is that it seems to be – I mean that is how I interpret it – let us have the law first and then Singaporeans will understand the law, that the law is good for them and all that.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: We already have them, they are all there.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Can the Minister point out a few examples, do not quote all the foreign countries example, quote Asian countries example, examples of Asian countries that have suffered from foreign interference.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Because as an ordinary citizen watching the TV and all that, all the foreign interferences in Taiwan and Australia, for example, seem to be a joke.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: It was just a theatre of actions and all that but in the end, all the foreign interference seems to be unravelled.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, I ask the Minister to quote us some examples and educate us.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: The third question is, we spend a lot of time talking about judicial review.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: What the Minister seems to be saying is "Trust me, trust me".

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: I ask two questions with regard to that.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Well, Sir, I will answer to the extent that I understand the questions.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: On the first point, what is the hurry?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I assume now, Mr Leong, we are talking about the same legislation because the legislation you talked about just now seemed to be a very different one.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Do you understand that almost everything you said earlier about this Bill is actually untrue and inaccurate?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Okay, what I have said is according to the legal advice that my Party had gotten from senior lawyers.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, you say those are not accurate, they are not right.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Then, that is exactly what we have been saying or I have been saying in this Parliament.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: The discussion and the debate in this Parliament actually should not be conducted in a way that is just interpretation by you.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Let us have a Committee, let the experts trash it out and then bring it to this main Chamber.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: We might as well call this legislative Chamber, legal Chamber.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: The legal experts who are advising me disagree with you.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: If I can request both Members to direct your comments through me.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Detention without trial, trial in absence and no judicial review for such detention.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Since his senior lawyers have advised it, he should be able to tell me which clause.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: I am not going to go into all these legal interpretation.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: If we want to argue, we argue out of this.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: But most of the things that I have said is in section 99, and I did not say detention without trial.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: I say he can arrest you, of course, through due process, but after he arrests you, you are not bailable and all that, those are provided in section 99.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: But, anyway, I am not going down that line.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Minister, let us go on with the other questions.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That phrase is there, I am sure it is captured in the Hansard.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Detention without trial, trial in absentia and no judicial review.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, I just order and the person is arrested and detained, and he has got no rights of review.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He reads English, I read English, I can tell him that neither clause 99 nor any other clause in the Bill has detention without trial.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Not just that, he says "There he goes again".

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: When Mr Leong refers to provisions in FICA, I asked him which provisions.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: When Mr Leong says you can detain without trial, he says it, I asked him which clauses.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, we will take it that his position is that clause 99 allows the Minister to detain without trial.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I can assure the House, he is reading something which I do not know anything about.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Mr Leong, would you like to respond to that?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I did not say there was little consultation with Singaporeans nor did I say let us have the law first and then, go and explain to Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think I said a number of things in context and I would ask Mr Leong not to misquote me.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I did not say it in those terms nor did I mean it in those terms.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The second the question is, is FICA effective in protecting us, given all the other resources that the Government has at its disposal?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And Mr Leong says give us examples of Asian countries which have suffered such an attack.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But is the suggestion that somehow because we are Asian, Asian countries will not be affected by foreign interference?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I will suggest Mr Leong reads the French report and that he reads the Select Committee report.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And I can tell him in the annexes we gave out this afternoon, while the names are not there, some of those countries are Asian.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is absolutely shocking to hear that the suggestion of foreign interference in Taiwan and Australia are jokes.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think, in the case of Taiwan, of course, it is a territory, or it is said to be a territory; in the case of Australia, it is a country.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Those places will be very surprised that someone in Singapore thinks the attacks on them, for which Australia has passed legislation, very draconian legislation on reporting requirements.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I said this afternoon, you are an ex-parliamentarian, your obligations are very onerous.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think no one who knows the facts will say what Mr Leong has said, that it is a joke that these places have suffered foreign interference.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Whether they have suffered it from the countries they have named, we do not express a view because it is not our business to go and say they were attacked by X or Y or Z.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But all the evidence that was laid out this afternoon – I talked about an Australian parliamentarian who was said to have been suborned by foreign money and making a statement on South China Sea that is contrary to his own party's position – what do you call that?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: When we say that Singapore itself has been subject to foreign interference recently, are you saying that what we are saying is untrue?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There are reports that the Indian electric infrastructure was brought down as a result of an attack from outside of India.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There are reports of foreign inspired attacks in a number of Asian countries, which I think you can see both in the Select Committee report and if you read the newspapers.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The third point he makes is, well, the Judge is appointed by the Minister and basically the approach is, trust me.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Leong asks why is it possible that other countries can have judicial review and we cannot.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is a question of what those countries can do and if you look at New Zealand, they have not had to face very severe threats.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: For the first time now, they are facing different types of threats.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In the absence of an Internal Security Act, they have to allow this man to be free for years outside and one day, he goes into a supermarket and knifes people.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I said there were 22 incidents, including the Charlie Hebdo incident.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: One is that the appointment of the tribunal is recommended by the Cabinet, right, to the President?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: In that case, does the President have the power to reject the appointment?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Second question is, just now I asked for some examples of Asian countries that are affected by foreign interference.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: I am looking for examples where there are more permanent damage, like really affected a national election and things like that.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: But what the Minister has pointed is this one senator being found with connections with a country.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Those things in the normal course of our security operation, we can identify already.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Similarly, our healthcare system data was compromised some years ago.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Is FICA needed before we can prevent all these things?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Or even with FICA, are we going to be able to prevent these kind of events?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think Mr Leong has got to, I would suggest he goes and listen again or reads and the answers are all there.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I suggest he read some material that has been given.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Nor did you answer his questions when he asked you earlier.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: You can sit down now, I will call you again later.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: I know the hour is late, I will try and keep it short.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: The first two are actually related to my speech and I do not think the Minister answered them, that is, unless I missed them.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: The first one is the subject of a Part 3 Direction or POL declaration can apply within a 30-day timeframe to the Minister for an appeal for reconsideration.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: But does the Minister have a timeframe within which he must respond on that; so, would the Minister commit to that?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: The second question is relating to clause 93, those who are designated as PSPs or PSEs issued directives on the Parts 5 and 6 may only appeal against that decision to the Minister.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: They have no right to appeal to the Tribunal, I believe, unlike those who are issued Part 3 Directions.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: The third question is in relation to what the Minister mentioned about my speech and speeches that I have made over the years.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: He talked about the trust deficit in countries like the UK and the US which have things like ombudsman and Freedom of Information Act, and so on and so forth.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: And would he not agree that maybe if we took some of the kind of laws that we have in Singapore and applied it to those countries, it may not necessarily increase trust in those countries?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: And would he not agree that perhaps in Singapore, if we put in place laws a little bit more balanced, along the lines that we have argued today in Parliament, that might possibly increase the trust levels that we have here, even though those trust levels, you think are high.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: So, that is sort of the third question.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: The fourth question and the last one, is on the part of my speech where I talked about who checks the checkers.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Essentially, I asked what recourse does a concerned citizen have in Singapore if they feel that very senior officials – Prime Minister, Minister of Home Affairs himself – has been suborned by a foreign power?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: What is their channel to redress that, to have that addressed?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: On the trust levels, I think finally we are beginning to get to some sort of narrowing of the gap.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, let us agree, you have all these institutions, Freedom of Information and the kind of media that they have and the ombudsman, does not automatically mean trust levels go up.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And I think there is a kernel of accuracy in what Mr Perera said.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And the kernel that I extract is this: each country has got to look at its own situation and decide what works for it.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: A country like China with 5,000 years and a single race – different considerations.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: A country like the US – different considerations.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: A country like Singapore with 700 square kilometres – different consideration.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think if we can agree on that and that therefore, we need to factor in what works for us, then the next question is, why have trust levels been so high in Singapore?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There is a trust based on how leaders behave.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There is a trust based on how powers are exercised.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, anytime there is abuse, there is corruption, there is lack of probity, there is a performance deficit, trust will dissipate.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I believe in Singapore, it will dissipate very quickly because we are such a small place, everyone understands everything pretty much in broad terms.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Whether bringing in some of these institutions will add to trust is a conversation we can have as long as it is not a priori argument: if you have it, trust will increase.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
